The curve ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(1,3)$ and $B(5,3).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,i+(x-1)^{2}\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector  ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.

*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free.*"] ["question-d222c5e4-f6d8-59cd-b06f-5764984195b7" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:

- $F$ is a source-free vector field.

- $∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$

- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\in D$ is zero.

- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s.
$$

- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$

First, notice that

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{{y}^{3}})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((x-1)^{2})=0+0=0,
$$

which shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.

Since $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where ${C}_{2}$ is the straight line from $A(1,3)$ to $B(5,3)$ and ${n}_{2}$ is its unit normal, shown in the diagram below.

![](images/3d/3d64ffb0e4cc313a2857d1c20922c1202619d0bdeb3d97f2808b4995c99f7f9f.png)

Notice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.

To calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply the formula,

- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$

Parametrizing ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+3\,j+t\cdot [(5\,i+3\,j)-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(4t+1)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in [0,1].$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-\sqrt{{y}^{3}}=-\sqrt{(3)^{3}}=-\sqrt{27}, \\ Q(x,y) & =(x-1)^{2}=((4t+1)-1)^{2}=16{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)=4, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the flux integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-\sqrt{27})\cdot (0)-(16{t}^{2})\cdot (4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-64{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{64{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s=-\frac{64}{3}.
$$"] ["question-d222c5e4-f6d8-59cd-b06f-5764984195b7" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-441e4f24-d3a1-5f34-b559-dd35657f1f13" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-7e8f43e3-d7f0-593f-9f61-7957ca2c311e" :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables with the joint probability density function 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}, & -1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x<-1,\,y>2.$"] ["question-7e8f43e3-d7f0-593f-9f61-7957ca2c311e" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables with the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.
$$

Let's draw the region $D$ in the $uv$-plane where the function $f(u,v)$ is nonzero. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x<-1,\,y>2,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/04/04eee4bcf3263318946503732ed7715913e12949659cacb84e93d1696ee7f2e1.png)

For the purposes of computation, we're only interested in the region inside $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. This is given by

$$
D\cap Δ=∅.
$$

 

So there is nowhere in our region $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v & ={∬}_{Δ}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v=0.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7e8f43e3-d7f0-593f-9f61-7957ca2c311e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-29f3fcfe-72a9-5dde-8a8a-0d962e42b063" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Let $X$ and $Y$ be continuous random variables with the joint probability density function 

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{7}{y}^{2}, & 2\le x\le 3,\,1\le y\le 2, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $x<1,\,-4<y<1.$"] ["question-ca240843-51e6-5695-9d1f-64a8db44b027" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables with the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.
$$

Let's draw the region $D$ in the $uv$-plane where the function $f(u,v)$ is nonzero. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $x<1,\,-4<y<1,$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/0c/0c027a6d656653ee1158bdff681405afe99748d734555f515de563099146849e.png)

For the purposes of computation, we're only interested in the region inside $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. This is given by

$$
D\cap Δ=∅.
$$

 

So there is nowhere in our region $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v & ={∬}_{Δ}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v=0.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ca240843-51e6-5695-9d1f-64a8db44b027" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-b648352b-9cfb-5d5c-8ea0-b1cb8e46e03c" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$

Find the expression for the corresponding joint CDF when $1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$"] ["question-64924153-c273-5495-a9b7-e1268d0994d0" :question/worked-solution "If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables with the joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the corresponding joint CDF is given by

$$
F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v.
$$

Let's draw the region $D$ in the $uv$-plane where the function $f(u,v)$ is nonzero. Let's also consider a point $(x,y)$ where $1\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{2},$ and a region $Δ$ that lies below and to the left of this point.

![](images/00/00e0dcbd7ea22f09db76b03fc4d7bda328f1b1f17ceeb998cf039241dafd8da3.png)

For the purposes of computation, we're only interested in the region inside $Δ$ where $f(x,y)$ is nonzero. This is given by

$$
D\cap Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le x,\,0\le v\le y\}.
$$

 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(u,v)\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v & ={\int }_{0}^{y}{\int }_{1}^{x}\frac{1}{4}u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡v{\int }_{1}^{x}u\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡v{[\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}]}_{u=1}^{u=x}\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{cos}⁡v({x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1){\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)[\operatorname{sin}⁡v]_{v=0}^{v=y} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-64924153-c273-5495-a9b7-e1268d0994d0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2184ddd6-bb84-56f9-ac10-b6a376a8e0a3" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Let the joint CDF of $X$ and $Y$ be $F(x,y),$ where

$$
F(8,6)=0.8,\,F(8,2)=0.5,\,F(2,6)=0.4,\,F(2,2)=0.2.
$$

Find $P(2\le X\le 8,2\le Y\le 6).$"] ["question-392c7844-059b-541a-9161-f7e9d9b52570" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $F(x,y)=P(X\le x,Y\le y)$ is the probability that the pair $(X,Y)$ will lie inside the infinite rectangular region that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes.

Let's sketch the region corresponding to the probability we wish to find.

![](images/15/1524afeeaea3cc0fd4ee51b9572222bdd846fba378e029e4fa20a272a4fe6353.png)

Geometrically, this region can be obtained as follows:

1\. Take the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(8,6).$

2\. Subtract the infinite rectangles that have their top-right corners at $(8,2)$ and $(2,6).$

3\. Finally, we need to *add back* the infinite rectangle that has its top-right corner at $(2,2).$ This is because we subtracted this region twice in step 2.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2\le X\le 8,2\le Y\le 6) & =\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(8,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 8,Y\le 6)}} \\  & \,-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(8,2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 8,Y\le 2)}}-\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,6)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 6)}} \\  & \,+\overset{\text{top-right corner at }(2,2)}{\overset{⏞}{P(X\le 2,Y\le 2)}} \\  & =F(8,6)-F(8,2)-F(2,6)+F(2,2) \\  & =0.8-0.5-0.4+0.2 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-392c7844-059b-541a-9161-f7e9d9b52570" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d3273a24-dde6-50e8-9d77-b0d57e06622e" :answer-field/id #uuid <td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>"] ["question-23c462cc-da9f-5356-aacb-68452f1af0c8" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2 \\ -8 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-2t)={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}(-2t){\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-2t{e}^{-2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}(1+2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(2t) \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & =-8{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(-8t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}1-4t & 2t \\ -8t & 1+4t\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-23c462cc-da9f-5356-aacb-68452f1af0c8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-03ccd2db-1552-543e-9102-8cfc8d2f158f" :answer-field/id #uuid "step-0de063b2-395e-543a-987f-5a9f09cd0abc"] ["question-30b095cd-424c-553d-bb7d-82a5c5e826eb" :question/id #uuid "30b095cd-424c-553d-bb7d-82a5c5e826eb"] ["question-30b095cd-424c-553d-bb7d-82a5c5e826eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-127225"] ["question-30b095cd-424c-553d-bb7d-82a5c5e826eb" :question/problem "According to the flux form of Green's theorem, the flux of the vector field 
$F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{3}+{y}^{2},\,{x}^{2}y⟩$
across the triangle $C$ with vertices $(1,0),(0,2),$ and $(-1,2)$ can be represented as

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise, $n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C,$ and $D$ is the region bounded by $C.$ Calculate the function $f(x,y).$"] ["question-30b095cd-424c-553d-bb7d-82a5c5e826eb" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/84/848dfedddea9803dcf39b4624f2966b63f080920ed19b875dc691e8fe9d3b038.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}+{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}y.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the flux form of Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

["question-d5c8c9fb-a926-5fe7-b24d-28d3915fc2cf" :question/math-academy-id "q-127230"] ["question-d5c8c9fb-a926-5fe7-b24d-28d3915fc2cf" :question/problem "Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(-1,-2),(3,-2),$ and $(3,0),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}\,i-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral."] ["question-d5c8c9fb-a926-5fe7-b24d-28d3915fc2cf" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/e1/e1e4386f3cc75afb63823d74daa27b517e8e47d51fa08c5c9e5bf3ca6f3ca88c.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{6}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{6},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 3,\,-2\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{6}-3{y}^{2}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-2}^{0}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}({y}^{4}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d5c8c9fb-a926-5fe7-b24d-28d3915fc2cf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-8bc52748-240b-5997-9e36-b5b9d7c36232" :answer-field/id #uuid Given that $M$ is the midpoint of $\overset{―}{LN}$ with $LM=7-x$ and $LN=11-x$, what is the value of $LN?$"] ["question-99403fe1-1721-56c5-b69a-61a8a55f3486" :question/worked-solution "We have the following diagram.

![](images/7c/7c89598fe6a0450eddfe8af4ed274d4110fd7cb2de796bb5a749798b44c7e94a.png)

  

Since $M$ is the midpoint of $\overset{―}{LN}$, the segment $\overset{―}{LN}$ is twice the length of the segment $\overset{―}{LM}.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}2LM & =LN \\ 2(7-x) & =11-x \\ 14-2x & =11-x \\ 14-2x+2x & =11-x+2x \\ 14 & =11+x \\ 14-11 & =11+x-11 \\ 3 & =x \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  by plugging this value into the expression for $LN$, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}LN & =11-x \\  & =11-3 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-99403fe1-1721-56c5-b69a-61a8a55f3486" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-edc3d773-9201-5181-846a-f801f1bee199" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
ax=bx
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a=b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax=bx.$ In this case, 

$$
a=7m,\,b=-14.
$$

Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
7m=-14.
$$

Solving this for $m,$ we get

$$
m=-2.
$$"] ["question-021c858c-ff29-5406-946e-12cf5966af05" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-5b7c28ee-4474-52da-a1df-71e406689457" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-4a0694b1-4a4b-5ce3-895a-155c5691ef32" :question/math-academy-id "q-69041"] ["question-4a0694b1-4a4b-5ce3-895a-155c5691ef32" :question/problem "Eleanor made a call to her parents, which lasted for $\frac{1}{4}$ of an hour. For this call, she paid $\frac{1}{2}$ of a dollar. How many dollars would she pay for a $5$ hour call?"] ["question-4a0694b1-4a4b-5ce3-895a-155c5691ef32" :question/worked-solution "To find the number of dollars that Eleanor would pay for a $5$ hour call, we can first find the unit rate of dollars per hour, and then multiply the unit rate by $5$ hours.

To find the unit rate of dollars per hour, we divide the number of dollars, $\frac{1}{2},$ by the number of hours, $\frac{1}{4},$ as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2}÷\frac{1}{4}
$$

Dividing one fraction by another is equivalent to multiplying the fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}÷\frac{1}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}\times \frac{4}{1} \\  & =\frac{1\times 4}{2\times 1} \\  & =\frac{4}{2} \\  & =4÷2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the unit rate is $2$ dollars per hour. To find the number of dollars that Eleanor would pay for a $5$ hour call, we multiply the unit rate by $5$ hours and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2\times 5 & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, Eleanor would pay $10$ dollars for a $5$ hour call."] ["question-4a0694b1-4a4b-5ce3-895a-155c5691ef32" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-d8eb4941-b3e2-55e9-b6fe-f87579a51eed" :question/math-academy-id "q-152026"] ["question-d8eb4941-b3e2-55e9-b6fe-f87579a51eed" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true? 

I. The sum of ${x}^{2}+x+1$ and ${x}^{2}-2x-1$ is a trinomial.

II. The sum of ${x}^{2}+3x+1$ and $3{x}^{2}-x-5$ is a trinomial.

III. The sum of two trinomials is not necessarily a trinomial."] ["question-d8eb4941-b3e2-55e9-b6fe-f87579a51eed" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
({x}^{2}+x+1)+({x}^{2}-2x-1)=2{x}^{2}-x,
$$

which is *not* a trinomial (it's a binomial).

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
({x}^{2}+3x+1)+(3{x}^{2}-x-5)=4{x}^{2}+2x-4,
$$

which is a trinomial.

- Statement III is true. The sum of two trinomials *could be* a trinomial (see, for example, statement II). 

 However, the sum of two trinomials is *not always* a trinomial (see, for example, statement I). 

 So, the sum of two trinomials is not necessarily a trinomial.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""] ["question-d8eb4941-b3e2-55e9-b6fe-f87579a51eed" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] "question-09d0b1bd-784f-5b5f-a562-190332d09cbb"] [17592186060293 :question/worked-solution "Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](images/75/75e75d1190cda98916cc6071cb2c0c2d25985fabafeda774cfafa5d3e60a7cb8.png)

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $3,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
x=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{3\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{3}=\sqrt{3}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $\sqrt{3}.$"] [17592186060293 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186058380 :answer-field/correct 17592186058383] ["question-97290040-c817-56ab-b0de-389c63e1806d" :question/id #uuid "97290040-c817-56ab-b0de-389c63e1806d"] ["question-97290040-c817-56ab-b0de-389c63e1806d" :question/math-academy-id "q-99763"] ["question-97290040-c817-56ab-b0de-389c63e1806d" :question/problem "$\frac{11}{(\frac{3}{4})}=$"] ["question-97290040-c817-56ab-b0de-389c63e1806d" :question/worked-solution "First, remember that a fraction represents a division:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{11}{(\frac{3}{4})}=11÷\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $11=\frac{11}{1}$ and dividing by $\frac{3}{4}$ is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal $\frac{4}{3}.$ We can use these facts to simplify the fraction above: 

$$
\begin{aligned}11÷\frac{3}{4} & = \\ \frac{11}{1}\times \frac{4}{3} & = \\ \frac{11\times 4}{1\times 3} & = \\ \frac{44}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{11}{(\frac{3}{4})}=\frac{44}{3}.
$$"] ["question-97290040-c817-56ab-b0de-389c63e1806d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-202889fe-fbdf-5866-9db5-d7e0eb76934f" :answer-field/id #uuid Find the equation of the line that passes through the points $(2,1)$ and $(5,7).$"] ["question-abb200c5-68bb-537e-9baa-018c760a0ae2" :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$

First, we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{7-1}{5-2} \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the slope $m=2$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach

$$
y=2x+b.
$$

We now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x+b \\ 1 & =2(2)+b \\ 1 & =4+b \\ 1-4 & =b \\ -3 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the line is $y=2x-3.$"] ["question-abb200c5-68bb-537e-9baa-018c760a0ae2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] :question/problem "Solve the equation $\frac{12}{7}=-\frac{4}{3n}.$"] ["question-b1ef5b0e-d9e2-581a-b9df-9ba5373d94d3" :question/worked-solution "First, note that $n=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

To solve the equation, we move the negative sign onto the numerator of the fraction and then apply cross-multiplication:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{7} & =-\frac{4}{3n} \\ \frac{12}{7} & =\frac{-4}{3n} \\ 12\cdot 3n & =7\cdot (-4) \\ 36n & =-28\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}36n & =-28 \\ n & =-\frac{28}{36} \\ n & =-\frac{28÷4}{36÷4} \\ n & =-\frac{7}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Since  $n=-\frac{7}{9}$ is different from $n=0,$ we can accept it as a solution. Therefore, the solution is $n=-\frac{7}{9}.$"] ["question-b1ef5b0e-d9e2-581a-b9df-9ba5373d94d3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4471834c-aadc-52a5-8221-0fc8082126bf" $△ABC$ is $9.$ What is the perimeter of the isosceles triangle $△ABD$ with base $\overset{―}{AB}$ if $AD=5?$"] ["question-9e670b5a-5fbf-5bcb-b259-10c91c8115bb" :question/worked-solution "Let's illustrate the triangles.

![](images/2e/2e18009a3a454e83e42f9f21840c6821605ac2eb8f4e3d493c8468a5fe5f5acc.png)

 

We're told that the perimeter of the equilateral triangle $△ABC$ is ${p}_{1}=9,$ and since all $3$ sides have equal length, we get

$$
AB=\frac{{p}_{1}}{3}=\frac{9}{3}=3.
$$

Since  $△ABD$  is an isosceles triangle with base $\overset{―}{AB},$ we have $AD=BD=5.$ 

Now, we have enough information to compute the perimeter of the triangle $△ABD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BD+AD \\  & =3+5+5 \\  & =13\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-9e670b5a-5fbf-5bcb-b259-10c91c8115bb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e0dcc2e6-1bc5-592f-996a-6b8e9f9cebf3" :answer-field/id #uuid in interval notation as"] ["question-974c4026-e9d5-5cd6-80d1-e15772e57911" :question/worked-solution "Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "or equal to" symbols. So, the endpoints $1$ and $5$ *are* included. 

$$
1\,\,\le \,\,x\,\,\le \,\,5
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
[1,5]
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in [1,5].
$$"] ["question-974c4026-e9d5-5cd6-80d1-e15772e57911" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-37038cfb-4364-58c7-8027-27793c04b330" :answer-field/id #uuid \end{aligned}

Find the function $g(t).$"] [17592186317324 :question/worked-solution "To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$

Comparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $y(t)=-2{e}^{-3t}+u(t-3)\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as

$$
g(t)=\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3(t-3)}+\frac{3t-10}{9}.
$$"] [17592186230233 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Laplace transforms to handle **time-delayed forcing**, where the forcing function turns on at some time $t=a>0$.

We represent this “turning on” using the **unit step function** $u_a(t)=u(t-a)$.

To see what this looks like, consider the initial value problem

$$

$$

Here, the forcing is $0$ for $t<2$ and becomes $e^{t-2}$ for $t\ge 2$.

To find the Laplace transform of the forcing term, we note that

$$
u_2(t)\cdot e^{t-2}
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=2$ and $f(t)=e^{t-2}.$

Now, recall that the **second shifting theorem** (time-shifting property) states

$$
\mathcal L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\} = e^{-as} \cdot \mathcal L\{f(t+a)\}.

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-2)\cdot {e}^{t-2}} & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot L{{e}^{(t+2)-2}} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot L{{e}^{t}} \\  & ={e}^{-2s}\cdot \frac{1}{s-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

After this step, we proceed as usual: we take the Laplace transform of the entire differential equation, solve for $Y(s)=\mathcal L\{y(t)\}$, and then (when needed) take $\mathcal L^{-1}$ to recover $y(t)$."] [17592186230231 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to solve the initial value problem

$$

$$

where $u_2(t)=u(t-2)$ is the unit step function.

First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the linearity properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{'}-4y} & =L{{u}_{2}(t)\cdot {e}^{t-2}} \\ L{{y}^{'}}-4L{y} & =L{{u}_{2}(t)\cdot {e}^{t-2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To compute $\mathcal L\{y'\},$ we use the derivative formula and the initial condition $y(0)=0{:}$

$$
\mathcal L\{y'\} = sY(s) - y(0) = sY(s).
$$

To compute the right-hand side, we note that

$$
u_2(t)\cdot e^{t-2}
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=2$ and $f(t)=e^{t-2}.$

Now, recall that the **second shifting theorem** (time-shifting property) states

$$
\mathcal L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}=e^{-as}\cdot \mathcal L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$

$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation and solve for $Y(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}sY(s)-4Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s-1} \\ (s-4)Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s-1} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{(s-1)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Taking the inverse Laplace transform of $Y(s)$ will give us the solution to our initial value problem."] [17592186230240 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' + 3y = u_\pi(t)\cdot \cos(t-\pi)\,, \qquad y(0)=2,
$$

where $u_\pi(t)=u(t-\pi)$ is the unit step function.

Assume we are given that the Laplace transform $Y(s) = \mathcal L\{y(t)\}$ is

$$
Y(s) = \dfrac{2}{s+3} + \dfrac{s\,e^{-\pi s}}{(s^2+1)(s+3)}
$$

and that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as 

$$
y(t) = 2e^{-3t} + \dfrac{1}{10} u(t-\pi)\cdot g(t).
$$

Our goal is to find the function $g(t).$ To do this, we'll need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the second term in $Y(s).$ We can use the following standard results:

$$
\mathcal L\{\sin\omega t\} = \dfrac{\omega}{s^2+\omega^2}, \qquad 
\mathcal L\{\cos\omega t\} = \dfrac{s}{s^2+\omega^2}, \qquad
s > 0.
$$

We focus on the term with the exponential $e^{-\pi s}$ and identify its rational function part:

$$
F(s) = \dfrac{s}{(s^2+1)(s+3)}.
$$

We'll find the inverse transform in three steps.

**Step 1. Partial fraction decomposition**

To handle the rational function $F(s),$ we use *partial fraction decomposition*. Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $(s^2+1),$ the decomposition takes the form

$$
\dfrac{s}{(s^2+1)(s+3)} = \dfrac{A}{s+3} + \dfrac{Bs+C}{s^2+1}.
$$

To find the constants, we clear the denominators:

$$
s = A(s^2+1) + (Bs+C)(s+3).
$$

Now, we find the constants $A, B,$ and $C.$

- Setting $s=-3,$ we have

$$
-3 = A\bigl((-3)^2+1\bigr) + 0 \implies 10A = -3 \implies A = -\dfrac{3}{10}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of $s^2,$ we have

$$
0 = A + B \implies B = -A = \dfrac{3}{10}.
$$

- Comparing the coefficients of $s,$ we have

$$
1 = 3B + C \implies 1 = 3\!\left(\dfrac{3}{10}\right) + C \implies C = \dfrac{1}{10}.
$$

Thus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as

$$
F(s)= -\dfrac{3}{10}\cdot\dfrac{1}{s+3} + \dfrac{3}{10}\cdot\dfrac{s}{s^2+1} + \dfrac{1}{10}\cdot\dfrac{1}{s^2+1}.
$$

**Step 2. Finding the inverse of the base function**

We find the inverse transform $f(t) = \mathcal L^{-1}\{F(s)\}$ using standard transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={L}^{-1}{-\frac{3}{10}\cdot \frac{1}{s+3}+\frac{3}{10}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}+\frac{1}{10}\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} \\  & =-\frac{3}{10}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{3}{10}\operatorname{cos}t+\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}t \\  & =\frac{1}{10}(-3{e}^{-3t}+3\operatorname{cos}t+\operatorname{sin}t).\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3. Applying the time-shifting property**

Finally, we use the *second shifting theorem* to handle the $e^{-\pi s}$ factor. The theorem states:

$$
\mathcal L^{-1} \{ e^{-as}F(s) \} = u(t-a) \cdot f(t-a).
$$

In our case, $a=\pi.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\pi):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-\pi )f(t-\pi ) & =u(t-\pi )\cdot \frac{1}{10}[-3{e}^{-3(t-\pi )}+3\operatorname{cos}(t-\pi )+\operatorname{sin}(t-\pi )] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}u(t-\pi )\cdot [-3{e}^{-3(t-\pi )}+3(-\operatorname{cos}t)+(-\operatorname{sin}t)]\end{aligned}
$$

Using the trigonometric identities $\cos(t-\pi)=-\cos t$ and $\sin(t-\pi)=-\sin t,$ we simplify:

$$
u(t-\pi)f(t-\pi) = \dfrac{1}{10}u(t-\pi)\cdot \left(-3e^{-3(t-\pi)} - 3\cos t - \sin t\right).
$$

**Conclusion: Identifying g(t)**

This result is the inverse transform of the second term in $Y(s).$ The problem statement gives the complete solution in the form

$$
y(t) = 2e^{-3t} + \dfrac{1}{10} u(t-\pi)\cdot g(t).
$$

The first term, $2e^{-3t},$ is the inverse transform of $\dfrac{2}{s+3}.$ By comparing our calculated term with the form above, we can identify **$g(t)$**:

$$
g(t)= -3e^{-3(t-\pi)} - 3\cos t - \sin t.
$$"] [17592186096559 :question/problem "Calculate the volume of a cylinder given that the circumference of the base is $10\pi \,\textrm{m}$ and the ratio of its height to its radius is $\dfrac{4}{5}$."] [17592186096559 :question/worked-solution "First, we find the radius $r$ using the formula $C=2\pi r$, where $C$ is the circumference, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C &= 2πr \\
10π &= 2πr \\
r &= 5m
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the height $h$, we use the fact that the ratio of the height to the radius is

$$
\dfrac{4}{5}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{h}{r} &= \frac{4}{5} \\
\frac{h}{5} &= \frac{4}{5} \\
h &= 4m
\end{aligned}
$$

The volume of a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h$ is given by

$$
V = \pi r^2h
$$

Substituting

$$
r = 5\,\textrm{m}
$$

and

$$
h = 4\,\textrm{m}
$$

into the formula, we get

$$
V = \pi(5)^2(4) = 100\pi\,\textrm{m}^3
$$"] [17592186096558 :question/problem "Calculate the radius $r$ of the cylinder below given that its volume is $200\pi \,\textrm{mm}^3$ and its height is $2\,\textrm{mm}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{r}{h} &= 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Our goal is to express $h$ in terms of $V$. Therefore, we need to isolate $r$ in the above equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}

r &= 4h
\end{aligned}
$$

The volume of a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h$ is given by

$$

Therefore, substituting $r = 4h$ into the formula and solving for $h$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}

V &= π(4h)^{2}h \\
V &= 16πh^{3} \\
h^{3} &= \frac{V}{16π} \\

Suppose we have a square system of linear equations

where ![](images/c7/c7ef883a1d4dd8c1fc0fc8fbde5ed80c9a5229650fc77c77559b71552370c35b.svg) Then Cramer's rule states that

$$

$$

is the unique solution of the system, where
![](images/b1/b13ecd10395fe0977d04d627179667cbca207fcf4015a89d43df0e69765f1f5e.svg)

For example, let's use Cramer's rule to solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x-2y &=-1 \\ -1x+2y &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by finding the **determinant of the coefficient matrix**:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $D_x$ and $D_y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 2-3\cdot (-2) \\  & =4 \\ {D}_{y} & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the solution to the system is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D}=\frac{4}{4}=1, \\ y & =\frac{{D}_{y}}{D}=\frac{8}{4}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

> A scientific calculator is required to answer this question."] [17592186093374 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we’ll learn how **Newton’s method** (also known as the **Newton–Raphson method**) constructs such an approximation step by step. Our focus will be on the single-variable case, where the goal is to find a real number $x$ such that $f(x) = 0$.

To apply Newton’s method, we begin by choosing an initial guess for the root, which we’ll denote by $x_0$. This guess might come from intuition or a rough sketch of the graph.

Below, we see the graph of $f(x)$ along with the initial guess $x_0$.

![](images/e2/e2d794aa00d7b0d84a70344c89872aa48736182ff6dbf334d1201c0451c215b6.png)

The idea is to simplify the problem by replacing the curve with a straight line near our guess.
Recall that the equation of the tangent line $y = F(x)$ to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $x = x_0$ is

$$
F(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0).
$$

Since $F(x)$ closely approximates $f(x)$ near $x_0$, we solve the simpler linear equation $F(x) = 0$ instead of the original nonlinear equation $f(x) = 0$. This gives us a new estimate for the root that is easier to compute.

To find where this tangent intersects the $x$-axis, we set $F(x) = 0{:}$

$$
0 = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0)
$$

Next, we isolate the term $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}({x}_{0})(x-{x}_{0}) & =-f({x}_{0}) \\ x-{x}_{0} & =-\frac{f({x}_{0})}{{f}^{'}({x}_{0})} \\ x & ={x}_{0}-\frac{f({x}_{0})}{{f}^{'}({x}_{0})}\end{aligned}
$$

This new value becomes our next guess, which we call $x_1$. So, we write

$$
x_1 = x_0 - \frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}.
$$

In the figure below, the dashed line is the tangent at $x_0$. We follow it down to the $x$-axis to find our next guess, $x_1$.

![](images/8e/8e19765a4f180f1acc95c6460fb63b95ca9c4af811d13a3035d4e66ba26471a1.png)

To keep improving our estimate, we now repeat the same process, this time starting from $x_1$ instead of $x_0$. Applying the same idea gives the next guess

$$
x_2 = x_1 - \frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)}
$$

as shown below.

![](images/e7/e789ff357b039591d7bb00d05e48456f3e11ea172b9f04723a670101c1a1c15a.png)

Continuing this process, we generate a sequence of values 

$$
x_0, \quad
x_1, \quad
x_2, \quad
x_3, 
\dots
$$

 
that, under suitable conditions, converges to a root of $f(x)$.
At each step, the next approximation is computed using the update rule

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
$$

In practice, we stop iterating when the change between consecutive guesses is very small, meaning we’re close enough to the actual root for our purposes."] [17592186092418 :activity/title "The Newton-Raphson Method"] [17592186069008 :question/problem "What is the quotient of $3x^{3} - 2x^{2} - x - 1$ divided by $x^{2} + x + 1$?"] [17592186065481 :answer-field/choices 17592186065482] [17592186065481 :answer-field/choices 17592186065483] [17592186065481 :answer-field/choices 17592186065484] [17592186065481 :answer-field/choices 17592186065485] [17592186065481 :answer-field/choices 17592186065486] [17592186069010 :question/problem "What is the remainder when $-12x^{4} + 28x^{3} - 47x^{2} + 25x - 9$ is divided by $6x^{2} - 5x + 4$?"] [17592186065493 :answer-field/choices 17592186065494] [17592186065493 :answer-field/choices 17592186065495] [17592186065493 :answer-field/choices 17592186065496] [17592186065493 :answer-field/choices 17592186065497] [17592186065493 :answer-field/choices 17592186065498] [17592186069009 :question/problem "What is the remainder when $-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1$ is divided by $2x^{2} - x + 5$?"] [17592186065487 :answer-field/choices 17592186065489] [17592186065487 :answer-field/choices 17592186065490] [17592186065487 :answer-field/choices 17592186065492] [17592186221995 :question/problem "$A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}, e^{At} = \begin{bmatrix}e^{2t} & te^{2t} \\ 0 & e^{2t}\end{bmatrix}$

31207} {:db/id 17592186167702 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168092 :tutorial/content "The derivatives of the inverse reciprocal hyperbolic functions are shown below:\n$\\newcommand{\\arsinh}{\\mathop{\\rm arsinh}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\arcosh}{\\mathop{\\rm arcosh}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\artanh}{\\mathop{\\rm artanh}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\sech}{\\mathop{\\rm sech}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\csch}{\\mathop{\\rm csch}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\coth}{\\mathop{\\rm coth}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\arsech}{\\mathop{\\rm arsech}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\arcsch}{\\mathop{\\rm arcsch}\\nolimits}\n\\newcommand{\\arcoth}{\\mathop{\\rm arcoth}\\nolimits}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\operatorname{arcsch}⁡x) & =-\\frac{1}{|x|\\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\\in (-\\infty ,0)\\cup (0,\\infty ) \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\operatorname{arsech}⁡x) & =-\\frac{1}{x\\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}, &  & x\\in (0,1) \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}x}(\\operatorname{arcoth}⁡x) & =\\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}, &  & have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A-20I & =[\\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\\\ -10 & 10\\end{aligned}]-20[\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}-10 & -10 \\\\ -10 & -10\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\\,A-20I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector\n\n$$\n{v}_{1}=[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\n- For ${\\lambda }_{2}={\\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A-0I & =[\\begin{aligned}10 & -10 \\\\ -10 & A\\mathbf{v}_i,\n$$\n\n \n\nwhere $\\mathbf u_i$ and $\\mathbf v_i$ are the $i$th columns of the orthogonal matrices $U$ and $V,$ respectively.  \n\nThe formula above works whenever $\\sigma_i\\neq 0.$ But how do we find the $i$th column of $U$ in cases where $\\sigma_i = 0?$ It turns out that we can find the corresponding left singular vector using the geometric properties of singular values.\n\nFor example, suppose that\n\n![](images/fa/fab8a223fc22100592865eeb8b147313f4a635ffa3791863826ca6330730cc58.svg)\n\nand $A=U \\Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ where\n![](images/58/58af793e95fd96171530b2b63e74d12e965fb02eb81af42c8fdb3c9289a04b11.svg)\nThe matrices $\\Sigma$ and $V$ can be found using the methods we've seen before. So, our task now is to find the matrix $U.$ \n\nFrom $\\Sigma,$ we deduce that the singular values of $A$ are $\\sigma_1=4$ and $\\sigma_2=0.$ Therefore, the first column of $U$ is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{4}[\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{3} & 1 \\\\ 3 & \\sqrt{3}\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{2} \\\\ \\frac{1}{2}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{2} \\\\ \\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nSince the second singular value is $\\sigma_2=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ However, we know that $U$ is an orthogonal matrix. Hence, we must find a vector\n\n![](images/78/781532700996b7a60101f204b934483da264ecab6acd6bfeda97141669308b6c.svg)\n\nsuch that \n\n$$\n\\mathbf{u}_1 \\cdot \\mathbf{u}_2 = 0 \\qquad \\textrm{and} \\qquad \\|\\mathbf{u}_2\\|=1.\n$$\n\n \n\nLet's consider each condition in turn:\n\n- The equation $\\mathbf{u}_1 \\cdot \\mathbf{u}_2 = 0$  is equivalent to\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{{2}} x_1 + :step/next {:db/id 17592186167657}} {:db/id 17592186167657 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168073 :tutorial/content "It follows from the definitions that a $2\\times 2$ matrix $A$ has two repeated singular values $\\sigma_1= \\sigma_2= \\sigma$ if and only if the matrix  $A^TA$ has two repeated eigenvalues $\\lambda_1=\\lambda_2 = \\sigma^2.$  Thus, since $A^TA$ is diagonalizable (because it is symmetric), the eigenspace corresponding to $\\sigma^2$ must be two-dimensional. Therefore, \n\n![](images/df/df266614e2576526353248439b7a17431d5e9e43153e1ba225adab3a89321373.svg)\n\nConsequently, we can use any pair of unit orthogonal vectors as a basis for the eigenspace corresponding to $\\sigma^2.$ \n\nLet's illustrate this with an example. Consider the following matrix:\n\n![](images/ee/ee74c3d4ed7e32388d06b47ed79789d768b54dee61e64d6db57c3eeb582089ae.svg)\n\nLet's find a singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.\n\n- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \\! A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A & ={[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}13 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 13\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that since $A^T \\! A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are \n\n$$\n\\sigma_1 = \\sigma_2 = \\sqrt{13}.\n$$\n\n- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \\! A$): Since the singular values are equal, we can always take as solutions of $(A^T\\!A-13I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ the unit eigenvectors \n![](images/d1/d1770843817b2557b032743e186dd27106374fef90a2a8e8bb3cfe77b2eb0398.svg)\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\mathbf u_1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{13}} \\\\ -\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{13}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute $\\mathbf u_2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{13}} \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{13}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\\Sigma,$ and $V\\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c9/c950cf3aff8f9ab47ede762fa9c4451c5e7fc1e78e12fca064ee87d89fcb571e.svg)\n\n**Note:** By swapping the order of eigenvectors in step 3, we swap the vectors $\\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\\mathbf{u}_2$ in step 4. :tutorial/content "It follows from the definitions that a $2\\times 2$ matrix $A$ has two repeated singular values $\\sigma_1= \\sigma_2= \\sigma$ if and only if the matrix  $A^TA$ has two repeated eigenvalues $\\lambda_1=\\lambda_2 = \\sigma^2.$  Thus, since $A^TA$ is diagonalizable (because it is symmetric), the eigenspace corresponding to $\\sigma^2$ must be two-dimensional. Therefore, \n\n![](images/df/df266614e2576526353248439b7a17431d5e9e43153e1ba225adab3a89321373.svg)\n\nConsequently, we can use any pair of unit orthogonal vectors as a basis for the eigenspace corresponding to $\\sigma^2.$ \n\nLet's illustrate this with an example. Consider the following matrix:\n\n![](images/ee/ee74c3d4ed7e32388d06b47ed79789d768b54dee61e64d6db57c3eeb582089ae.svg)\n\nLet's find a singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.\n\n- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \\! A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A & ={[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}13 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 13\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that since $A^T \\! A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are \n\n$$\n\\sigma_1 = \\sigma_2 = \\sqrt{13}.\n$$\n\n- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T \\! A$): Since the singular values are equal, we can always take as solutions of $(A^T\\!A-13I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ the unit eigenvectors \n![](images/d1/d1770843817b2557b032743e186dd27106374fef90a2a8e8bb3cfe77b2eb0398.svg)\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\mathbf u_1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -3\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{13}} \\\\ -\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{13}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute $\\mathbf u_2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\\\ -3 & 2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{13}}[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{13}} \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{13}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\\Sigma,$ and $V\\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c9/c950cf3aff8f9ab47ede762fa9c4451c5e7fc1e78e12fca064ee87d89fcb571e.svg)\n\n**Note:** By swapping the order of eigenvectors in step 3, we swap the vectors $\\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\\mathbf{u}_2$ in step 4. is the $m\\times n$ matrix\n\n$$\n\\frac{\\text{d}f}{\\text{d}x}=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\\\ \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ \\frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \\frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\\end{aligned}]\\in {R}^{m\\times n}.\n$$\n\nIn our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{3}\\end{aligned}]\\in {R}^{3}$, we get\n\n$$\nf(x)=[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{3}\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\\\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\nSo, the total derivative is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\,\\,\\,\\frac{\\text{d}f}{\\text{d}x} & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\\\ \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\\\ \\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\\\ \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\\\ \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 1\\end{aligned}].\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix."} {:db/id exploring the *total derivative* of a vector-valued function, which generalizes the derivative to functions with multiple inputs and outputs.\n\nSuppose a transformation $\\boldsymbol{f}:\\mathbb variables.\n\nIf $\\boldsymbol f$ is differentiable at $\\mathbf{x},$ then the **total derivative** of $\\boldsymbol f$ at $\\mathbf{x},$ denoted $\\boldsymbol{f}'(\\mathbf{x}),$ is given by the $m \\times n$ matrix\n\n![](images/c8/c8fbc309a129b8e19db46aebff637e47259b629ef83c282a38b3b318c3a4f269.svg)\n\nThis is sometimes called the **Jacobian matrix** of $\\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\\mathbf{x}$. Each row corresponds to the derivative of one component function $f_i$, and each column corresponds to the rate of change of all the components of $\\boldsymbol f$ with respect to one input variable $x_j$. This is sometimes called the **numerator layout** for derivatives because each row corresponds to each function component, which appears in the numerator positions of the partial derivatives.\n\nNotice that if $f: \\mathbb{R}^n \\to \\mathbb{R}$ is a scalar-valued function, then the total derivative is a row vector given by\n  ![](images/6e/6ef756e82eb71d528a8f279863fd86efc8669658456a65879fba73d08e964bd5.svg)\n\nOn the other hand, if $\\boldsymbol{f}: \\mathbb{R} \\to \\mathbb{R}^m$ is a vector-valued function of a single variable, then the total derivative is a column vector\n  ![](images/cd/cd232968d5ffff3040294f8093a42c91bccd3207f91bfc2f784cb53cad00441d.svg)\n\nNow let’s get some practice by working through a few examples of total derivatives." :tutorial/id #uuid "56f24ef3-119b-5459-90a4-c9d67357d755" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12299 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :step/next {:db/id 17592186205009}} {:db/id 17592186205009 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205189 :tutorial/content "We've learned that the derivative of a vector-valued function is a Jacobian matrix. Now imagine the input to our function $\\mathbf f$ is a matrix instead of a vector. In such cases, the Jacobian matrix must expand to account for two input dimensions.\n\nSuppose we have a transformation $\\boldsymbol{f} : \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n} \\to \\mathbb{R}^p$ that maps a matrix $\\mathbf{A} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{m \\times n}$ to a vector $\\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{A}) \\in \\mathbb{R}^p$, defined as\n\n![](images/f7/f7b9ca5880f164c28b490fd4a215a56769e426bdde8111a24e6530c03d83b937.svg)\n\nwhere each $f_i$ is a scalar-valued function of all the entries of the matrix $\\mathbf{A}.$\n\nSince the input $\\mathbf{A}$ varies along two dimensions (rows and columns), and the output $\\mathbf{f}(\\mathbf{A})$ varies along one (a vector with $p$ components), the total derivative of $\\mathbf f,$ which we denote as \n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{f}}{\\textrm{d}\\mathbf{A}}\n$$\n\nis naturally represented as a *three-dimensional object!* The technical name for this object is a **tensor**. Since it is a three-dimensional object, this particular tensor is a **third-order tensor** (or $3$-**tensor**).\n\nTo capture a meaningful derivative, we must differentiate each component $f_i$ with respect to *every element of the matrix* $\\mathbf A.$ We can visualize this as a stack of matrices, or layers, as shown below.\n\n![](images/d5/d533d4d2e387c8c9f177b9dafe939b58c1f1d7db2f03e9df2059fa9f7cbe22c5.png)\n\nLet's apply this concept to a specific example in the next slide." :tutorial/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186222322}} {:db/id 17592186222322 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222501 :tutorial/content "Recall that when we shift coordinates by defining\n\n$$\nu = x - x^\\ast,\\qquad v = y - y^\\ast,\n$$\n\nwe translate the coordinate system so that the equilibrium $(x^\\ast, y^\\ast)$ becomes $(0,0).$\n\nThis translation preserves several important properties of the system. Shifting coordinates does not change the dynamics of the system, it only changes where the equilibrium appears in the coordinate plane. In particular:\n\n1\\. *Eigenvalues do not change:*\n\n  After shifting a linear system, the eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors are unchanged.\n\n2\\. *Stability type is preserved:*\n\n  The equilibrium retains its original classification (saddle, node, spiral, center, etc.). Shifting does not alter the local behavior near the equilibrium.\n\n3\\. *Trajectory shapes are unchanged up to translation:*\n\n  Trajectories in the $(u,v)$-plane have the same shapes as those in the $(x,y)$-plane. Only their location changes.\n\n4\\. *Equilibria correspond one-to-one:*\n\n  The target equilibrium $(x^\\ast, y^\\ast)$ maps to $(u,v) = (0,0).$ The shift does not create or remove equilibria.\n\n5\\. *Nullclines translate but retain the same shape:*\n\n  The geometric structure of the vector field is preserved under translation.\n\nLet's proceed to some examples." :tutorial/id elementary $2\\times 2$ matrices, each elementary $3\\times 3$ matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as $E.$ To illustrate, let's consider the matrix \n\n![](images/a1/a1c71fda15d78cc8c6ae95862c95b73a1cca1830cdf3b54f8e7e151653b82df1.svg)\n\nTo find the inverse of $E,$ we proceed as follows:\n\n**Step 1:** Write down $\\color{blue}E$ and the identity matrix $I_3$ side-by-side, as shown below:\n![](images/1e/1ef9574c45fb103c7fa2b32af13018de53da495fdf9e6e2da729897a521cead9.svg)\n\n**Step 2:** Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.$ We apply the operation to entire row (not only the left part):\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[E\\,|\\,{I}_{3}] & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -4 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =[{I}_{3}\\,|\\,{E}^{-1}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe conclude that $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1$ transforms $E$ back into the identity matrix. Likewise, when this row operation is applied to the identity matrix, it generates $E^{-1}.$\n\nThe matrix $E^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,\n![](images/fa/fa0e6c42fc8efaf80c3a37640261b1ec8247c2d598f14d7af4865a7c57691654.svg)\n\nWe can work out the inverse of all elementary $3\\times 3$ matrices in a similar way." :tutorial/id #uuid "90445bd9-d2af-593e-a10d-9e7c94156e49" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3169 :tutorial/title "The Inverse of an Elementary Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "e927ae81-0817-515b-8603-18914b2317b0" :step/math-academy-id 17237 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116141}} {:db/id 17592186116141 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115254 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115083 :question/id #uuid "c27359a0-0784-5750-9323-b35d9d7b5f62" :question/math-academy-id "e-4728"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "dd71abb1-455e-50d0-aae4-082b41821ef1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115745} {:db/id 17592186115860} {:db/id 17592186247107} {:db/id 17592186345042} {:db/id 17592186380601} {:db/id 17592186386522} {:db/id 17592186386529} {:db/id 17592186393493} {:db/id 17592186437048} {:db/id 17592186437049}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Inverse of an Elementary 3x3 Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "0ad61d7d-e259-50fa-af0b-671e9d0310ef" :step/math-academy-id 17238 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116139}}] :activity/title "Elementary 3x3 Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186115477} {:db/id 17592186116137 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116499 :tutorial/content "Just like for $2\\times 2$ matrices, there are also **elementary $3\\times 3$ matrices**. 17592186116140 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116500 :tutorial/content "As we saw before for elementary $2\\times 2$ matrices, each elementary $3\\times 3$ matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as $E.$ To illustrate, let's consider the matrix \n\n![](images/a1/a1c71fda15d78cc8c6ae95862c95b73a1cca1830cdf3b54f8e7e151653b82df1.svg)\n\nTo find the inverse of $E,$ we proceed as follows:\n\n**Step 1:** Write down $\\color{blue}E$ and the identity matrix $I_3$ side-by-side, as shown below:\n![](images/1e/1ef9574c45fb103c7fa2b32af13018de53da495fdf9e6e2da729897a521cead9.svg)\n\n**Step 2:** Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.$ We apply the operation to entire row (not only the left part):\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}[E\\,|\\,{I}_{3}] & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -4 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =[{I}_{3}\\,|\\,{E}^{-1}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe conclude that $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1$ transforms $E$ back into the identity matrix. Likewise, when this row operation is applied to the identity matrix, it generates $E^{-1}.$\n\nThe matrix $E^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,\n![](images/fa/fa0e6c42fc8efaf80c3a37640261b1ec8247c2d598f14d7af4865a7c57691654.svg)\n\nWe can work out the inverse of all elementary $3\\times 3$ matrices in a similar way." :tutorial/id #uuid "90445bd9-d2af-593e-a10d-9e7c94156e49" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3169 :tutorial/title "The Inverse of an Elementary Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "e927ae81-0817-515b-8603-18914b2317b0" :step/math-academy-id 17237 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116141}} {:db/id 17592186116139 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115253 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115082 :question/id #uuid "18e5d6e0-a024-503b-87f5-b20080980b51" :question/math-academy-id "e-4727"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "41954d0a-b8ce-52a0-a2c0-002b0078a37d" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115746} {:db/id 17592186115862} {:db/id 17592186247119} {:db/id 17592186247120} {:db/id 17592186345054} {:db/id 17592186380608} {:db/id 17592186382284} {:db/id 17592186386536} {:db/id 17592186393507} {:db/id 17592186437046}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Product Involving an Inverse of an Elementary 3x3 Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "8f9639d5-a5fb-5b6c-8aca-eb75b34a00ab" :step/math-academy-id 17236} {:db/id 17592186116500 :tutorial/content "As we saw before for elementary $2\\times 2$ matrices, each elementary $3\\times 3$ matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as $E.$ To illustrate, let's consider the matrix \n\n![](images/a1/a1c71fda15d78cc8c6ae95862c95b73a1cca1830cdf3b54f8e7e151653b82df1.svg)\n\nTo find the inverse of $E,$ we proceed as follows:\n\n**Step 1:** Write down $\\color{blue}E$ and the identity matrix $I_3$ side-by-side, as shown below:\n![](images/1e/1ef9574c45fb103c7fa2b32af13018de53da495fdf9e6e2da729897a521cead9.svg)\n\n**Step 2:** Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. Riemann Sum in Sigma Notation"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "The area under the curve $y=(x+1)^{3}$ between $x=0$ and $x=4$ and the $x$-axis is approximated by a right Riemann sum using $n$ subintervals of equal length. What is the expression for the Riemann sum in sigma notation?" :question/worked-solution "The right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is\n\n$$\n{\\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f({x}_{j})Δx,\n$$\n\nwhere ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx$ with $Δx=\\frac{b-a}{n}.$ \n\nWe're told that there are $n$ subintervals. The endpoints indicate that $a=0$ and $b=4.$ So, we have\n\n$$\nΔx=\\frac{4-0}{n}=\\frac{4}{n}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f({x}_{j})Δx & ={\\sum }_{j=1}^{n}f(a+jΔx)Δx \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[f(0+j\\cdot \\frac{4}{n})\\cdot \\frac{4}{n}] \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[f(\\frac{4j}{n})\\cdot \\frac{4}{n}] \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[\\frac{4}{n}{(\\frac{4j}{n}+1)}^{3}].\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186233552 :question/id #uuid So the root $x=-1$ has multiplicity $3$.\n- The factor $(x-2)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $P(x)$. So the root $x=2$ has multiplicity $2$.\n- The factor $(x+3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $P(x)$. "Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x - 12$ have multiplicity $1$?" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to factor the polynomial. For this polynomial, we can factor by grouping:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\np(x) &= x^{3} + 3x^{2} - 4x - 12 \\\\\n&= x^{2}(x + 3) - 4(x + 3) \\\\\n&= (x^{2} - 4)(x + 3) \\\\\n&= (x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:\n\n- The factor $(x-2)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x)$. So the root $x=2$ has multiplicity $1$.\n- The factor $(x+2)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x)$. So the root $x=-2$ has multiplicity $1$.\n- The factor $(x+3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x)$. So the root $x=-3$ has multiplicity $1$.\n\nIn conclusion, the roots $x=2,-2,-3$ all have multiplicity $1$."} {:db/id 17592186048272} {:db/id 17592186055480 :question/id #uuid the roots of the polynomial are $x=5$ and $x=-8$.\n\nThe **multiplicity** of a root of a polynomial equals the number of times the corresponding factor appears in the fully factored form of the polynomial.\n\nFor the polynomial $p(x)$ above, we have the following:\n\n- The factor $(x-5)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x)$. Therefore, it appears only once, and the multiplicity of the root $x=-8$ is $1$.\n\nIf the multiplicity of a root is $1$, like $x=-8$ in the example above, then the root is called a **simple root**. \nGiven that $D={P}^{T}\\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that\n\n$$\nA=PD{P}^{T},\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,\n\n$$\nD={P}^{T}AP.\n$$\n\nMoreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.\n\nFirst, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$\n\nFrom the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\\lambda }_{1}=0,$ ${\\lambda }_{2}=1,$ and ${\\lambda }_{3}=3.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\\lambda }_{2}=1.$ \n\nNow, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-1I,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-1I & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\\\ -1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 1\\end{bmatrix}-1\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 & 0 \\\\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector \n\n$$\n{v}_{2}=\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix},\n$$\n\nwhere $‖{v}_{2}‖=\\sqrt{2}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P:$ \n\n$$\n\\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{\\sqrt{2}}{2} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{\\sqrt{2}}{2}\\end{bmatrix}\n$$"} {:db/id Equivalently,\n\n$$\nD={P}^{T}AP.\n$$\n\nMoreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.\n\nFirst, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$\n\nFrom the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\\lambda }_{1}=6,$ ${\\lambda }_{2}=6,$ and ${\\lambda }_{3}=12.$ So, the first and second columns of $P$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\\lambda }_{2}.$ \n\nNow, we need to find eigenvectors that correspond to ${\\lambda }_{1}={\\lambda }_{2}=6.$ Computing $A-6I,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-6I & =\\begin{bmatrix}7 & -1 & 2 \\\\ -1 & 7 & -2 \\\\ 2 & -2 & 10\\end{bmatrix}-6\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\\\ -1 & 1 & -2 \\\\ 2 & -2 & 4\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSeeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives two eigenvectors: \n\n$\\,$ ${v}_{1}=\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix}\\,$ and $\\,{v}_{2}=\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix}$\n\nNotice that eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. We set \n\n$$\n{e}_{1}={v}_{1}=\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix},\n$$\n\nand we find ${e}_{2}$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{e}_{2} & ={v}_{2}-\\frac{{v}_{2}\\cdot {e}_{1}}{{e}_{1}\\cdot {e}_{1}}{e}_{1} \\\\  & ={v}_{2}+\\frac{2}{5}{e}_{1} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{bmatrix}+\\frac{2}{5}\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 1 \\\\ \\frac{2}{5}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, dividing ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ by their respective norms, we obtain the first and second columns of \\frac{\\sqrt{5}}{5}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\ \\frac{{e}_{2}}{‖{e}_{2}‖} & =\\frac{1}{(\\frac{\\sqrt{30}}{5})}\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 1 \\\\ \\frac{2}{5}\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{\\sqrt{30}}{30} \\\\ \\frac{\\sqrt{30}}{6} \\\\ \\frac{\\sqrt{30}}{15}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186364530 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that\n\n$$\nA=PDP^T,\n$$\n\nwhere $D$ is a diagonal matrix.\n\nMoreover, a real matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.\n\nThe procedure for finding an orthogonal diagonalization of a $3 \\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A$ is similar to diagonalizing a regular (diagonalizable) $3\\times 3$ matrix:\n\n- **Step 1**: Find the eigenvalues of $A.$\n\n- **Step 2**: Find a basis of  $\\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of *unit orthogonal* eigenvectors of $A.$\n\n- **Step 3**: Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$\n\nAs an example, consider the matrix \n![](images/ac/acba5373e2f2470930adec855df9958508d9f41aba5d3fc6988b0001c07a9dfd.svg)\n\nThis matrix is symmetric. So let's apply our diagonalization algorithm.\n\n- **Step 1.**  We find the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving $\\det(A-\\lambda I)=0.$ This gives\n\n$$\n\\lambda_1=3, \\qquad \\lambda_2=-6, \\qquad \\lambda_3=-9.\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** We need to find an eigenvector basis of $\\mathbb R^3.$ Seeking a nonzero solution of $|A-\\lambda_i I| = 0$ for $i=1,2,3,$ we get the corresponding eigenvectors\n![](images/cd/cddf44571b3aba21dca82cc12664733469c17f30ed3a9a9cfc62acb12230caef.svg)\nNotice that the eigenvectors are mutually orthogonal. \nNow, an orthogonal diagonalization requires each eigenvector to be normalized. So, dividing each eigenvector by its norm, we obtain the following unit orthogonal eigenvectors:\n![](images/e4/e4bfc5b51cea64bd5cb8d340fbeab1a126aaa3f48ae42b991c2b5af2a25480b3.svg)\n\n- **Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ as follows:\n![](images/4b/4b4a8c98b7c4688fab231510b6b1d615f47bed070310d39f3e812cd9fb811395.svg)\n\n**Watch out!** In this example, we automatically get orthogonal eigenvectors because $A$ has three *distinct* eigenvalues. However, in the case of repeated eigenvalues, the corresponding eigenvectors might not be orthogonal." :tutorial/id #uuid "0ff932ad-00a4-58cd-952f-55c21e02ef43" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4881 :step/math-academy-id 30597 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162870}} {:db/id 17592186162915 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163249 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the algorithm for diagonalizing a $3\\times 3$ symmetric matrix $A.$\n\n- **Step 1**: Find the eigenvalues of $A.$\n\n- **Step 2**: Find a basis of  $\\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of unit orthogonal eigenvectors of $A.$\n\n- **Step 3**: Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$\n\nNote the following important points regarding step 2 of this process:\n\n- If $A$ has mutually distinct eigenvalues, the eigenvectors will automatically be orthogonal, so we only need to normalize them.\n\n- If $A$ has *repeated* eigenvalues, then the eigenvectors corresponding to these repeated eigenvalues *may not* be orthogonal. Therefore, we have to apply the Gram-Schmidt process to obtain orthogonal vectors.\n\nFor example, consider the following matrix:\n\n![](images/28/2807ddab01a673d01c385b0dcc1b77d007896f803376006e7f81f639930fecdc.svg)\n\nThis matrix is symmetric. Let's apply our diagonalization algorithm.\n\n- **Step 1.**  We find the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving $\\det(A-\\lambda I)=0\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\lambda_1=4, \\qquad \\lambda_2=4, \\qquad \\lambda_3=-2\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $\\mathbb R^3.$ Seeking a nonzero solution of $|A-\\lambda_i I| = 0$ for $i=1,2,3,$ we get the corresponding eigenvectors\n![](images/95/95d0808a376ad679118ee26b9387cc3037862b74f12945db886a2ffd7738d525.svg)\nNotice that $\\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\\mathbf{v}_2$ are not orthogonal. So, we proceed using the Gram-Schmidt process. to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{C}\\,\\text{d}s=L.\n$$\n\nIn polar coordinates, the arc length element $\\text{d}s$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\text{d}s=\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta .\n$$\n\nSo, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\\theta )$ for ${\\theta }_{1}\\le \\theta \\le {\\theta }_{2},$ we have\n\n$$\nL={\\int }_{C}\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta .\n$$\n\nSince }_{\\pi /3}^{\\pi }\\sqrt{(1-2\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta )^{2}+(2\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta )^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta  \\\\  & ={\\int }_{\\pi /3}^{\\pi }\\sqrt{1-4\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta :step/math-academy-id 35543 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172997}} {:db/id 17592186172995 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173201 :tutorial/content "Recall that for a path $C$ in the $xy$-plane, the arc length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\nL = \\displaystyle\\int_C \\, \\textrm{d}s\n$$\n\nNow, if $C$ is defined parametrically as \n\n$$\n\\mathbf r(t) = \\langle x(t),\\, y(t)\\rangle, \\quad a\\leq t \\leq b ,\n$$\n\nthen we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as\n\n$$\nL = \\int_{a}^{b}||\\mathbf r'(t)||\\,\\textrm d t = \\int_{a}^{b}\\sqrt{\\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2 + \\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2}\\,\\textrm d t\\,.\n$$\n\nBy comparing our two expressions for $L,$ we say that the **arc-length element** $\\textrm ds$ for a parametrically defined curve is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm ds = \\sqrt{\\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2 + \\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2}\\,\\textrm d t\\,.\n$$\n\nGeometrically, we can think of $\\textrm ds$ as representing the change in arc length that arises due to a vanishingly small change in $t.$ By summing (integrating) all of these small changes, we arrive at the arc length of $C.$ We'll explore this in more detail at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "56e8bdd3-5303-5eeb-82d3-ef837773c38f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5797 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "65361afd-5d8b-59a0-8bed-041764bc0685" :step/math-academy-id 35544 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172996}} {:db/id 17592186172996 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173202 :tutorial/content "Now suppose that a curve $C$ is defined using plane polar coordinates as\n\n$$\nr = r(\\theta), \\qquad \\theta_1\\leq\\theta\\leq\\theta_2.\n$$\n\nWe've already seen that a polar curve is just a special type of parametric curve in the parameter $\\theta,$ where\n\n$$\nx = r(\\theta)\\cos\\theta, \\qquad y = r(\\theta)\\sin\\theta, \\qquad \\theta_1\\leq\\theta\\leq\\theta_2.\n$$\n\nUsing the usual formula for the arc length of a polar curve, the arc length of $C$ can be calculated as\n\n$$\nL = \\int_{\\theta_1}^{\\theta_2}\\sqrt{r^2 + \\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d r}{\\textrm d \\theta}\\right)^2}\\,\\textrm d \\theta\n$$\n\nwhich is the same as the line integral\n\n$$\nL = \\displaystyle\\int\\limits_C \\, \\textrm{d}s.\n$$\n\nBy comparing our two expressions for $L,$ the arc-length element $\\textrm ds$ for a curve can also be defined using polar coordinates as follows:\n\n$$\n\\textrm ds = \\sqrt{r^2 + \\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d r}{\\textrm d \\theta}\\right)^2}\\,\\textrm d \\theta\n$$\n\nWe'll build up a geometric understanding of this result at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's use this result to calculate some line integrals across polar curves." :tutorial/id #uuid "4850750a-5b8d-5c03-88c1-a2b832a313ce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5801 :tutorial/title "The Arc Length Element for Polar Curves"} :step/id #uuid "665cda4d-3863-540c-afb3-a1cde7ebd6d9" :step/math-academy-id 35565 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172993}} {:db/id 17592186172997 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173203 :tutorial/content "Let's now build up a geometric understanding of what the arc length element $\\textrm d s$ means. First, we'll consider the case of a parametric curve defined as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf r(t) = \\langle x(t),\\, y(t)\\rangle.\n$$\n\nSuppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\\mathbf r.$\n\n![](images/2b/2b302806eef01fd6e8160ee6e3183959537c0e9f5c6907238a2eea1d208d3da7.png)\n\nNow consider a small change $\\Delta t$ in the parameter $t.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\\mathbf r + \\Delta\\mathbf r,$ where $\\Delta \\mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. \n\n![](images/0b/0b1eb1dcc7be637e4e6024b5a8e9e13a4ea5c3e7439be7a2e3083f5ec274ef71.png)\n\nAccording to the diagram we have\n\n$$\n\\Delta x = x(t+\\Delta t) - x(t), \\qquad \\Delta y = y(t+\\Delta t) - y(t),\n$$\n\nwhere $\\Delta x$ and $\\Delta y$ are the changes in $x$ and $y,$ respectively, corresponding to the change in $t.$\n\nUsing the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, these quantities can be approximated as\n\n$$\n\\Delta x \\approx \\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\Delta t, \\qquad \\Delta y \\approx \\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\Delta t.\n$$\n\nThe change in arc length $\\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\\Delta \\mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\\\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\\\  & ≈{(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\\\  & ={(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\\\  & =[{(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\Delta s\n\n\\approx\n\n\\sqrt{\\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2  + \\left( \\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2}\\, \\Delta t.\n$$\n\nIf we imagine the limiting case where $\\Delta t \\to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\\textrm d s\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\textrm d s\n\n=\n\n\\sqrt{\\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2  + \\left( \\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2}\\, \\textrm d t\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65578a76-05f7-551a-acbd-956ae6831965" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5802 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of the Arc Length Element for a Parametric Curve"} :step/id #uuid "46feb8c2-5068-5992-a3a2-858b37d8c39e" :step/math-academy-id 35569 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172998}} {:db/id 17592186172998 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173204 :tutorial/content "Now, let's derive the formula for the arc length element $\\textrm d s$ for a curve defined using plane polar coordinates. We will use a similar geometric approach.\n\nConsider a curve $r= r(\\theta)$ defined using polar coordinates. Suppose that the point $P$ lies on this curve and has position vector $\\mathbf r.$\n\n![](images/7f/7fa77b8d4ad159967f917b438096f472cbd7f541495847e11b919a6843e6259b.png)\n\nNow consider a small change $\\Delta \\theta$ in the parameter $\\theta.$ This change gives a new point $P'$ on the curve with position vector $\\mathbf r + \\Delta\\mathbf r,$ where $\\Delta \\mathbf r$ gives the total change (as a vector) in moving from $P$ to $P',$ as shown below. \n\n![](images/10/105112a2bb993a13282c5f36190ca99a46d80a22a4203f653f7f67060e486d48.png)\n\nFrom here, we see that the vector $\\Delta \\mathbf r$ can be approximated as the vector addition of two components:\n\n- a vector of length $\\Delta r$ acting parallel to $\\mathbf r,$ and\n\n- a vector of length $r\\Delta \\theta$ acting perpendicular to $\\mathbf r.$\n\n![](images/08/080fa1112410328ba369e1c2e5d70fc2e5ddba97606a2fdeaa90d61e3e20d874.png)\n\nNote that $\\Delta r$ is simply the difference of the radial lengths between the points $P$ and $P'.$ The expression $r\\Delta \\theta$ comes from the formula for the arc length of a sector of a circle.\n\nNow, the change in arc length $\\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\\Delta \\mathbf r.$ Since our two components are perpendicular, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\\\  & ≈(Δr)^{2}+(rΔ\\theta )^{2} \\\\  & =Δ{r}^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\\theta )^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nUsing the fact that a difference quotient can be approximated as derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\Delta r = r(\\theta + \\Delta\\theta) - r(\\theta) = \\dfrac{\\textrm d r}{\\textrm d \\theta}\\Delta\\theta.\n$$\n\nSubstituting this into our expression for $(\\Delta s)^2$ above, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}(Δ\\theta )^{2}+{r}^{2}(Δ\\theta )^{2} \\\\  & ={r}^{2}(Δ\\theta )^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}(Δ\\theta )^{2} \\\\  & =[{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}](Δ\\theta )^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\Delta s = \\sqrt{r^2 + \\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d r}{\\textrm d \\theta}\\right)^2}\\Delta\\theta.\n$$\n\nIf we imagine the limiting case where $\\Delta \\theta \\to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\\textrm d s\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\textrm d s\n\n=\n\n\\sqrt{r^2 + \\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d r}{\\textrm d \\theta}\\right)^2}\\textrm d\\theta\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b310dc84-9da7-5492-9639-145086fe7403" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5803
