t.\n$$\n\nThe change in arc length $\\Delta s$ can be approximated as the magnitude of $\\Delta \\mathbf r.$ Therefore, by the Pythagorean theorem, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(Δs)^{2} & ≈||Δr|{|}^{2} \\\\  & ={(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2} \\\\  & ≈{(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t}Δt)}^{2} \\\\  & ={(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}(Δt)^{2} \\\\  & =[{(\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t})}^{2}](Δt)^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\Delta s\n\n\\approx\n\n\\sqrt{\\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2  + \\left( \\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2}\\, \\Delta t.\n$$\n\nIf we imagine the limiting case where $\\Delta t \\to 0,$ we arrive at the arc length element $\\textrm d s\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\textrm d s\n\n=\n\n\\sqrt{\\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2  + \\left( \\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2}\\, \\textrm d t\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid length $L$ of $C$ can be computed as the line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\nL = \\displaystyle\\int_C \\, \\textrm{d}s\n$$\n\nNow, if $C$ is defined parametrically as \n\n$$\n\\mathbf r(t) = \\langle x(t),\\, y(t)\\rangle, \\quad a\\leq t \\leq b ,\n$$\n\nthen we can also calculate the arc length of $C$ as\n\n$$\nL = \\int_{a}^{b}||\\mathbf expressions for $L,$ we say that the **arc-length element** $\\textrm ds$ for a parametrically defined curve is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm ds = \\sqrt{\\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d x}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2 + \\left(\\dfrac{\\textrm d y}{\\textrm d t}\\right)^2}\\,\\textrm d t\\,.\n$$\n\nGeometrically, we can think of $\\textrm ds$ as representing the change in arc length that arises due to }_{1}\\le \\theta \\le {\\theta }_{2},$ we have\n\n$$\nL={\\int }_{C}\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{\\theta }_{1}}^{{\\theta }_{2}}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta .\n$$\n\nWhere $1+\\operatorname{sin}⁡4\\theta>0$, $r=\\sqrt{1+\\operatorname{sin}⁡4\\theta }\\,$ gives\n\n$$\n\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta }=\\frac{2\\operatorname{cos}⁡4\\theta }{\\sqrt{1+\\operatorname{sin}⁡4\\theta }}.\n$$\n\nApplying the arc-length formula piecewise between the finitely many zeros of $r$, the expression for our line }_{2}}\\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\\frac{\\text{d}r}{\\text{d}\\theta })}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}\\theta .\n$$\n\nWhere $1+\\operatorname{sin}⁡4\\theta>0$, $r=\\sqrt{1+\\operatorname{sin}⁡4\\theta }\\,$ :topic/math-academy-id 4166} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199256 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199454 :tutorial/content "Recall that a lamina's *center of mass* is the point $(\\overline{x}, \\overline{y})$ where its total mass could be concentrated to give the same total moment about the coordinate axes as the original lamina. \n\nThe center of mass of a lamina $D$ with the mass density function $\\lambda(x,y)$ is given by \n\n$$\n(\\overline{x},\\overline{y}) = \\left( \\dfrac{M_y}{m}, \\dfrac{M_x}{m} \\right),\n$$\n\nwhere \n\n- $\\displaystyle m = \\iint \\limits_D \\lambda (x,y) \\: \\textrm{d}A$ is the mass of the lamina,\n\n- $\\displaystyle M_x = \\iint\\limits_D y \\, \\lambda (x,y) \\: \\textrm{d}A\\:$ is the moment of the lamina about the $x$-axis, and\n\n- $\\displaystyle M_y = \\iint\\limits_D x \\, \\lambda (x,y) \\: \\textrm{d}A$ is the moment of the lamina about the $y$-axis.\n\nRemember that if we could place a fulcrum under our lamina at its center of mass, it would balance perfectly." :tutorial/id #uuid "dbc92201-9cb2-54d6-9ac9-8ee49bf8c4e5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4905 :tutorial/title "Center of Mass"} :step/id #uuid "274308ee-bab4-54df-9e77-953f260e7982" :step/math-academy-id 30624 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199258}} {:db/id 17592186199257 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199455 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we'll learn how to determine the center of mass of a thin lamina whose mass is unevenly distributed. \n\nWe describe the mass distribution across a lamina using its mass density function $\\lambda (x,y).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit area* at any point $(x,y)$ on the lamina.\n\nFor example, consider a thin plate with mass density function $\\lambda(x,y) = 6xy$ occupying the finite rectangular region $D$ between the lines $x=1,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ and $y=1.$ What is the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis?\n\nTo answer this, consider a point $(x,y) \\in D$ on the plate and a small rectangular piece with its bottom-left corner at $(x,y)$ and area $\\Delta{A},$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/8c/8cd947e542aaf7eb787abc7a846e87a2d03ccafa0987f3422928fdcba115da9e.png)\n\nIf $\\Delta{A}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the moment of this piece about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{y} & ≈x\\cdot Δm \\\\  & ≈x\\cdot 6xy\\,ΔA \\\\  & =6{x}^{2}y\\,ΔA.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the total moment of the plate about the axis, we add together the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\\Delta{A} \\to 0.$ By doing this, we get\n\n$$\nM_y =  \\iint\\limits_D 6x^2y \\: \\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\n \n\nCarrying out the integration, we find that the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{1}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}y\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{1}^{2}3{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{1}2y\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\\\  & =(8-1)\\cdot (1-0) \\\\  & =7.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe moment about the $x$-axis can be found similarly.\n\nIn general, the moments $M_x$ and $M_y$ of a lamina $D$ with mass density function $\\lambda(x,y)$ about the $x$-axis and about the $y$-axis, respectively, are given by the following formulas:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\\,\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\ {M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\\,\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7aa18cfe-acd7-5e17-982c-58eabc063404" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4906 :tutorial/title 17592186199259 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199456 :tutorial/content "When a lamina's mass density is constant, the center of mass depends only on the shape of the lamina. In cases like these, the center of mass is called the **centroid** of the lamina. The centroid of a shape corresponds to its geometrical center.\n\nSo, $\\lambda$ is constant, then the mass of the plate is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda \\,dA \\\\  & =\\lambda {∬}_{D}\\,dA \\\\  & =\\lambda \\cdot {A}_{D},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $A_D$ denotes the area of $D.$ As a result, \n\n$$\nm = \\lambda \\cdot A_D \\qquad \\Longrightarrow \\qquad \\dfrac{\\lambda}{m} = \\dfrac{1}{A_D}.\n$$\n\nSubstituting the above into the formula for the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass, we obtain \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{M}_{y}}{m} & =\\frac{1}{m}{∬}_{D}x\\,\\lambda \\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{\\lambda }{m}{∬}_{D}x\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{{A}_{D}}{∬}_{D}x\\,\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can similarly compute the $y$-coordinate.\n\nIn general, the centroid of a lamina $D$ with area $A_D$ is given by $(x_c, y_c),$ where\n\n$$\n\\displaystyle x_c = \\dfrac{1}{A_D} \\iint\\limits_D x \\, \\: \\textrm{d}A, \\qquad \n\\displaystyle y_c = \\dfrac{1}{A_D} \\iint\\limits_D y \\, \\: \\textrm{d}A.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "aea964ff-901c-5b76-9fca-721d53f04354" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4907 :tutorial/title $\\Delta{A}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the moment of this piece about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{y} & ≈x\\cdot Δm \\\\  & ≈x\\cdot 6xy\\,ΔA \\\\  & =6{x}^{2}y\\,ΔA.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the total moment of the plate about the axis, we add together the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\\Delta{A} \\to 0.$ By doing this, we get\n\n$$\nM_y =  \\iint\\limits_D 6x^2y \\: \\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\n \n\nCarrying out the integration, we find that the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{1}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}y\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{1}^{2}3{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{1}2y\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\\\  & =(8-1)\\cdot (1-0) \\\\  & =7.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe moment about the $x$-axis can be found similarly.\n\nIn general, the moments $M_x$ and $M_y$ of a lamina $D$ with mass density function $\\lambda(x,y)$ about the $x$-axis and about the $y$-axis, respectively, are given by the following formulas:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\\,\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\ {M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\\,\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7aa18cfe-acd7-5e17-982c-58eabc063404" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4906 :tutorial/title \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{y}_{c} & =\\frac{1}{{A}_{D}}{∬}_{D}y\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}y\\,\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}y{\\int }_{0}^{\\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}\\text{d}x\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}y[x]_{x=0}^{x=\\sqrt{{y}^{3}}}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}y\\cdot \\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{5/2}\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{2}{[\\frac{2{y}^{7/2}}{7}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{5}{2}\\cdot \\frac{2}{7} \\\\  & Round the slope and the $y$-intercept to $1$ decimal place if necessary." :question/worked-solution "The equation of the regression line is given by\n\n$$\ny = mx+b\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nm &= \\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, b = y^(―) - mx^(―)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's compute $m{:}$\n\n- First, we compute the sum in the numerator:\n$S_{xy}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)); = (1 - 4)(6 - 3) + (2 - 4)(4 - 3); = + (4 - 4)(2 - 3) + (9 - 4)(0 - 3); = (-3)(3) + (-2)(1) + (0)(-1) + (5)(-3); =-9 - 2 - 0 - 15; =-26$\n- Second, we compute the sum in the denominator:\n$S_{xx}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2}; = (1 - 4)^{2} + (2 - 4)^{2} + (4 - 4)^{2} + (9 - 4)^{2}; = 9 + 4 + 0 + 25; = 38$\n\nNow, substituting into the formula for $m$, we obtain\n\n$$\nm = \\dfrac{-26}{38} = -\\dfrac{13}{19} \\approx -0.7\n$$\n\nNext, we substitute into the formula for $b{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nb &= y^(―) - mx^(―) \\\\\n&= 3 - (-\\frac{13}{19}) \\cdot 4 \\\\\n&= \\frac{109}{19} \\\\\n&\\approx 5.7\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation of the regression line is\n\n$$\ny = -0.7x + 5.7\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186048914} {:db/id 17592186049126} {:db/id 17592186050516} {:db/id 17592186097076 :question/id #uuid "1408fd26-8bc6-5a7f-ac9b-cc4b2ac4505f" :question/math-academy-id "q-134205"} {:db/id 17592186097079 :question/id #uuid "cd1fc976-0e05-50eb-b31c-b09094b91627" :question/math-academy-id "q-134556"} {:db/id 17592186096823 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096595 :question/id #uuid "9c9247a2-0a43-5dec-b477-bb60f8f57c0d" :question/math-academy-id "e-9716"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f904b9b7-b565-5bee-8f6f-c319a7cb9d7b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050210}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097078 :question/id #uuid "c8d3e7fb-7b7e-5708-a3c3-52c0d9f411c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-134208"} {:db/id 17592186097080 :question/id #uuid "f29883d6-68c5-5a81-b553-e109dd4bd8fd" :question/math-academy-id "q-134618"}] :knowledge-point/title "Making Predictions by Calculating a Regression Line"} {:db/id 17592186096595 :question/id #uuid "9c9247a2-0a43-5dec-b477-bb60f8f57c0d" :question/math-academy-id "e-9716" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186096823 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f904b9b7-b565-5bee-8f6f-c319a7cb9d7b" :knowledge-point/title "Making Predictions by Calculating a Regression Line"}] :question/problem "| **Years ($x$)** | $0$ | $1$ | $3$ | $4$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| **Value ($y$)** | **$35$** | **$26$** | **$19$** | **$16$** |\n\nThe table above gives the value of a car a few years after it was purchased (in thousands of dollars). = y^(―) - mx^(―)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nLet's compute $m{:}$\n\n- First, we compute the sum in the numerator:\n$S_{xy}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)); = (0 - 2)(35 - 24) + (1 - 2)(26 - line is\n\n$$\ny = -4.5x+33\n$$\n\nFinally, we can estimate the required value by substituting $y=10$ into the equation of the trend line and solving for $x{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\ny &= -4.5x + 33 \\\\\n10 &= -4.5x + 33 \\\\\n- 23 &= -4.5x \\\\\n&= x \\mid \\approx 5\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, according to this model, it takes approximately $5$ years for the car's value to drop to [{:db/id 17592186097755 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097892 :tutorial/content "For a set of $n$ paired observations $x_i$ and $y_i$, the trend line is the straight line that best fits the data.\n\n![](images/a2/a23a1411b40f723b19446d0838346dd74dd7bf75da918859cc688171e808b44a.png)\n\nFinding the equation of the trend line is called **linear regression**. The trend line is commonly called the **regression line** or **line of best fit.**\n\nWe can show that the equation of the trend line is given by\n\n$$\ny = mx+b\n$$\n\nwhere:\n\n- The slope $m$ is given by\n$m = \\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$.\n- The $y$-intercept $b$ is given by\n$b = \\overline{y} - m \\overline{x}$.\n- $\\overline{x}$ and $\\overline{y}$ are the means of the data sets:\n$\\overline{x} = \\dfrac1n \\sum_{i=1}^n x_i, \\qquad \\overline{y} = \\dfrac1n \\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$\n\n- The quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by\n$S_{xx} = \\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\\overline{x})^2, \\qquad S_{xy} = \\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\\overline{x})(y_i-\\overline{y})$.\n\nThere's some nice intuition behind the formula for $b$. The trend line *always* passes through the point $(\\overline{x}, \\overline{y})$. Therefore, this point must satisfy the trend line equation\n\n$$\ny = mx+b\n$$\n\nWe can then solve this equation for $b$.\n\nAlso, notice that $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are the summation terms that feature in the formulas for the variance and covariance, respectively." :tutorial/id #uuid "13ca983a-da47-572a-911a-813833c034d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5967 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :tutorial/content "For a set of $n$ paired observations $x_i$ and $y_i$, the trend line is the straight line that best fits the data.\n\n![](images/a2/a23a1411b40f723b19446d0838346dd74dd7bf75da918859cc688171e808b44a.png)\n\nFinding the equation of the trend line is called **linear regression**. The trend line is commonly called the **regression line** or **line of best fit.**\n\nWe can show that the equation of the trend line is given by\n\n$$\ny = mx+b\n$$\n\nwhere:\n\n- The slope $m$ is given by\n$m = \\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}$.\n- The $y$-intercept $b$ is given by\n$b = \\overline{y} - m \\overline{x}$.\n- $\\overline{x}$ and $\\overline{y}$ are the means of the data sets:\n$\\overline{x} = \\dfrac1n \\sum_{i=1}^n x_i, \\qquad \\overline{y} = \\dfrac1n \\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$\n\n- The quantities $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are given by\n$S_{xx} = \\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\\overline{x})^2, \\qquad S_{xy} = \\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\\overline{x})(y_i-\\overline{y})$.\n\nThere's some nice intuition behind the formula for $b$. The trend line *always* passes through the point $(\\overline{x}, \\overline{y})$. Therefore, this point must satisfy the trend line equation\n\n$$\ny = mx+b\n$$\n\nWe can then solve this equation for $b$.\n\nAlso, notice that $S_{xx}$ and $S_{xy}$ are the summation terms that feature in the formulas for the variance and covariance, respectively." :tutorial/id #uuid "13ca983a-da47-572a-911a-813833c034d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5967 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "77b46578-dd53-5487-a176-6e3dc8e5c0e5" :step/math-academy-id 511836 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097756}} {:db/id 17592186097892 :tutorial/content "For a set of $n$ paired observations $x_i$ and $y_i$, the trend line is the straight line that best fits the data.\n\n![](images/a2/a23a1411b40f723b19446d0838346dd74dd7bf75da918859cc688171e808b44a.png)\n\nFinding the equation of the trend line is called **linear regression**. {:db/id 17592186148590 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148714 :tutorial/content "A **polyhedron** is a $3$-dimensional shape where each side is a polygon. These flat polygonal sides are called **faces**.\n\n**Prisms** are polyhedrons made of two identical polygonal faces (called **bases**) connected by equal parallel line segments. If these line segments are perpendicular to the bases, we have a **right** prism.\n\nLet's take a look at some common prisms.\n\n- A **triangular (right) prism** consists of two identical triangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments.\n\n![](images/95/9563bd4f9c40ff5921998ed5840f8e5b43fb1af579a64a06a14782be4a86ece2.png)\n\n- A **rectangular (right) prism** consists of two identical rectangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments. :question/problem "Find the Laplace transform $Y(s) = \\mathcal L\\{y(t)\\}$ if \n\n$$\ny' - 3y = 2u_{\\pi/2}(t)\\cdot \\sin\\!\\left(2t-\\pi\\right)\\,, \\qquad y(0)=-2,\n$$\n\nwhere $u_{\\pi/2}(t)=u\\!\\left(t-\\dfrac{\\pi}{2}\\right)$ is the unit step function.\n\nYou may make use of the following result:\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L\\{\\sin\\omega t\\} = \\dfrac{\\omega}{s^2+\\omega^2}, \\qquad s > 0\n$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}-3y} & =L{2{u}_{\\pi /2}(t)\\cdot sin\\,(2t-\\pi )} \\\\ L{{y}^{′}}-3L{y} & =L{2{u}_{\\pi /2}(t)\\cdot sin\\,(2t-\\pi )}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo calculate $\\mathcal L\\left\\{y' \\right\\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=-2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\mathcal{L}\\left\\{y' \\right\\}  = sY(s) - y(0)   = sY(s) + 2\n$$\n\nTo find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term \n\n$$\n2u_{\\pi/2}(t)\\cdot \\sin\\!\\left(2t-\\pi\\right)\n$$\n\nis in the form $u(t-a)\\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\\dfrac{\\pi}{2}$ and $f(t)=2\\sin(2t-\\pi).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. \n\nNow, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L\\{u(t-a)\\cdot f(t)\\} = e^{-as} \\cdot \\mathcal L\\{f(t+a)\\}.\n$$\n\n  \n\nSo, by the second shifting theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{u\\,(t-\\frac{\\pi }{2})\\cdot 2\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\\pi )} & ={e}^{-(\\pi /2)s}\\cdot L{2sin\\,(2\\,(t+\\frac{\\pi }{2})-\\pi )} \\\\  & ={e}^{-(\\pi /2)s}\\cdot L{2\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)} \\\\  & ={e}^{-(\\pi /2)s}\\cdot 2\\cdot \\frac{2}{{s}^{2}+4} \\\\  & =\\frac{4{e}^{-\\pi s/2}}{{s}^{2}+4}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}-3L{y} & =L{2{u}_{\\pi /2}(t)\\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t-\\pi )} \\\\ (sY(s)+2)-3Y(s) & =\\frac{4{e}^{-\\pi s/2}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\\\ (s-3)Y(s)+2 & =\\frac{4{e}^{-\\pi s/2}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\\\ (s-3)Y(s) & =-2+\\frac{4{e}^{-\\pi s/2}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\\\ Y(s) & =-\\frac{2}{s-3}+\\frac{4{e}^{-\\pi s/2}}{({s}^{2}+4)(s-3)}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states\n\n$$\nL{u(t-a)\\cdot f(t)}={e}^{-as}\\cdot L{f(t+a)}.\n$$\n\n  \n\nSo, by the second shifting theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{u(t-2)\\cdot {e}^{t-2}} & ={e}^{-2s}\\cdot L{{e}^{(t+2)-2}} \\\\  & ={e}^{-2s}\\cdot L{{e}^{t}} \\\\  & ={e}^{-2s}\\cdot \\frac{1}{s-1} \\\\  & =\\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s-1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =L{{u}_{2}(t)\\cdot {e}^{t-2}} \\\\ }(t)=u(t-\\pi )$ is the unit step function.\n\nYou may make use of the following result:\n\n$$\nL{\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\omega t}=\\frac{\\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\\omega }^{2}},\\,s>0\n$$\n\n$Y(s)=$\n{{field-1}},$\\,s>0$" :question/worked-solution "First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}+y} & =L{{u}_{\\pi }(t)\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\\pi )} \\\\ L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =L{{u}_{\\pi }(t)\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\\pi )}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo calculate $L{{y}^{′}},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0:$\n\n$$\nL{{y}^{′}}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)\n$$\n\nTo find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term \n\n$$\n{u}_{\\pi }(t)\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\\pi )\n$$\n\nis in the form $u(t-a)\\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\\pi $ and $f(t)=\\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\\pi ).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. \n\nNow, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states\n\n$$\nL{u(t-a)\\cdot f(t)}={e}^{-as}\\cdot L{f(t+a)}.\n$$\n\n  \n\nSo, by the second shifting theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{u(t-\\pi )\\cdot \\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\\pi )} & ={e}^{-\\pi s}\\cdot L{\\operatorname{sin}⁡((t+\\pi )-\\pi )} \\\\  & ={e}^{-\\pi s}\\cdot L{\\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)} \\\\  & ={e}^{-\\pi s}\\cdot \\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1} \\\\  & =\\frac{{e}^{-\\pi s}}{{s}^{2}+1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{{y}^{′}}+L{y} & =L{{u}_{\\pi }(t)\\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-\\pi )} \\\\ sY(s)+Y(s) & =\\frac{{e}^{-\\pi s}}{{s}^{2}+1} \\\\ (s+1)Y(s) & =\\frac{{e}^{-\\pi s}}{{s}^{2}+1} \\\\ Y(s) & =\\frac{{e}^{-\\pi s}}{({s}^{2}+1)(s+1)}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id problem:\n\n$$\ny' + 4y = u_3(t)\\cdot (t-3)\\,, \\qquad y(0)=-2,\n$$\n\nwhere $u_3(t)=u(t-3)$ is the unit step function.\n\nYou're given that the Laplace transform $Y(s) = \\mathcal L\\{y(t)\\}$ is\n\n$$\nY(s) = -\\dfrac{2}{s+4} + \\dfrac{e^{-3s}}{s^2(s+4)}\n$$\n\nand that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as \n\n$$\ny(t) = -2e^{-4t} + u(t-3)\\cdot g(t).\n$$\n\nFind the function $g(t).$" :question/worked-solution "To find the function $g(t),$ we need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the term containing the time delay in $Y(s).$\n\nWe focus on the term with the exponential $e^{-3s}$ (which corresponds to the step function in the time domain) and identify the rational function part:\n\n$$\nF(s) = \\dfrac{1}{s^2(s+4)}.\n$$\n\nWe'll solve this in three steps.\n\n**Step 1.** Partial fraction decomposition\n\nSince the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+4)$ and a repeated linear factor $s^2,$ the decomposition takes the form\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{1}{s^2(s+4)} = \\dfrac{A}{s} + \\dfrac{B}{s^2} + \\dfrac{C}{s+4}.\n$$\n\nTo find the constants, we clear the denominators:\n\n$$\n1 = As(s+4) + B(s+4) + Cs^2.\n$$\n\nNow, we find the constants $A, B,$ and $C.$\n\n- Setting $s=0,$ we have\n\n$$\n1 = A(0) + B(4) + C(0) \\implies B = \\dfrac{1}{4}.\n$$\n\n- Setting $s=-4,$ we have\n\n$$\n1 = A(0) + B(0) + C(16) \\implies C = \\dfrac{1}{16}.\n$$\n\n- Comparing the coefficients of $s^2,$ we have\n\n$$\n0 = A + C \\implies A = -C = -\\dfrac{1}{16}.\n$$\n\nThus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as\n\n$$\nF(s) = -\\dfrac{1}{16s} + \\dfrac{1}{4s^2} + \\dfrac{1}{16(s+4)}.\n$$\n\n**Step 2.** Finding the Inverse of the base function\n\nWe find the inverse transform $f(t) = \\mathcal L^{-1}\\{F(s)\\}$ using standard transforms:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={L}^{-1}{-\\frac{1}{16s}+\\frac{1}{4{s}^{2}}+\\frac{1}{16(s+4)}} \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{16}+\\frac{t}{4}+\\frac{1}{16}{e}^{-4t}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3.** Applying the time-shifting property\n\nFinally, we address the $e^{-3s}$ term. By the second shifting theorem, we have\n\n$$\ne^{-as}\\cdot F(s)  = \\mathcal L\\{u(t-a)\\cdot f(t-a)\\}.\n$$\n\nTaking the inverse Laplace transform gives\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L^{-1} \\{ e^{-as}F(s) \\} = u(t-a) \\cdot f(t-a).\n$$\n\nIn our case, $a=3.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-3){:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u(t-3)f(t-3) & =u(t-3)[-\\frac{1}{16}+\\frac{t-3}{4}+\\frac{1}{16}{e}^{-4(t-3)}] \\\\  & =u(t-3)(\\frac{1}{16}{e}^{-4(t-3)}+\\frac{4t-13}{16}).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComparing this to the second term of the form given in the problem statement $y(t) = -2e^{-4t} + u(t-3)\\cdot g(t),$ we identify $g(t)$ as\n\n$$\ng(t) = \\dfrac{1}{16}e^{-4(t-3)} + \\dfrac{4t-13}{16}.\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186050768} {:db/id 17592186230063 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230233 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we will use Laplace transforms to handle **time-delayed forcing**, where the forcing function turns on at some time $t=a>0$.\n\nWe represent this “turning on” using the **unit step function** $u_a(t)=u(t-a)$.\n\nTo see what this looks like, consider the initial value problem\n\n$$\ny' - 4y = u_2(t)\\cdot e^{t-2}, \\qquad y(0)=0.\n$$\n\nHere, the forcing is $0$ for $t<2$ and becomes $e^{t-2}$ for $t\\ge 2$.\n\nTo find the Laplace transform of the forcing term, we note that\n\n$$\nu_2(t)\\cdot e^{t-2}\n$$\n\nis in the form $u(t-a)\\cdot f(t)$ where $a=2$ and $f(t)=e^{t-2}.$\n\nNow, recall that the **second shifting theorem** (time-shifting property) states\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L\\{u(t-a)\\cdot f(t)\\} = e^{-as} \\cdot \\mathcal L\\{f(t+a)\\}.\n$$\n\nSo, by the second shifting theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}L{u(t-2)\\cdot {e}^{t-2}} & ={e}^{-2s}\\cdot L{{e}^{(t+2)-2}} \\\\  & L{{y}^{'}}-4L{y} & =L{{u}_{2}(t)\\cdot {e}^{t-2}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo compute $\\mathcal L\\{y'\\},$ we use the derivative formula and the initial condition $y(0)=0{:}$\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L\\{y'\\} often appears in the $s$-domain as a factor of $e^{-as}$.\n\nSuppose $F(s)=\\mathcal L\\{f(t)\\}.$ Then the second shifting theorem can be written as\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L\\{u(t-a)\\cdot f(t-a)\\} = e^{-as}\\,F(s), \\qquad a>0.\n$$\n\nEquivalently, we can read this rule *backwards* as an inverse Laplace transform statement:\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L^{-1}\\{e^{-as}F(s)\\}=u(t-a)\\cdot f(t-a), \\qquad a>0.\n$$\n\nSo, if $Y(s)$ contains a term like $e^{-as}F(s)$, we can handle it using the following steps.\n\n- **Step 1:** Compute $f(t)=\\mathcal L^{-1}\\{F(s)\\}$.\n\n- **Step 2:** Shift the function by replacing $t$ with $(t-a)$.\n\n- **Step 3:** Multiply by the unit step function $u(t-a)$.\n\nWe consider the concrete example below." :tutorial/id #uuid "f9ee51be-d7c5-57bd-9302-41618fa57ab0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14745 :tutorial/title "Taking the Inverse Transform and Applying the Second Shifting Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "03a9dbab-bfb2-5a17-8b2a-da80a0acc614" :step/math-academy-id 600529 :step/next {:db/id 17592186230100}} {:db/id 17592186230100 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230240 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem:\n\n$$\ny' + 3y = u_\\pi(t)\\cdot \\cos(t-\\pi)\\,, \\qquad y(0)=2,\n$$\n\nwhere $u_\\pi(t)=u(t-\\pi)$ is the unit step function.\n\nAssume we are given that the Laplace transform $Y(s) = \\mathcal L\\{y(t)\\}$ is\n\n$$\nY(s) = \\dfrac{2}{s+3} + \\dfrac{s\\,e^{-\\pi s}}{(s^2+1)(s+3)}\n$$\n\nand that the solution to the initial value problem can be expressed as \n\n$$\ny(t) = 2e^{-3t} + \\dfrac{1}{10} u(t-\\pi)\\cdot g(t).\n$$\n\nOur goal is to find the function $g(t).$ To do this, we'll need to compute the inverse Laplace transform of the second term in $Y(s).$ We can use the following standard results:\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L\\{\\sin\\omega t\\} = \\dfrac{\\omega}{s^2+\\omega^2}, \\qquad \n\\mathcal L\\{\\cos\\omega t\\} = \\dfrac{s}{s^2+\\omega^2}, \\qquad\ns > 0.\n$$\n\nWe focus on the term with the exponential $e^{-\\pi s}$ and identify its rational function part:\n\n$$\nF(s) = \\dfrac{s}{(s^2+1)(s+3)}.\n$$\n\nWe'll find the inverse transform in three steps.\n\n**Step 1. Partial fraction decomposition**\n\nTo handle the rational function $F(s),$ we use *partial fraction decomposition*. Since the denominator contains a linear factor $(s+3)$ and an irreducible quadratic factor $(s^2+1),$ the decomposition takes the form\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{s}{(s^2+1)(s+3)} = \\dfrac{A}{s+3} + \\dfrac{Bs+C}{s^2+1}.\n$$\n\nTo find the constants, we clear the denominators:\n\n$$\ns = A(s^2+1) + (Bs+C)(s+3).\n$$\n\nNow, we find the constants $A, B,$ and $C.$\n\n- Setting $s=-3,$ we have\n\n$$\n-3 = A\\bigl((-3)^2+1\\bigr) + 0 \\implies 10A = -3 \\implies A = -\\dfrac{3}{10}.\n$$\n\n- Comparing the coefficients of $s^2,$ we have\n\n$$\n0 = A + B \\implies B = -A = \\dfrac{3}{10}.\n$$\n\n- Comparing the coefficients of $s,$ we have\n\n$$\n1 = 3B + C \\implies 1 = 3\\!\\left(\\dfrac{3}{10}\\right) + C \\implies C = \\dfrac{1}{10}.\n$$\n\nThus, we can rewrite $F(s)$ as\n\n$$\nF(s)= -\\dfrac{3}{10}\\cdot\\dfrac{1}{s+3} + \\dfrac{3}{10}\\cdot\\dfrac{s}{s^2+1} + \\dfrac{1}{10}\\cdot\\dfrac{1}{s^2+1}.\n$$\n\n**Step 2. Finding the inverse of the base function**\n\nWe find the inverse transform $f(t) = \\mathcal L^{-1}\\{F(s)\\}$ using standard transforms:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(t) & ={L}^{-1}{-\\frac{3}{10}\\cdot \\frac{1}{s+3}+\\frac{3}{10}\\cdot \\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+1}+\\frac{1}{10}\\cdot \\frac{1}{{s}^{2}+1}} \\\\  & =-\\frac{3}{10}{e}^{-3t}+\\frac{3}{10}\\operatorname{cos}t+\\frac{1}{10}\\operatorname{sin}t \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{10}(-3{e}^{-3t}+3\\operatorname{cos}t+\\operatorname{sin}t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3. Applying the time-shifting property**\n\nFinally, we use the *second shifting theorem* to handle the $e^{-\\pi s}$ factor. The theorem states:\n\n$$\n\\mathcal L^{-1} \\{ e^{-as}F(s) \\} = u(t-a) \\cdot f(t-a).\n$$\n\nIn our case, $a=\\pi.$ Therefore, we shift $f(t)$ by replacing every instance of $t$ with $(t-\\pi):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}u(t-\\pi )f(t-\\pi ) & =u(t-\\pi )\\cdot \\frac{1}{10}[-3{e}^{-3(t-\\pi )}+3\\operatorname{cos}(t-\\pi )+\\operatorname{sin}(t-\\pi )] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{10}u(t-\\pi )\\cdot [-3{e}^{-3(t-\\pi )}+3(-\\operatorname{cos}t)+(-\\operatorname{sin}t)]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nUsing the trigonometric identities $\\cos(t-\\pi)=-\\cos t$ and $\\sin(t-\\pi)=-\\sin t,$ we simplify:\n\n$$\nu(t-\\pi)f(t-\\pi) = \\dfrac{1}{10}u(t-\\pi)\\cdot \\left(-3e^{-3(t-\\pi)} - 3\\cos t - \\sin t\\right).\n$$\n\n**Conclusion: Identifying g(t)**\n\nThis result is the inverse transform of the second term in $Y(s).$ The problem statement gives the complete solution in the form\n\n$$\ny(t) = 2e^{-3t} + \\dfrac{1}{10} u(t-\\pi)\\cdot g(t).\n$$\n\nThe first term, $2e^{-3t},$ is the inverse transform of $\\dfrac{2}{s+3}.$ By comparing our calculated term with the form above, we can identify **$g(t)$**:\n\n$$\ng(t)= -3e^{-3(t-\\pi)} - 3\\cos t - \\sin t.\n$$" :tutorial/id 3\\cos t - \\sin t\\right).\n$$\n\n**Conclusion: Identifying g(t)**\n\nThis result is the inverse transform of the second term in $Y(s).$ The problem statement gives the complete solution in the form\n\n$$\ny(t) = 2e^{-3t} + \\dfrac{1}{10} u(t-\\pi)\\cdot g(t).\n$$\n\nThe first term, $2e^{-3t},$ is the inverse transform of $\\dfrac{2}{s+3}.$ By comparing our calculated term with the form above, we can identify **$g(t)$**:\n\n$$\ng(t)= -3e^{-3(t-\\pi)} - \\sum_{k=0}^\\infty c_k A^k\n$$\n\nFor example, recall that the Maclaurin series of $f(x) = e^x$ is\n\n$$\ne^x = \\sum_{k=0}^\\infty \\dfrac{x^k}{k!}.\n$$\n\nThen, for a square matrix $A,$ we define the matrix exponential as\n\n$$\ne^A = \\sum_{k=0}^\\infty \\dfrac{1}{k!}A^k.\n$$\n\nIn the next slide, we'll see how to apply matrix functions to square matrices." :tutorial/id #uuid with a Maclaurin series expansion, $f(D)$ is the diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $f(\\lambda_1), \\ldots, f(\\lambda_n){:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}f({\\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ 0 & f({\\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\\lambda }_{n})\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nFor example, given the matrix\n$\\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}$\nand the function $f(x) = e^x,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}f(2) & 0 \\\\ 0 & f(1)\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nThis rule works because raising a diagonal matrix to a power is equivalent to raising each diagonal entry to the same power.\n\nIndeed, if\n$\\displaystyle\nf(x) = \\sum_{k=0}^\\infty c_k x^k$\nis the Maclaurin series of $f,$ then, by the definition of $f(D),$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(D) & ={\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}{D}^{k} \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}{\\begin{bmatrix}{\\lambda }_{1} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ 0 & {\\lambda }_{2} & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\\lambda }_{n}\\end{bmatrix}}^{k} \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}\\begin{bmatrix}{\\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ 0 & {\\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\\lambda }_{n}^{k}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}{\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}{\\lambda }_{1}^{k} & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ 0 & {\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}{\\lambda }_{2}^{k} & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & {\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}{\\lambda }_{n}^{k}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}f({\\lambda }_{1}) & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ 0 & f({\\lambda }_{2}) & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & 0 & ⋯ & f({\\lambda }_{n})\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da162714-f641-5ded-aec8-6f24c0d5cbb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10689 :tutorial/title "Function of a Diagonal $J_n(\\lambda)$ is an $n\\times n$ Jordan block where the main diagonal entries are all $\\lambda{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}\\lambda  & 1 & 0 & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\lambda  & 1 & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & \\lambda  & 1 \\\\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & \\lambda \\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nFor a scalar function $f$ analytic at $\\lambda$ (i.e., has a Taylor series expansion at $\\lambda$), $f(J_n(\\lambda))$ is the matrix\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}f(\\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\\lambda ) & \\frac{{f}^{''}(\\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \\frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\\\ 0 & f(\\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\\lambda ) & ⋯ & \\frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\\\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\\lambda ) & {f}^{'}(\\lambda ) \\\\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\\lambda )\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nTo demonstrate, let's find $f(J_3(2))$ for $f(x) = \\ln x.$\n\nSince $J_3(2)$ is a $3\\times 3$ matrix, we will need the first $3-1=2$ derivatives of $f{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\\operatorname{ln}x \\\\ {f}^{'}(x) & =\\frac{1}{x} \\\\ {f}^{''}(x) & =-\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, we have\n\n![](images/43/439d1a1c3c2c315510fd293e8bb8e1467e149222025359a0e0d899270eb07e12.svg)\n\nNow that we can compute the value of a function of a Jordan block, we can also find the value of a function of a Jordan matrix.\n\nThe matrix [math]f(J_n(\\lambda))[/math] for [math]n=2,3,[/math] and [math]4[/math] are as follows.\n\n* For [math]2\\times 2[/math] Jordan blocks, we have\n\\[\nf(J_2(\\lambda)) =\n\\begin{bmatrix}\n\tf(\\lambda) & f'(\\lambda) \\\\\n\t0 & f(\\lambda)\n\\end{bmatrix}.\n\\]\n\n* For [math]3\\times 3[/math] Jordan blocks, we have\n\\[\nf(J_3(\\lambda)) =\n\\begin{bmatrix}\n\tf(\\lambda) & f'(\\lambda) & \\dfrac12f''(\\lambda) \\\\\n\t0 & f(\\lambda) & f'(\\lambda) \\\\\n\t0 & 0 & f(\\lambda)\n\\end{bmatrix}.\n\\]\n\n* For [math]4\\times 4[/math] Jordan blocks, we have\n\\[\nf(J_4(\\lambda)) =\n\\begin{bmatrix}\n\tf(\\lambda) & f'(\\lambda) & \\dfrac12f''(\\lambda) & \\dfrac16f'''(\\lambda) \\\\\n\t0 & f(\\lambda) & f'(\\lambda) & \\dfrac12f''(\\lambda) \\\\\n\t0 & 0 & f(\\lambda) & f'(\\lambda) \\\\\n\t0 & 0 & 0 & f(\\lambda)\n\\end{bmatrix}.\n\\]" :tutorial/id #uuid "7972371e-9205-5e74-b277-6dfcab332f9b" series expansion, we have\n\n$$\nf(SAS^{-1}) = Sf(A)S^{-1}.\n$$\n\nIndeed, given the Maclaurin series $\\displaystyle f(x) = \\sum_{k=0}^\\infty c_kx^k,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(SA{S}^{-1}) & ={\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}(SA{S}^{-1})^{k} \\\\  & ={\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}S{A}^{k}{S}^{-1} \\\\  & =S({\\sum }_{k=0}^{\\infty }{c}_{k}{A}^{k}){S}^{-1} \\\\  & =Sf(A){S}^{-1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo far, we have seen how to evaluate functions for diagonal matrices and Jordan blocks. With the formula above, we will now be able to\n\n- evaluate $f(B)$ for diagonalizable $B$ using a diagonalization $B=PDP^{-1},$ and\n\n- evaluate $f(B)$ for non-diagonalizable $B$ using a Jordan decomposition $B=PJP^{-1}.$\n\nLet's see how with an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4241af18-972e-530c-b06b-388437001b24" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10692 :tutorial/title "Function of a Jordan 17592186158424 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158466 :tutorial/content "Consider a Jordan matrix formed by the direct sum of blocks $J_{n_1}(\\lambda_1) {\\textstyle\\:\\oplus\\:} \\cdots {\\textstyle\\:\\oplus\\:} J_{n_k}(\\lambda_k)$ and a function $f.$ By applying the rule for diagonal matrices to this block diagonal matrix, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\\lambda }_{1})\\,⊕\\,⋯\\,⊕\\,{J}_{{n}_{k}}({\\lambda }_{k})) & =f(\\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{{n}_{1}}({\\lambda }_{1}) & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & ⋯ & {J}_{{n}_{k}}({\\lambda }_{k})\\end{bmatrix}) \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\\lambda }_{1})) & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & ⋯ & f({J}_{{n}_{k}}({\\lambda }_{k}))\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\\lambda }_{1}))\\,⊕\\,⋯\\,⊕\\,f({J}_{{n}_{k}}({\\lambda }_{k})).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis allows us to compute functions of any matrix in Jordan Normal Form by applying the function to each Jordan block individually.\n\nFor example, suppose $J = J_2(2) \\oplus J_1(3).$ Then, applying a function $f,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}f({J}_{2}(2)) & 0 \\\\ 0 & f({J}_{1}(3))\\end{bmatrix}\n$$" \\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nFor a scalar function $f$ analytic at $\\lambda$ (i.e., has a Taylor series expansion at $\\lambda$), $f(J_n(\\lambda))$ is the matrix\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}f(\\lambda ) & "Consider a Jordan matrix formed by the direct sum of blocks $J_{n_1}(\\lambda_1) {\\textstyle\\:\\oplus\\:} \\cdots {\\textstyle\\:\\oplus\\:} J_{n_k}(\\lambda_k)$ and a function $f.$ By applying the =f(\\begin{bmatrix}{J}_{{n}_{1}}({\\lambda }_{1}) & ⋯ & 0 \\\\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\\\ 0 & ⋯ & {J}_{{n}_{k}}({\\lambda }_{k})\\end{bmatrix}) \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}f({J}_{{n}_{1}}({\\lambda }_{1})) & ⋯ & 0 Therefore, we need to isolate $r$ in the above equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\frac{r}{h} &= 4 \\\\\nr &= 4h\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe volume of a cylinder with radius $r$ and height $h$ is given by\n\n$$\nV = \\pi r^2 h\n$$\n\nTherefore, substituting $r = 4h$ into the formula and solving for $h$, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nV &= πr^{2}h \\\\\nV &= π(4h)^{2}h \\\\\nV &= 16πh^{3} 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $3\\times 3$ matrix such that $|A|=0.$ Which of the following statements must be true?\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\n- **I.** $A$ has a zero column\n- **II.** $A$ has two proportional rows\n- **III.** One of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A$" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider our statements in turn.\n\n- Statements I and II are false. For example, consider the matrix \n\n$$\nA=\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 3\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nExpending across the $1$st column, we have that \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}|A| & =1\\cdot \\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3\\end{vmatrix}+1\\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{vmatrix} \\\\  & =(3-2)+(1-2) \\\\  & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nbut $A$ has neither a zero column nor two proportional rows.\n\n- Statement III is true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:\n\n$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"III only\"."} {:db/id 17592186420353 :question/id #uuid "d2486be8-75b8-51f1-882e-08f8a79961f2" :question/math-academy-id "q-42463"} {:db/id 17592186049875} {:db/id 17592186048750 :topic/difficulty equations:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=-2 \\\\ -{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2} &=4 \\\\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=2\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nIt is easy to show that the system is inconsistent (i.e., it has no solution). However, in real-world problems, we might want to find an approximate solution to the system. \n\nLet's formulate the problem a little more rigorously. Firstly, we write down the system in the form $A\\mathbf x = \\mathbf b\\mathbin{:}$\n![](images/22/22b8abd4638e579875755f482442cf1dbf89653bd9d396b4a802217e25177839.svg)\n\nWe are interested in vectors $\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ such that $A\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ is very close to $\\mathbf b.$ More precisely, we wish to *minimize the distance* between $A\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ and $\\mathbf b.$ Recall that the distance between $A\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ and $\\mathbf b$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\Vert  A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} - \\mathbf{b} \\Vert.\n$$\n\nThe smaller the value of $\\Vert  A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} - \\mathbf{b} \\Vert,$ the better our approximation $\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ will be. \n\nIn terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector $A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ that lies in $\\textrm{Col}(A)$ and is closest to $\\mathbf{b}.$\nTherefore, $A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$\n\n![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)\n\nIt can be shown that ${\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ is found by solving the corresponding **normal equation**, given by \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A\\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation $A {\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} = \\mathbf b$ by $A^T.$\n\nSince the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \\! A$ is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T \\! A)^{-1},$ we obtain\n\n$$\n{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \\! A)^{-1}A^T \\mathbf{b}.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the right-hand side as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\hat{x} & =({A}^{T}\\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\\\  & ={(\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -4 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & -4 \\\\ 2 & -1\\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -4 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & ={\\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\\\ 3 & 18\\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ -20\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{99}\\begin{bmatrix}18 & -3 \\\\ -3 & 6\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ -20\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{8}{33} \\\\ -\\frac{38}{33}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe vector ${\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ is called the **least-squares solution** of the given system.\n\n**Watch out!** We assumed that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, which guarantees that $A^T \\! A\\,$ is invertible. However, if the columns of $A$ are linearly *dependent,* then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem." :tutorial/id #uuid "548ecdec-2401-51e1-b2cf-d63f0b5a595d" Firstly, we write down the system in the form $A\\mathbf x = \\mathbf b\\mathbin{:}$\n![](images/22/22b8abd4638e579875755f482442cf1dbf89653bd9d396b4a802217e25177839.svg)\n\nWe are interested in vectors $\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ such that $A\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ is very close to $\\mathbf b.$ More precisely, we wish to *minimize the distance* between $A\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ and $\\mathbf b.$ Recall that the distance between $A\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ and $\\mathbf b$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\Vert  A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} - \\mathbf{b} \\Vert.\n$$\n\nThe smaller the value of $\\Vert  A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} - \\mathbf{b} \\Vert,$ the better our approximation $\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}$ will be. \n\nIn terms of vector subspaces, we wish to find a vector $A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ that lies in $\\textrm{Col}(A)$ and is closest to $\\mathbf{b}.$\nTherefore, $A{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ must be the orthogonal projection of $\\mathbf{b}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of $A.$\n\n![](images/3a/3a1c79036954f0e04212892b7e3d79c75f8cd7b81d7785441f090f89a4eb6faf.png)\n\nIt can be shown that ${\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ is found by solving the corresponding **normal equation**, given by \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A\\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe'll prove this at the end of the lesson. Note that the normal equation is obtained by left-multiplying the equation $A {\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} = \\mathbf b$ by $A^T.$\n\nSince the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix $A^T \\! A$ is invertible. Therefore, left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T \\! A)^{-1},$ we obtain\n\n$$\n{\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}} = (A^T \\! A)^{-1}A^T \\mathbf{b}.\n$$\n\nWe now compute the right-hand side as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\hat{x} & =({A}^{T}\\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\\\  & ={(\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -4 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & -4 \\\\ 2 & -1\\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\\,\\,\\,\\,\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -4 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 2\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & ={\\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\\\ 3 & 18\\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ -20\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{99}\\begin{bmatrix}18 & -3 \\\\ -3 & 6\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\\\ -20\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{8}{33} \\\\ -\\frac{38}{33}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe vector ${\\hat{\\mathbf{x}}}$ is called the **least-squares solution** of the given system.\n\n**Watch out!** We assumed that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, which guarantees that $A^T \\! A\\,$ is invertible. However, if the columns of $A$ are linearly *dependent,* then we have to use a different approach to solve the problem." :tutorial/id #uuid "548ecdec-2401-51e1-b2cf-d63f0b5a595d" :question/math-academy-id "q-140953" :question/problem "Consider the system $Ax=b$, where the matrix $A$ and the vector $b$ are shown below. Given that the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, find the minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖.$\n\n$$\nA=\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ 1 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 0 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{bmatrix},\\,b=\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ -1 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 3\\end{bmatrix}\n$$" :question/worked-solution "First of all, we write the given system in the form $Ax=b:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\overset{A}{\\overset{⏞}{\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ 1 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 0 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{bmatrix}}}\\overset{x}{\\overset{⏞}{\\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{2}\\end{bmatrix}}} & =\\overset{b}{\\overset{⏞}{\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ -1 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 3\\end{bmatrix}}} \\\\ Ax & =b\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can find the least-squares solution $\\hat{x}$ of the equation above by solving the corresponding normal equation, which we obtain by left-multiplying our original equation by ${A}^{T}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A\\hat{x} & ={A}^{T}b\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince the columns of $A$ are linearly independent, the matrix ${A}^{T}\\,A$ is invertible. Therefore, multiplying by $({A}^{T}\\,A)^{-1}$ on the left, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\hat{x} & =({A}^{T}\\,A)^{-1}{A}^{T}b \\\\  & ={(\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ 1 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 0 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{bmatrix})}^{-1}\\,\\,\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1 & 2 & 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ 0 \\\\ -1 \\\\ 4 \\\\ 3\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & ={\\begin{bmatrix}7 & 2 \\\\ 2 & 7\\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\\begin{bmatrix}12 \\\\ -3\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{45}\\begin{bmatrix}7 & -2 \\\\ -2 & 7\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}12 \\\\ -3\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}2 \\\\ -1\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe minimum value of $‖Ax-b‖$ is attained when $x=\\hat{x},$ which is the least-squares solution of the system $Ax=b.$ In this case, $A\\hat{x}$ represents the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A,$ and $‖A\\hat{x}-b‖$ is the distance between the vector $b$ and the column space. testing), we often need to use standard cumulative distribution function (CDF) tables to carry out the test. \n\nIn this lesson, we'll learn how to construct CDF tables for the binomial distribution and use them to calculate probabilities. \n\nFirst, recall that the probability mass function of the binomial distribution $B(n,p)$ is given by\n\n$$\nf(x) = \\binom{n}{x} \\, p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \\qquad x=0,1,2,\\ldots, n\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success.\n\nAlso, recall that the CDF of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that\n\n$$\nF(x) = P(X \\leq x).\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's compute the value of $F(x)$ for the distribution $B(5,0.37)$ at $x=0$ and $x=1.$  \n\nTo do that, we use the definition of the cumulative distribution function:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}F(0) & =P(X\\le 0) \\\\  & =P(X=0) \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0})(0.37)^{0}(1-0.37)^{5-0} \\\\  & =1\\cdot (0.37)^{0}\\cdot (0.63)^{5} \\\\  & ≈0.0992 \\\\ F(1) & =P(X\\le 1) \\\\  & =P(X=0)+P(X=1) \\\\  & =(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{0})(0.37)^{0}(1-0.37)^{5-0}+(\\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{5}{1})(0.37)^{1}(1-0.37)^{5-1} \\\\  & =1\\cdot (0.37)^{0}\\cdot (0.63)^{5}+5\\cdot (0.37)^{1}\\cdot (0.63)^{4} \\\\  & ≈0.3907.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe CDF data is usually presented as a table. If we were to continue this process and calculate $F(2), F(3), F(4),$ and $F(5),$ our table would look as follows:\n\n| $\\quad x \\quad$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |\n| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |\n| $P(X\\leq x)$ | $\\,\\bbox[gainsboro, 3pt]{\\color{blue}0.0992}\\,$ | $\\,\\bbox[gainsboro, 3pt]{\\color{blue}0.3907}\\,$ | $\\,0.7330\\,$ | $\\,0.9340\\,$ | $\\,0.9931\\,$ | $\\,1.0000\\,$ |\n\nNote the following:\n\n- $F(x)$ is an increasing function.\n\n- Since $n$ is the largest possible value of the binomial distribution, we have $F(n) = 1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid The only difference is that now a neighborhood of a point is a disc.\n\nFor example, consider the set $S$ and points $A,$ $B, C,$ and $D,$ shown below.\n\n![](images/a7/a7e037fd998c235ff7b721e7187d44814700ac5f41a256920f34f248c798c520.png)\n\nLet's classify each of these as interior or boundary points (or neither):\n\n- $A$ is an interior point since *there exists* a neighborhood of $A$ that is fully contained inside the set.\n\n- $B$ is neither an interior nor a boundary point because *there exists* a neighborhood of $B$ that does not contain points from the set.\n\n- $C$ is a boundary point since *every* neighborhood of $C$ contains points that lie in the set and points that do not lie in the set.\n\n- $D$ is a boundary point since *every* neighborhood of $D$ contains points that lie in the set and points that do not lie in the set.\n\nNotice that although $C$ and $D$ are both boundary points, $C\\notin S$ and yet $D\\in S.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bfda97a2-2fe7-5c9a-a067-dbf903ba2111" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6825 :tutorial/title "Interior and Boundary Points of Sets in the Plane"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that $S$ is a set of real numbers. A point $x_0$ is called an **interior point** of $S$ if *some* neighborhood of $\\mathbf x_0$ is *fully contained* inside $S.$ \n\nFor example, consider the set $S=[0,1)$ and the points $A$ and $B,$ shown below.\n\n![](images/a1/a12c60b6f60ca7c35162fb1ddf0d0d507fe80e73e621c451c21f0b882034ae21.png)\n\nThe point $A$ is an interior point of $S,$ but $B$ is not:\n\n- The point $A$ is an interior point of $S$ since there exists a neighborhood of $A$ that is *fully contained* inside $S.$\n\n- The point $B$ is *not* an interior point of $S$ since there is no neighborhood of $B$ that is *fully contained* inside $S.$ In other words, any neighborhood of $B$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.\n\nNote that neither $x=0$ nor $x=1$ are interior points. To see why, let's draw a neighborhood of each point:\n\n![](images/a9/a923732241443a0fd6a5f53dab7de2d346f5704a0b034c276e64dc3df2746f4f.png)\n\n \n\nFrom here, we can deduce the following:\n\n- The point $x=0$ is *not* an interior point of $S$ since there is no neighborhood of $x=0$ that is *fully* contained inside $S.$\n\n- The point $x=1$ is also *not* an interior point of $S$ since there is no neighborhood of $x=1$ that is *fully* contained inside $S.$\n\nThe set containing all interior points of a set $S$ is called the **interior** of $S,$ and is denoted $\\textrm{int}\\,S.$ \n\nFor the set $[0,1),$ its interior is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{int}\\,S = (0,1).\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "da6d3c21-fe0a-566e-a6e0-117f10988923" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7685 :tutorial/title "Interior Points"} point $x_0$ is a **boundary point** of $S$ if *every* neighborhood of $x_0$ contains points that *are* in $S$ *and* points that are *not* in $S.$ \n\nLet's consider the set $S=[0,1),$ the points $x=0, x=1,$ and neighborhoods of these points.\n\n![](images/a9/a923732241443a0fd6a5f53dab7de2d346f5704a0b034c276e64dc3df2746f4f.png)\n\nBoth $x=0$ and $x=1$ are boundary points of $S{:}$\n\n- The point $x=0$ is a boundary point because *every* open neighborhood contains points that belong to $S$ and points that do not belong to $S.$\n\n- The point $x=1$ is a boundary point because *every* open neighborhood contains points that belong to $S$ and points that do not belong to $S.$\n\nThe set of all boundary points of a set $S$ is called the **boundary** of $S,$ and is denoted as $\\partial S.$\n\nFor the set $[0,1)$ above, its boundary contains two points only, namely $x=0$ and $x=1,$ and we write\n\n$$\n\\partial S = \\{0,1\\}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid The coordinates of $P(\\sqrt{2},1)$ satisfy the equation $\\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}=1.$ Hence, $P$ lies in the set $∂B,$ the boundary of $B.$\n\n- Statement II is false. The coordinates of $P(\\sqrt{2},1)$ do not satisfy the inequality $\\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}<1.$ Hence, $P$ does not belongs to $B.$\n\n- Statement III is true. :tutorial/content "If an $n\\!\\times \\!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.\n\nFor example, consider the matrix $A$ given below:\n\n![](images/6b/6bb8b64f7ed8730e641cdf88fc6fe7add40bc15061095c6b1f57c1b764b28feb.svg)\n\nThe second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\\ast$) may represent any number.\n\nLet's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-1)^{2+1}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+2}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+3}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =0+0+0 \\\\  & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero." :tutorial/id #uuid "cee0a552-60f2-5785-a506-63bd053364c7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6888 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b68428f5-f5bb-5090-b7f9-4971dc931914" :step/math-academy-id 41745 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134902}} {:db/id 17592186134902 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135152 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows but it has two identical rows:\n\n![](images/74/7477781b618ec384b1638d01707acf545e7d9882ffca5bbc0efde4e224b04308.svg)\n\nWe can subtract the $1$st row from the $3$rd row, as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 1\\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\\\  & ∼\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =B\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\\det(A) = \\det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\det(A) = \\det(B) = 0.\n$$\n\nNotice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:\n\n*If a square matrix has at least two identical rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "6813d49e-3908-5735-8196-8e1aad5a14e6" "Geometrically, the absolute value of an $n \\times n$ determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant. \n\nFor example:\n\n- Suppose the columns of a $3\\times 3$ matrix $A$ are ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{a}}, {\\color{black}\\mathbf{b}},$ and ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{c}}.$\n![](images/6e/6e046341b7a1b8f6760797f7db89a7e021a6ace6b5cdf28bd5217998cb450837.svg)\nThe $3$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $A$ is depicted below:\n\n![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)\n\nThe volume $V$ of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $A{:}$\n\n$$\nV = \\left|\\det(A)\\right|\n$$\n\n- Now suppose the columns of a $2\\times 2$ matrix $B$ are ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{p}}$ and ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{q}}.$\n![](images/f5/f593c123eb081da0399e74c665325774758b48c5f086a7475b959905e1de2763.svg)\nThe $2$-dimensional parallelepiped (i.e., the parallelogram) spanned by vectors $\\mathbf{p}$ and $\\mathbf{q}$ is shown below:\n\n![](images/4a/4af1971404b188df75bb3d62d47ac95340c5e1791066e5358370d743230baa45.png)\n\nThe two-dimensional volume $V$ (i.e., the area) of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $B{:}$\n\n$$\nV = \\left|\\det(B)\\right|\n$$\n\n- In general, the absolute value of the determinant of an $n\\times n$ matrix $M$ gives the $n$-dimensional volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $M.$\n\nIn this lesson, we studied the following property:\n\n*$\\det(A) = 0$ if and only if one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns of $A$.*\n\nWhat does this property mean in geometric terms?\n\nThe component $\\det(A) = 0$ implies that the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped formed by the columns of $A$ has zero volume. Conversely, when one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns, it indicates that the corresponding parallelepiped possesses at most $n-1$ distinct dimensions. \n\nConsider the following examples:\n\n- In the case of a $3$-dimensional parallelepiped, if the vector $\\mathbf{c}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\\mathbf{a}$ and $\\mathbf{b}$, then $\\mathbf{c}$ lies within the plane containing $\\mathbf{a}$ and $\\mathbf{b}$. In other words, the vectors $\\mathbf{a}$, $\\mathbf{b}$, and $\\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar. Consequently, we obtain a \"flat\" ($2$-dimensional) figure with a volume of $0$.\n\n- For the parallelogram example, if the vector $\\mathbf{q}$ is a linear combination of the vector $\\mathbf{p}$ (i.e., $\\mathbf{p}$ and $\\mathbf{q}$ are proportional), then $\\mathbf{q}$ resides on the line containing vector $\\mathbf{p}$. In other words, the vectors $\\mathbf{p}$ and $\\mathbf{q}$ are collinear. This results in a $1$-dimensional object with a $2$-dimensional volume (i.e., area) of $0$." :tutorial/id #uuid "1f7191c6-60ca-5c44-befc-8dbad7779b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6893 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of a Zero Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "8c5dbeea-b2e4-5fe9-9d8c-98750164b70c" :step/math-academy-id 41766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134907}}] :activity/title "Conditions When a Determinant Equals Zero" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134042} {:db/id 17592186134901 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135151 :tutorial/content "If an $n\\!\\times \\!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.\n\nFor example, consider the matrix $A$ given below:\n\n![](images/6b/6bb8b64f7ed8730e641cdf88fc6fe7add40bc15061095c6b1f57c1b764b28feb.svg)\n\nThe second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\\ast$) may represent any number.\n\nLet's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\\\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-1)^{2+1}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+2}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+3}(0)|\\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\\\ ∗ & ∗\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =0+0+0 \\\\  & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\\ast$). Reasons Why a Determinant Equals Zero"} :step/id #uuid "81571aa7-ce3d-5713-bf67-a49538fee0ef" :step/math-academy-id 41755} {:db/id 17592186135155 :tutorial/content "Geometrically, the absolute value of an $n \\times n$ determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant. \n\nFor example:\n\n- Suppose the columns of a $3\\times 3$ matrix $A$ are ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{a}}, {\\color{black}\\mathbf{b}},$ and ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{c}}.$\n![](images/6e/6e046341b7a1b8f6760797f7db89a7e021a6ace6b5cdf28bd5217998cb450837.svg)\nThe $3$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $A$ is depicted below:\n\n![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)\n\nThe volume $V$ of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $A{:}$\n\n$$\nV = \\left|\\det(A)\\right|\n$$\n\n- Now suppose the columns of a $2\\times 2$ matrix $B$ are ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{p}}$ and ${\\color{black}\\mathbf{q}}.$\n![](images/f5/f593c123eb081da0399e74c665325774758b48c5f086a7475b959905e1de2763.svg)\nThe $2$-dimensional parallelepiped (i.e., the parallelogram) spanned by vectors $\\mathbf{p}$ and $\\mathbf{q}$ is shown below:\n\n![](images/4a/4af1971404b188df75bb3d62d47ac95340c5e1791066e5358370d743230baa45.png)\n\nThe two-dimensional volume $V$ (i.e., the area) of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $B{:}$\n\n$$\nV = \\left|\\det(B)\\right|\n$$\n\n- In general, the absolute value of the determinant of an $n\\times n$ matrix $M$ gives the $n$-dimensional volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $M.$\n\nIn this lesson, we studied the following property:\n\n*$\\det(A) = 0$ if and only if one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns of $A$.*\n\nWhat does this property mean in geometric terms?\n\nThe component $\\det(A) = 0$ implies that the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped formed by the columns of $A$ has zero volume. Conversely, when one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns, it indicates that the corresponding parallelepiped possesses at most $n-1$ distinct dimensions. \n\nConsider the following examples:\n\n- In the case of a $3$-dimensional parallelepiped, if the vector $\\mathbf{c}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\\mathbf{a}$ and $\\mathbf{b}$, then $\\mathbf{c}$ lies within the plane containing $\\mathbf{a}$ and $\\mathbf{b}$. In other words, the vectors $\\mathbf{a}$, $\\mathbf{b}$, and $\\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar. Consequently, we obtain a \"flat\" ($2$-dimensional) figure with a volume of $0$.\n\n- For the parallelogram example, if the vector $\\mathbf{q}$ is a linear combination of the vector $\\mathbf{p}$ (i.e., $\\mathbf{p}$ and $\\mathbf{q}$ are proportional), then $\\mathbf{q}$ resides on the line containing vector $\\mathbf{p}$. In other words, the vectors $\\mathbf{p}$ and $\\mathbf{q}$ are collinear. This results in a $1$-dimensional object with a $2$-dimensional volume (i.e., area) of $0$." :tutorial/id #uuid "1f7191c6-60ca-5c44-befc-8dbad7779b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6893 :tutorial/title :question/math-academy-id "q-43307" :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $3\\times 3$ matrix such that $|A|=0.$ Which of the following statements must be true?\n\nSelect all that apply.\n\n- **I.** $A$ has statements in turn.\n\n- Statements I and II are false. For example, consider the matrix \n\n$$\nA=\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 2 & 3\\end{bmatrix}.\n$$\n\nExpending across the $1$st column, we have that \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}|A| & =1\\cdot \\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\\\ 2 & 3\\end{vmatrix}+1\\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{vmatrix} \\\\  & =(3-2)+(1-2) \\\\  & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nbut $A$ has neither a zero column nor two proportional rows.\n\n- Statement III is true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:\n\n$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is matrices. \n\nRemember, $\\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$ if $A\\mathbf{v} = \\lambda\\mathbf{v}$ for some non-zero vector $\\mathbf{v}$. This implies that the equation\n\n$$\n(A-\\lambda I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}\n$$\n\nhas a non-trivial solution, which means that the matrix $A-\\lambda I$ is singular, and consequently\n$\\textrm{det}(A-\\lambda I)=0.$\nTherefore, if we want to find the eigenvalues of a $n\\!\\times\\! n$ matrix $A,$ we have to find the solutions of the characteristic equation\n\n$$\n\\textrm{det}(A-\\lambda I)=0.\n$$\n\nLet's go through this process in the case of the matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/21/21e0994519fbba32a84020ce4661e98600c1307947083ddc3afe9902658143c1.svg)\n\nFirst, we write down the matrix $A-\\lambda I{:}$\n\n﻿﻿﻿\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}A-\\lambda I & =\\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -8 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 5\\end{bmatrix}-\\begin{bmatrix}\\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & \\lambda  & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & \\lambda \\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}-2-\\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -8-\\lambda  & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 5-\\lambda \\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we set and solve the characteristic equation $\\,\\textrm{det}(A-\\lambda I)=0.$ Using the fact that the determinant of a triangular (or diagonal) matrix is given by the product of the elements on the main diagonal, we get the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}det(A-\\lambda I) & =0 \\\\ \\begin{vmatrix}-2-\\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -8-\\lambda  & 0 \\\\ 0 & 0 & 5-\\lambda \\end{vmatrix} & =0 \\\\ (-2-\\lambda )(-8-\\lambda )(5-\\lambda ) & =0 \\\\ (\\lambda +2)(\\lambda +8)(\\lambda -5) & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\\lambda=-2,$ $\\lambda=-8,$ and $\\lambda=5.$" :tutorial/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186121027 :tutorial/content "**Cramer's Rule** is a method for solving a linear system of equations using determinants.\n\nSuppose we have a square system of linear equations\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}{a}_{11}x+{a}_{12}y &={b}_{1} \\\\ {a}_{21}x+{a}_{22}y &={b}_{2},\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nwhere ![](images/c7/c7ef883a1d4dd8c1fc0fc8fbde5ed80c9a5229650fc77c77559b71552370c35b.svg) Then Cramer's rule states that\n\n$$\nx =  \\dfrac{D_x}{D}, \\qquad y = \\dfrac{D_y}{D}\n$$\n\nis the unique solution of the system, where\n![](images/b1/b13ecd10395fe0977d04d627179667cbca207fcf4015a89d43df0e69765f1f5e.svg)\n\nFor example, let's use Cramer's rule to solve the following system of equations:\n\n$$\n\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}3x-2y &=-1 \\\\ -1x+2y &=3\\end{aligned}\\right.\n$$\n\nWe start by finding the **determinant of the coefficient matrix**:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}D & =|\\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\\\ -1 & 2\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =3\\cdot 2-(-1)\\cdot (-2) \\\\  & =4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we compute $D_x$ and $D_y\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\\\ 3 & 2\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =(-1)\\cdot 2-3\\cdot (-2) \\\\  & =4 \\\\ {D}_{y} & =|\\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\\\ -1 & 3\\end{aligned}| \\\\  & =3\\cdot 3-(-1)\\cdot (-1) \\\\  & =8\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, the solution to the system is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x & =\\frac{{D}_{x}}{D}=\\frac{4}{4}=1, \\\\ y & =\\frac{{D}_{y}}{D}=\\frac{8}{4}=2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIt is common to write the solutions to a linear system as a vector. So, in this case, we have\n\n$$\n\\left< x,y \\right> = \\left< 1,2 \\right>.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3adc5c1c-58e5-5c0a-a8f7-da6abd6f06e2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3102 :tutorial/title the Newton-Raphson process starting from the point $x_0 = 1.$ Round your answer to three decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The formula for the Newton-Raphson method is\n\n$$\nx_{n+1} = x_n - \\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\n$$\n\nwhere $f'(x_n)$ is the derivative of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n.$\n\nIn our case, we have\n\n$$\nf'(x) = (5^{2x}-20)' = 2\\ln (5)\\cdot 5^{2x}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\\frac{{5}^{2{x}_{n}}-20}{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\\cdot {5}^{2{x}_{n}}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nStarting with $x_0 = 1,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-\\frac{{5}^{2{x}_{0}}-20}{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\\cdot {5}^{2{x}_{0}}}. \\\\  & =1-\\frac{{5}^{2}-20}{2\\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)\\cdot {5}^{2}}. \\\\  & case, we have\n\n$$\nf'(x) = (e^x-x^3-3)' = e^x-3x^2.\n$$\n\nTherefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\\frac{{e}^{{x}_{n}}-{x}_{n}^{3}-3}{{e}^{{x}_{n}}-3{x}_{n}^{2}}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nStarting with $x_0 = 5,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-\\frac{{e}^{{x}_{0}}-{x}_{0}^{3}-3}{{e}^{{x}_{0}}-3{x}_{0}^{2}} \\\\  & =5-\\frac{{e}^{5}-{5}^{3}-3}{{e}^{5}-3(5)^{2}} \\\\  & =4.721\\,941…\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFor the second iteration, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-\\frac{{e}^{{x}_{1}}-{x}_{1}^{3}-3}{{e}^{{x}_{1}}-3{x}_{1}^{2}} \\\\  & =(4.721\\,941…)-\\frac{{e}^{4.721\\,941…}-(4.721\\,941…)^{3}-3}{{e}^{4.721\\,941…}-3(4.721\\,941…)^{2}} \\\\  & ≈4.632,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nrounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186092658 Round your final answer to two decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The formula for the Newton-Raphson method is\n\n$$\nx_{n+1} = x_n - \\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\n$$\n\nwhere $f'(x_n)$ is the derivative of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n.$\n\nIn our case, we have\n\n$$\nf'(x) = (x^5-2)' = 5x^4.\n$$\n\nTherefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\\frac{{x}_{n}^{5}-2}{5{x}_{n}^{4}} \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}_{n}(5{x}_{n}^{4})-({x}_{n}^{5}-2)}{5{x}_{n}^{4}} \\\\  & =\\frac{4{x}_{n}^{5}+2}{5{x}_{n}^{4}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nStarting with $x_0 = 1,$ we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\\frac{4{x}_{0}^{5}+2}{5{x}_{0}^{4}} \\\\  & =\\frac{4(1)^{5}+2}{5(1)^{4}} \\\\  & =\\frac{6}{5} \\\\  & =1.2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimilarly, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\\frac{4{x}_{1}^{5}+2}{5{x}_{1}^{4}} \\\\  & =\\frac{4(1.2)^{5}+2}{5(1.2)^{4}} \\\\  & =1.152… \\\\ {x}_{3} & =\\frac{4{x}_{2}^{5}+2}{5{x}_{2}^{4}} \\\\  & =\\frac{4(1.152…)^{5}+2}{5(1.152…)^{4}} \\\\  & =1.148….\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that the last two approximations $x_2 \\approx 1.15$ and $x_3 \\approx 1.15$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.\n\nTherefore, the root of the function is $x \\approx 1.15,$ rounded to two decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186092660 :question/id #uuid "d82ea011-ddd7-5eaf-8739-fbc1e56a9b6f" [{:db/id 17592186093302 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093491 :tutorial/content "In many problems, we are interested in finding the **roots** of functions, that is, solving equations of the form\n\n$$\nf(x) = 0.\n$$\n\nSometimes, this can be done **analytically**. For example, to find the roots of $f(x) = x^2 - 1$, we solve the equation\n\n$$\nx^2 - 1 = 0,\n$$\n\nwhich gives the exact solutions $x = \\pm 1.$\n\nHowever, in many cases, finding the roots analytically is either too difficult or simply not possible. For example, the roots of the function\n\n$$\nf(x) = x^2 + x \\sin{x} - 1\n$$\n\ncannot be found using standard algebraic techniques. When that happens, we turn to methods that provide good approximations rather than exact answers.\n\nIn the next slide, we will look at an example of how to apply such a method to this function." :tutorial/id #uuid "71728479-0258-589a-8972-828adf2b2ea0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7535 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "72821eb7-cd78-568d-9f90-3bbd6e3839d7" :step/math-academy-id 593950 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093303}} {:db/id 17592186093303 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093374 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we’ll learn how **Newton’s method** (also known as the **Newton–Raphson method**) constructs such an approximation step by step. Our focus will be on the single-variable case, where the goal is to find a real number $x$ such that $f(x) = 0$.\n\nTo apply Newton’s method, we begin by choosing an initial guess for the root, which we’ll denote by $x_0$. This guess might come from intuition or a rough sketch of the graph.\n\nBelow, we see the graph of $f(x)$ along with the initial guess $x_0$.\n\n![](images/e2/e2d794aa00d7b0d84a70344c89872aa48736182ff6dbf334d1201c0451c215b6.png)\n\nThe idea is to simplify the problem by replacing the curve with a straight line near our guess.\nRecall that the equation of the tangent line $y = F(x)$ to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $x = x_0$ is\n\n$$\nF(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0).\n$$\n\nSince $F(x)$ closely approximates $f(x)$ near $x_0$, we solve the simpler linear equation $F(x) = 0$ instead of the original nonlinear equation $f(x) = 0$. This gives us a new estimate for the root that is easier to compute.\n\nTo find where this tangent intersects the $x$-axis, we set $F(x) = 0{:}$\n\n$$\n0 = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0)\n$$\n\nNext, we isolate the term $x,$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}({x}_{0})(x-{x}_{0}) & =-f({x}_{0}) \\\\ x-{x}_{0} & =-\\frac{f({x}_{0})}{{f}^{'}({x}_{0})} \\\\ x & ={x}_{0}-\\frac{f({x}_{0})}{{f}^{'}({x}_{0})}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis new value becomes our next guess, which we call $x_1$. So, we write\n\n$$\nx_1 = x_0 - \\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}.\n$$\n\nIn the figure below, the dashed line is the tangent at $x_0$. We follow it down to the $x$-axis to find our next guess, $x_1$.\n\n![](images/8e/8e19765a4f180f1acc95c6460fb63b95ca9c4af811d13a3035d4e66ba26471a1.png)\n\nTo keep improving our estimate, we now repeat the same process, this time starting from $x_1$ instead of $x_0$. Applying the same idea gives the next guess\n\n$$\nx_2 = x_1 - \\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)}\n$$\n\nas shown below.\n\n![](images/e7/e789ff357b039591d7bb00d05e48456f3e11ea172b9f04723a670101c1a1c15a.png)\n\nContinuing this process, we generate a sequence of values \n\n$$\nx_0, \\quad\nx_1, \\quad\nx_2, \\quad\nx_3, \n\\dots\n$$\n\n \nthat, under suitable conditions, converges to a root of $f(x)$.\nAt each step, the next approximation is computed using the update rule\n\n$$\nx_{n+1} = x_n - \\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.\n$$\n\nIn practice, we stop iterating when the change between consecutive guesses is very small, meaning we’re close enough to the actual root for our purposes." :tutorial/id #uuid "667de2d9-42aa-5db9-94b4-145c571f13e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13225 :tutorial/title "Newton's Method"} :step/id #uuid "b728d6c4-abd9-5e4a-9057-13f1a6631ed5" :step/math-academy-id 593951 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093304}} {:db/id 17592186093304 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093371 :tutorial/content "Suppose we know that the function\n\n$$\nf(x) = 0.1 x^2 - 3\n$$\n\nhas a root somewhere in the interval $[5, 6]$, and we want to use Newton’s method to estimate that root.\n\nWhile the root of $f(x)$ can be found analytically, we’ll apply Newton’s method to see how well it approximates the root after a few steps.\n\nThe formula for the Newton-Raphson method is\n\n$$\nx_{n+1} = x_n - \\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\n$$\n\nwhere $f'(x_n)$ is the derivative of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n.$\n\nIn our case, we have\n\n$$\nf'(x) = (0.1 x^2-3)' = 0.2 x\n$$\n\nTherefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\\frac{0.1{x}_{n}^{2}-3}{0.2{x}_{n}} \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}_{n}(0.2{x}_{n})-(0.1{x}_{n}^{2}-3)}{0.2{x}_{n}} \\\\  & =\\frac{0.1{x}_{n}^{2}+3}{0.2{x}_{n}} \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}_{n}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{n}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe take $x_0 = 5$ as our initial guess, since it falls within the interval where the root is located:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\\frac{{x}_{0}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{0}} \\\\  & =\\frac{{5}^{2}+30}{2\\cdot 5} \\\\  & =5.5.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimilarly, we have the following updates:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{1}} \\\\  & =\\frac{(5.5)^{2}+30}{2(5.5)} \\\\  & =5.477\\,272… \\\\ {x}_{3} & =\\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{2}} \\\\  & =\\frac{(5.477\\,272…)^{2}+30}{2(5.477\\,272…)} \\\\  & =5.477\\,225…\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that the last two approximations $x_2 \\approx 5.477$ and $x_3 \\approx 5.477$ are the same when rounded to three decimal places.\n\nTherefore, we can take for the root of the function the value $x \\approx 5.477,$ rounded to three decimal places. The actual root is $x = \\sqrt{30} = 5.477\\,225 \\ldots,$ which is pretty close to our result just after $3$ iterations." :tutorial/id #uuid "3d1426e8-8d76-5c5c-8957-2ea9bc0606cb" :step/next {:db/id 17592186093308}} {:db/id 17592186093308 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093373 :tutorial/content "Now that we’ve seen how Newton’s method works in practice, it’s important to understand the conditions under which it actually succeeds. While the method can converge very quickly, it doesn’t always work as expected.\n\nFor Newton’s method to work reliably, a few key conditions need to be met:\n\n- The derivative $f'(x_n)$ must not be zero or close to zero.  \n\nIf the slope is flat, the tangent line becomes nearly horizontal, and the update step can either move very little or jump far in the wrong direction. In the figure below, we can see this effect in action. \n\nOur initial guess $x_1$ happens to lie in a region where the slope of the function is close to zero. If we follow the tangent line from that point to where it intersects the $x$-axis, the resulting guess $x_2$ ends up farther from the actual root than where we started ($d_1 < d_2$). This illustrates how a poor initial guess can lead Newton’s method in the wrong direction.\n\n![](images/8c/8cdfdcec6f1eab45635dd78e2b7ed567dca82dd4edc0fb65c0ad56e8678b6349.png)\n\n- The initial guess must be reasonably close to the root.  \n\nNewton’s method relies on local linear approximation. If the guess is too far from the root, the tangent might not reflect the behavior of the function in the right region.\n\n- The function must be smooth near the root.  \n\nSharp corners, discontinuities, or erratic changes in slope can break the assumptions behind the method. In such cases, the tangent might not be a good approximation even near the root.\n\nIf any of these conditions fail, Newton’s method can behave unpredictably. It may diverge entirely, bounce back and forth between values without settling down, converge to the wrong root, or get stuck in a region where the derivative is nearly zero and the update steps become ineffective." :tutorial/id #uuid "c3f1ef50-2c0c-5951-bcec-a03e3606ccc9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13124 :tutorial/title "Limitations of Newton’s Method"} :step/id #uuid "65b743ce-75a0-58a3-bafa-87a7d05ef58c" :step/math-academy-id 593963}] :activity/title "The Newton-Raphson Method" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186092418} {:db/id 17592186093302 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093491 :tutorial/content "In many problems, we are interested in finding the **roots** of functions, that is, solving equations of the form\n\n$$\nf(x) = 0.\n$$\n\nSometimes, this can be done **analytically**.
