This guess might come from intuition or a rough sketch of the graph.\n\nBelow, we see the graph of $f(x)$ along with the initial guess $x_0$.\n\n![](images/e2/e2d794aa00d7b0d84a70344c89872aa48736182ff6dbf334d1201c0451c215b6.png)\n\nThe idea is to simplify the problem by replacing the curve with a straight line near our guess.\nRecall that the equation of the tangent line $y = F(x)$ to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $x = x_0$ is\n\n$$\nF(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0).\n$$\n\nSince $F(x)$ closely approximates $f(x)$ near $x_0$, we solve the simpler linear equation $F(x) = 0$ instead of the original nonlinear equation $f(x) = 0$. This gives us a new estimate for the root that is easier to compute.\n\nTo find where this tangent intersects the $x$-axis, we set $F(x) = 0{:}$\n\n$$\n0 = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0)\n$$\n\nNext, we isolate the term $x,$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}({x}_{0})(x-{x}_{0}) & =-f({x}_{0}) \\\\ x-{x}_{0} & =-\\frac{f({x}_{0})}{{f}^{'}({x}_{0})} \\\\ x & ={x}_{0}-\\frac{f({x}_{0})}{{f}^{'}({x}_{0})}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThis new value becomes our next guess, which we call $x_1$. So, we write\n\n$$\nx_1 = x_0 - \\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}.\n$$\n\nIn the figure below, the dashed line is the tangent at $x_0$. We follow it down to the $x$-axis to find our next guess, $x_1$.\n\n![](images/8e/8e19765a4f180f1acc95c6460fb63b95ca9c4af811d13a3035d4e66ba26471a1.png)\n\nTo keep improving our estimate, we now repeat the same process, this time starting from $x_1$ instead of $x_0$. Applying the same idea gives the next guess\n\n$$\nx_2 = x_1 - \\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)}\n$$\n\nas shown below.\n\n![](images/e7/e789ff357b039591d7bb00d05e48456f3e11ea172b9f04723a670101c1a1c15a.png)\n\nContinuing this process, we generate a sequence of values \n\n$$\nx_0, \\quad\nx_1, \\quad\nx_2, \\quad\nx_3, \n\\dots\n$$\n\n \nthat, under suitable conditions, converges to a root of $f(x)$.\nAt each step, the next approximation is computed using the update rule\n\n$$\nx_{n+1} = x_n - \\frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.\n$$\n\nIn practice, we stop iterating when the change between consecutive guesses is very small, meaning we’re close enough to the actual root for our purposes." :tutorial/id #uuid "667de2d9-42aa-5db9-94b4-145c571f13e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13225 :tutorial/title "Newton's Method"} :step/id #uuid "b728d6c4-abd9-5e4a-9057-13f1a6631ed5" :step/math-academy-id 593951 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093304}} {:db/id 17592186093374 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we’ll learn how **Newton’s method** (also known as the **Newton–Raphson method**) constructs such an approximation step by step. 3\n$$\n\nhas a root somewhere in the interval $[5, 6]$, and we want to use Newton’s method to estimate that root.\n\nWhile the root of $f(x)$ can be found analytically, we’ll apply Newton’s method to see how well it approximates the root after a few steps.\n\nThe formula for the Newton-Raphson method is\n\n$$\nx_{n+1} = x_n - \\dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\n$$\n\nwhere $f'(x_n)$ is the derivative of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n.$\n\nIn our case, we have\n\n$$\nf'(x) = (0.1 x^2-3)' = 0.2 x\n$$\n\nTherefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\\frac{0.1{x}_{n}^{2}-3}{0.2{x}_{n}} \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}_{n}(0.2{x}_{n})-(0.1{x}_{n}^{2}-3)}{0.2{x}_{n}} \\\\  & =\\frac{0.1{x}_{n}^{2}+3}{0.2{x}_{n}} \\\\  & =\\frac{{x}_{n}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{n}}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe take $x_0 = 5$ as our initial guess, since it falls within the interval where the root is located:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\\frac{{x}_{0}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{0}} \\\\  & =\\frac{{5}^{2}+30}{2\\cdot 5} \\\\  & =5.5.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimilarly, we have the following updates:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{1}} \\\\  & =\\frac{(5.5)^{2}+30}{2(5.5)} \\\\  & =5.477\\,272… \\\\ {x}_{3} & =\\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}+30}{2{x}_{2}} \\\\  & =\\frac{(5.477\\,272…)^{2}+30}{2(5.477\\,272…)} \\\\  & =5.477\\,225…\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that the last two approximations $x_2 \\approx 5.477$ and $x_3 \\approx 5.477$ are the same when rounded to three decimal places.\n\nTherefore, we can take for the root of the function the value $x \\approx 5.477,$ rounded to three decimal places. The actual root is $x = \\sqrt{30} = 5.477\\,225 \\ldots,$ which is pretty close to our result just after $3$ iterations." :tutorial/id #uuid "3d1426e8-8d76-5c5c-8957-2ea9bc0606cb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 12764 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "28d8b753-9c24-5632-b4cf-26ab877d1b09" :step/math-academy-id 593952 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093305}} {:db/id 17592186093371 :tutorial/content "Suppose we know that the function\n\n$$\nf(x) = 0.1 x^2 - seen how Newton’s method works in practice, it’s important to understand the conditions under which it actually succeeds. While the method can converge very quickly, it doesn’t always work as expected.\n\nFor Newton’s method to work reliably, a few key conditions need to be met:\n\n- The derivative $f'(x_n)$ must not be zero or close to zero.  \n\nIf the slope is flat, the tangent line becomes nearly horizontal, and the update step can either move very little or jump far in the wrong direction. In the figure below, we can see this effect in action. \n\nOur initial guess $x_1$ happens to lie in a region where the slope of the function is close to zero. If we follow the tangent line from that point to where it intersects the $x$-axis, the resulting guess $x_2$ ends up farther from the actual root than where we started ($d_1 < d_2$). This illustrates how a poor initial guess can lead Newton’s method in the wrong direction.\n\n![](images/8c/8cdfdcec6f1eab45635dd78e2b7ed567dca82dd4edc0fb65c0ad56e8678b6349.png)\n\n- The initial guess must be reasonably close to the root.  \n\nNewton’s method relies on local linear approximation. If the guess is too far from the root, the tangent might not reflect the behavior of the function in the right region.\n\n- The function must be smooth near the root.  \n\nSharp corners, discontinuities, or erratic changes in slope can break the assumptions behind the method. In such cases, the tangent might not be a good approximation even near the root.\n\nIf any of these conditions fail, Newton’s method can behave unpredictably. It may diverge entirely, bounce back and forth between values without settling down, converge to the wrong root, or get stuck in a region where the derivative is nearly zero and the update steps become ineffective." :tutorial/id #uuid "c3f1ef50-2c0c-5951-bcec-a03e3606ccc9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13124 :tutorial/title "Limitations of Newton’s Method"} :step/id #uuid "65b743ce-75a0-58a3-bafa-87a7d05ef58c" :step/math-academy-id 593963} {:db/id 17592186093373 :tutorial/content "Now that we’ve seen how Newton’s method works in practice, it’s important to understand the conditions under which it actually succeeds. :topic/math-academy-id 427} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069669 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069974 :tutorial/content "The long division method allows us to divide a polynomial by another nonlinear polynomial.\n\nFor example, suppose we want to find the quotient and remainder of the following division problem:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{-4x^3+4x^2+x+4}{4x^2-1}\n$$\n\nHere, the divisor is the quadratic polynomial $4x^2-1$. \n\nAgain, we follow a step-by-step process.\n\n**Step 1**\n\nWe start by writing the dividend and the divisor as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**\n\nWe divide the leading term of the dividend $({\\color{red}{-4x^3}})$ by the leading term of the divisor $({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}).$ This gives $\\left(\\dfrac{\\color{red}{-4x^3}}{{\\color{blue}{4x^2}}}\\right)={\\color{#8b008b}{-x}}.$ We add this result to the quotient line:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we multiply the $\\color{#8b008b}-x$ we just found by the full divisor ${\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1.$ This gives ${\\color{#8b008b}-x}({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1)=-4x^3+x.$ We place this underneath the dividend, being sure to match the terms. Notice that we include a zero coefficient for the $x^2$ term.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we subtract $-4x^3+0x^2+x$ from $-4x^3+4x^2+x+4$ and get $4x^2+0x+4\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**\n\nWe now repeat the process. The new dividend is ${\\color{red}{4x^2}}+0x+4.$\n\nWe divide the leading term of the dividend $({\\color{red}{4x^2}})$ by the leading term of the divisor $({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}).$ This gives $\\left(\\dfrac{{\\color{red}{4x^2}}}{{\\color{blue}{4x^2}}}\\right)={\\color{#8b008b}{1}}.$ We  add this result to the quotient:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x+1 \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we multiply the ${\\color{#8b008b}{1}}$ we just found by the full divisor ${\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1.$ This gives ${\\color{#8b008b}{1}}({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1)=4x^2-1.$ We place this result underneath the dividend:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x+1 \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4 \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{4{x}^{2}+0x-1}_{―}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we subtract $4x^2+0x-1$ from $4x^2+0x+4$ to get ${\\color{red}{5}}\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x+1 \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4 \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{4{x}^{2}+0x-1}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,5\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe're left with the constant $\\color{red}5$, which has a smaller degree than the divisor. So, the division is complete.\n\nTherefore, we conclude that\n\n- the quotient of the polynomial division is ${\\color{blue}{-x+1}},$ and\n\n- the remainder is ${\\color{red}{5}}.$\n\nOur complete result can be summarized as follows:\n\n$$\n\\frac{-4x^3+4x^2+x+4}{4x^2-1}={\\color{blue}{-x+1}} + \\dfrac{\\color{red}5}{4x^2-1}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65b9f3fa-d1aa-5799-bc53-d2a843778980" Notice that we include a zero coefficient for the $x^2$ term.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we subtract $-4x^3+0x^2+x$ from $-4x^3+4x^2+x+4$ and get $4x^2+0x+4\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 3**\n\nWe now repeat the process. The new dividend is ${\\color{red}{4x^2}}+0x+4.$\n\nWe divide the leading term of the dividend $({\\color{red}{4x^2}})$ by the leading term of the divisor $({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}).$ This gives $\\left(\\dfrac{{\\color{red}{4x^2}}}{{\\color{blue}{4x^2}}}\\right)={\\color{#8b008b}{1}}.$ We  add this result to the quotient:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x+1 \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we multiply the ${\\color{#8b008b}{1}}$ we just found by the full divisor ${\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1.$ This gives ${\\color{#8b008b}{1}}({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1)=4x^2-1.$ We place this result underneath the dividend:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x+1 \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4 \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{4{x}^{2}+0x-1}_{―}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we subtract $4x^2+0x-1$ from $4x^2+0x+4$ to get ${\\color{red}{5}}\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x+1 \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{-\\,4{x}^{3}+0{x}^{2}+x}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,4{x}^{2}+0x+4 \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,{4{x}^{2}+0x-1}_{―} \\\\  & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,5\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe're left with the constant $\\color{red}5$, which has a smaller degree than the divisor. So, the division is complete.\n\nTherefore, we conclude that\n\n- the quotient of the polynomial division is ${\\color{blue}{-x+1}},$ and\n\n- the remainder is ${\\color{red}{5}}.$\n\nOur complete result can be summarized as follows:\n\n$$\n\\frac{-4x^3+4x^2+x+4}{4x^2-1}={\\color{blue}{-x+1}} + \\dfrac{\\color{red}5}{4x^2-1}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "65b9f3fa-d1aa-5799-bc53-d2a843778980" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3382 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "44a9504c-2712-520b-9afa-31a3bf6cea61" :step/math-academy-id 18896 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069670}} {:db/id 17592186069974 :tutorial/content "The long division method allows us to divide a polynomial by another nonlinear polynomial.\n\nFor example, suppose we want to find the quotient and remainder of the following division problem:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{-4x^3+4x^2+x+4}{4x^2-1}\n$$\n\nHere, the divisor is the quadratic polynomial $4x^2-1$. \n\nAgain, we follow a step-by-step process.\n\n**Step 1**\n\nWe start by writing the dividend and the divisor as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Step 2**\n\nWe divide the leading term of the dividend $({\\color{red}{-4x^3}})$ by the leading term of the divisor $({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}).$ This gives $\\left(\\dfrac{\\color{red}{-4x^3}}{{\\color{blue}{4x^2}}}\\right)={\\color{#8b008b}{-x}}.$ We add this result to the quotient line:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned} & \\,\\,\\,\\,\\,-x \\\\  & 4{x}^{2}-1\\,\\enclose{longdiv}{\\,\\,-\\,4{x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}+\\phantom{0}x+4\\,\\,}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNext, we multiply the $\\color{#8b008b}-x$ we just found by the full divisor ${\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1.$ This gives ${\\color{#8b008b}-x}({\\color{blue}{4x^2}}-1)=-4x^3+x.$ We place this underneath the dividend, being sure to match the terms. :topic/math-academy-id 1177} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186101757 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101918 :tutorial/content "We'll now give some intuition regarding why the second-degree coefficient in the second-order Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ is $\\dfrac12f''(a).$\n\nFirst, recall that the first-degree Taylor polynomial (linear approximation) about $x=a$ is given by\n\n$$\nP_1(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a).\n$$\n\nThis approximates the function $f(x)$ using a straight line. So, if we want to approximate $f(x)$ using a quadratic curve, we need an additional quadratic term:\n\n$$\nP_2(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + k(x-a)^2\n$$\n\nwhere $k$ is to be determined. Note: \n\n- We've chosen $(x-a)^2$ as the variable part of our quadratic term (not just $x^2$).\n\n- By doing this, the approximation $P_2(x)$ is *exact* at the point $x=a,$ because\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(a) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(a-a)+k(a-a)^{2} \\\\  & =f(a)+0+0 \\\\  & =f(a).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nOur task now is to find the coefficient $k.$\n\nLet's assume $x$ is sufficiently close to $a.$ Then, $P_2(x)$ gives a good approximation of $f(x){:}$\n\n$$\nf(x) \\approx P_2(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + k(x-a)^2\n$$\n\n \nDifferentiating once, we get\n\n$$\nf'(x) \\approx f'(a) + 2k(x-a).\n$$\n\n \nDifferentiating again, we get\n\n$$\nf''(x) \\approx 2k.\n$$\n\n \nThus, we have that\n\n$$\nk\\approx \\dfrac12 f''(x).\n$$\n\nWe're approximating $f(x)$ in the vicinity of $x=a$ using a quadratic curve. For any quadratic curve, the second derivative is constant. Thus, we can approximate $f''(x)$ by its value at $x=a.$ Thus:\n\n$$\nk\\approx \\dfrac12 f''(a).\n$$\n\nFinally, we have\n\n$$\nf(x) \\approx P_2(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \\dfrac12 f''(a)(x-a)^2\n$$\n\nas required." :tutorial/id #uuid "ba95c570-dcd4-5b69-a3af-11edd8515abb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10949 :tutorial/title "Justification for the Second Term"} :step/id #uuid "8f0f9e05-b472-5ffd-8cc6-97dffafb967d" :step/math-academy-id 230993} {:db/id 17592186101769 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101922 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can approximate a function $f(x)$ around the point $x=a$ using a linear approximation $L(x)\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\nf(x)\\approx L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a).\n$$\n\nThis approximates the function $f(x)$ using a straight line. But we can do even better! We can approximate $f(x)$ using a quadratic curve instead.\n\nThe quadratic approximation is called the **second-degree Taylor polynomial** $P_2(x),$ and is given by\n\n$$\nP_2(x) =  \\underbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}_{\\text{linear approximation}} + \\underbrace{\\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\\textrm{new quadratic term}}.\n$$\n\nNotice that we added another term to the linear approximation to get the second-degree Taylor polynomial. This new term is called the ** second-degree term** of the Taylor polynomial. \n\nThe *coefficient* of the second-degree term is $\\dfrac 1 2 f''(a).$ We'll discuss why the second-degree term is of this form at the end of the lesson.\n\nIn general, $P_2(x)$ is a more accurate estimate of the function $f(x)$ compared with $L(x),$ provided that $x$ is close to the value of $a.$\n\n**Note:** The phrase \"Taylor polynomial\" refers to a polynomial that's used to approximate a function. So, if we want to approximate $f(x)$ using a quadratic curve, we need an additional quadratic term:\n\n$$\nP_2(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + k(x-a)^2\n$$\n\nwhere $k$ is to be determined. Note: \n\n- We've chosen $(x-a)^2$ as the variable part of our quadratic term (not just $x^2$).\n\n- By doing this, the approximation $P_2(x)$ is *exact* at the point $x=a,$ because\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(a) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(a-a)+k(a-a)^{2} \\\\  & =f(a)+0+0 \\\\  & =f(a).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nOur task now is to find the coefficient $k.$\n\nLet's assume $x$ is sufficiently close to $a.$ Then, $P_2(x)$ gives a good approximation of $f(x){:}$\n\n$$\nf(x) \\approx P_2(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + k(x-a)^2\n$$\n\n \nDifferentiating once, we get\n\n$$\nf'(x) \\approx f'(a) + 2k(x-a).\n$$\n\n \nDifferentiating again, we get\n\n$$\nf''(x) \\approx 2k.\n$$\n\n \nThus, we have that\n\n$$\nk\\approx \\dfrac12 f''(x).\n$$\n\nWe're approximating $f(x)$ in the vicinity of $x=a$ using a quadratic curve. For any quadratic curve, the second derivative is constant. =f(\\frac{1}{6})+{f}^{′}(\\frac{1}{6})(x-\\frac{1}{6})+\\frac{{f}^{″}(\\frac{1}{6})}{2}{(x-\\frac{1}{6})}^{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe coefficient of ${(x-\\frac{1}{6})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is \n\n$$\n\\frac{{f}^{″}(\\frac{1}{6})}{2}.\n$$\n\nTo find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\pi x) \\\\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\\pi \\operatorname{cos}⁡(\\pi x) \\\\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-{\\pi }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\pi x)\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\\frac{1}{6}.$ This gives\n\n$$\n{f}^{″}(\\frac{1}{6})=-{\\pi }^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(\\frac{\\pi }{6})=-{\\pi }^{2}\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}=-\\frac{{\\pi }^{2}}{2}.\n$$\n\nFinally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\\frac{1}{6})}^{2},$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{f}^{″}(\\frac{1}{6})}{2} & =\\frac{(-\\frac{{\\pi }^{2}}{2})}{2}=-\\frac{{\\pi }^{2}}{4}\\end{aligned}\n$$"} That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s.\n$$\n\n- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$\n\nNote that $F(x,y)=x\\,i-y\\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=-y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\\,\\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's consider each statement.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=1+(-1)=0.\n$$\n\n- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.\n\n- Statement III is false. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s.\n$$\n\n- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$\n\nFirst, notice that\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x)+\\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-2y)=2-2=0,\n$$\n\nwhich shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.\n\nSince $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot {n}_{1}\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot {n}_{2}\\,\\text{d}s,\n$$\n\nwhere ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/51/5186fb872f03e73124d04c2e9ff07e77fb336bef121484a9ff1b697ea0cf8bcd.png)\n\nNotice that both }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot {n}_{2}\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\\,\\text{d}y-Q\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nTo apply the formula,\n\n- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\\in [a,b],$ and\n\n- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$\n\nWe have the parametrization\n\n$$\nr(t)=(1-2t)\\,i+(1-2t)\\,j,\\,t\\in [0,1].\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2x=2(1-2t)=2-4t, \\\\ Q(x,y) & =3-2y=3-2(1-2t)=1+4t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t} & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t} & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe evaluate the flux integral as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot {n}_{2}\\,\\text{d}s & ={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\\,\\text{d}y-Q\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}(P\\cdot \\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t}-Q\\cdot \\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}(2-4t)\\cdot (-2)-(1+4t)\\cdot (-2)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-2{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2-4t)-(1+4t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-2{\\int }_{0}^{1}1-8t\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot {[t-4{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot (1-4) \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot (-3) \\\\  & =6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we conclude that\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot {n}_{1}\\,\\text{d}s=6.\n$$"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186199478 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\\mathbf F,$ given by\n\n$$\n\\mathbf F(x,y)= P(x,y)\\,\\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y)\\,\\mathbf{j}\n$$\n\nwhich is defined on an open set $D\\subseteq \\mathbb R^2.$ Recall that a function $\\psi(x,y)$ is said to be a **stream function** of $\\mathbf F$ if it satisfies\n\n$$\nP = \\dfrac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial y}, \\qquad \nQ = -\\dfrac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial x}.\n$$\n\nIf a vector field $\\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ has a stream function $\\psi(x,y),$ then $\\mathbf{F}$ is called a **source-free vector field**. \n\nSource-free vector fields have some interesting properties, summarized below:\n\n- *The divergence of $\\mathbf{F}$ at any point of $D$ is zero:* \n\n$$\n\\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf{F} = \\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf F = \\dfrac{\\partial P}{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q}{\\partial y} = 0\n$$\n\n- *The *flux* of $\\mathbf{F}$ along any closed curve $C \\in D$ is zero:*\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\,\\textrm{d}s = 0\n$$\n\n- *Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves $C_1, C_2 \\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that*\n\n$$\n\\int\\limits_{C_1} \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n}  \\,\\textrm{d}s\n=\n\\int\\limits_{C_2} \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n}  \\,\\textrm{d}s.\n$$\n\nStream functions for source-free vector fields play a similar role to potential functions for conservative vector fields. So it's worth comparing them side-by-side.\n\n<table align=\"center\">\n<tbody><tr>\n<td>\n<table align=\"left\" cellpadding=\"10\" rules=\"all\">\n<tbody><tr>\n<th align=\"center\" bgcolor=\"#D6EAF8\" colspan=\"2\">Source-Free</th>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\" width=\"450\">Stream Function $\\psi$\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\mathbf F =  \\dfrac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial y}\\,\\mathbf i -  \\dfrac{\\partial \\psi}{\\partial x}\\,\\mathbf j$\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">Relationship between $\\psi$ and $\\mathbf F$\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\mathbf F$ is tangential to $\\psi$'s level curves\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">Divergence is zero\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\dfrac{\\partial P}{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q}{\\partial y} = 0$\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">Flux is zero along closed curves\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\,\\textrm{d}s = 0$\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">Flux integrals are path independent\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\displaystyle\\int\\limits_{C_1} \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\,\\textrm{d}s = \\int\\limits_{C_2} \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\,\\textrm{d}s$\n</td></tr>\n</tbody></table>\n</td>\n<td width=\"30\"></td>\n<td>\n<table align=\"left\" cellpadding=\"10\" rules=\"all\">\n<tbody><tr>\n<th align=\"center\" bgcolor=\"#D6EAF8\" colspan=\"2\">Conservative</th>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\" width=\"450\">Potential Function $\\phi$\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\mathbf F =  \\dfrac{\\partial \\phi}{\\partial x}\\,\\mathbf i +  \\dfrac{\\partial \\phi}{\\partial y}\\,\\mathbf j$\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">Relationship between $\\phi$ and $\\mathbf F$\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\mathbf F$ is perpendicular to $\\phi$'s level curves\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">(Scalar) curl is zero\n</td><td align=\"center\"> $\\dfrac{\\partial Q}{\\partial x} - \\dfrac{\\partial P}{\\partial y} = 0$ </td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">Circulation is zero along closed curves\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\displaystyle\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf{r}= 0$\n</td></tr>\n<tr>\n<td align=\"left\">Line integrals are path independent\n</td><td align=\"center\">$\\displaystyle\\int\\limits_{C_1} \\mathbf{F} \\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf{r} = \\int\\limits_{C_2} \\mathbf{F}\\cdot \\textrm d \\mathbf{r}$\n</td></tr>\n</tbody></table>\n</td>\n</tr>\n</tbody></table>" :tutorial/id #uuid "69005432-5588-5ac3-bf47-9dd734bb6953" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7703 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199328 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199485 :tutorial/content "Let's use what we know about source-free vector fields to calculate the flux of\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{F}(x,y)=2y\\,\\mathbf{i}-2x\\,\\mathbf{j}\n$$\n\nacross the curve $C,$ shown below.\n\n![](images/d6/d6adda2809af5d49c6b3dd0e81eae913dcdf02ceec0ae919fda0011d8a3dad2b.png)\n\nFirst, notice that this is a source-free vector field, since\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2y)+\\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x) \\\\  & =0+0 \\\\  & =0.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, since $\\mathbf{F}$ is source-free, the flux of $\\mathbf{F}$ across any closed curve is zero. piecewise-smooth curve $C$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\\,i+Q\\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:\n\n- $F$ is a source-free vector field.\n\n- $∇\\cdot F=\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$\n\n- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C⊂D$ is zero.\n\n- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}⊂D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s.\n$$\n\n- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$\n\nNote that $F(x,y)=x\\,i-y\\,j$ is a vector field with the simply connected domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=-y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\\,\\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWith that in mind, let's consider each statement.\n\n- Statement I is true. Indeed, we have that\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=1+(-1)=0.\n$$\n\n- Statement II is true. This follows from statement I.\n\n- Statement III is false. Since $F$ is source-free, the result ${\\int }_{C}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s=0$ is guaranteed for closed curves only.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and II only.\""} :step/id #uuid ${C}_{1}$ has endpoints $A(1,1)$ and $B(-1,-1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)=2x\\,i+(3-2y)\\,j$ through ${C}_{1}$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector ${n}_{1},$ as shown above.\n\n*Hint: You're given that $F$ is source-free, and the segment $\\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B$ can be parametrized as*\n\n$$\nr=(1-2t)\\,i+(1-2t)\\,j,\\,t\\in [0,1].\n$$" :question/worked-solution "If $F=P\\,i+Q\\,j$ is a vector field with simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2},$ then the following are equivalent:\n\n- $F$ is a source-free vector field.\n\n- $∇\\cdot F=\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.$\n\n- The flux ${∮}_{C}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s$ along any closed curve $C\\in D$ is zero.\n\n- Flux is path-independent. That is, given any two curves ${C}_{1},{C}_{2}\\in D$ with the same start and endpoints, we have that\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s.\n$$\n\n- There exists a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ for $F.$\n\nFirst, notice that\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=\\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x)+\\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-2y)=2-2=0,\n$$\n\nwhich shows that $F$ is a source-free vector field.\n\nSince $F$ is source-free, we know the flux of $F$ is independent of the path. In particular, as we have that \n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot {n}_{1}\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot {n}_{2}\\,\\text{d}s,\n$$\n\nwhere ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment $\\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from $A$ to $B,$ and ${n}_{2}$ is the unit normal to ${C}_{2},$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/51/5186fb872f03e73124d04c2e9ff07e77fb336bef121484a9ff1b697ea0cf8bcd.png)\n\nNotice that both ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotations of their respective unit tangent vectors.\n\nTo calculate the flux of $F$ across ${C}_{2},$ we will use the formula\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot {n}_{2}\\,\\text{d}s={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\\,\\text{d}y-Q\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nTo apply the formula,\n\n- the curve should be parametrized as $r(t)$ for $t\\in [a,b],$ and\n\n- the unit normal vector ${n}_{2}$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit normal tangent vector $T(t).$\n\nWe have the parametrization\n\n$$\nr(t)=(1-2t)\\,i+(1-2t)\\,j,\\,t\\in [0,1].\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =2x=2(1-2t)=2-4t, \\\\ Q(x,y) & =3-2y=3-2(1-2t)=1+4t.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t} & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2, \\\\ \\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t} & =\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}(1-2t)=-2.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe evaluate the flux integral as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\\cdot {n}_{2}\\,\\text{d}s & ={\\int }_{{C}_{2}}P\\,\\text{d}y-Q\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}(P\\cdot \\frac{\\text{d}y}{\\text{d}t}-Q\\cdot \\frac{\\text{d}x}{\\text{d}t})\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & ={\\int }_{0}^{1}(2-4t)\\cdot (-2)-(1+4t)\\cdot (-2)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-2{\\int }_{0}^{1}(2-4t)-(1+4t)\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =-2{\\int }_{0}^{1}1-8t\\,\\text{d}t \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot {[t-4{t}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot (1-4) \\\\  & =(-2)\\cdot (-3) \\\\  & =6\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we conclude that\n\n$$\n{\\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\\cdot {n}_{1}\\,\\text{d}s=6.\n$$"} :step/id #uuid 17592186176766 :step/content {:db/id 17592186177010 :tutorial/content "The **joint cumulative distribution function** (or joint CDF) of two continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as\n\n$$\nF(x,y)=P(X \\leq x,Y \\leq y).\n$$\n\nThe joint CDF gives the probability that the pair $(X,Y)$ will lie inside the infinite rectangular region $\\Delta$ that has its top-right corner at $(x,y)$ and whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes.\n\n![](images/ee/ee82c6b810f02f8b8380bd97c94cbe491095d17dbadc685ffdca1a54cf9828b8.png)\n\nThe joint CDF satisfies the following properties:\n\n- $0\\leq F(x,y)\\leq 1$\n\n- The **marginal CDF** of $X$ is given by $F_X(x)=F(x,\\infty).$\n\n- The **marginal CDF** of $Y$ is given by $F_Y(y)=F(\\infty,y).$\n\n- $F(\\infty, \\infty)=1$\n\n- $F(-\\infty ,y)=F(x,-\\infty)=0$\n\n- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, then \n$F(x,y)=F_X(x)\\cdot F_Y(y).$\n\nIf $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y)$, we have the following relationship between the joint PDF and joint CDF:\n\n$$\nF(x,y)=\\int^y_{-\\infty}\\int^x_{-\\infty} f(u,v)\\; \\textrm{d}u\\textrm{d}v.\n$$\n\nConsequently, if $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables that are nonzero only over the rectangle $[a, b] \\times [c, d]$, then the joint CDF is \n\n$$\nF(x,y)=\\int^d_{c}\\int^b_{a} f(u,v)\\; \\textrm{d}u\\textrm{d}v.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "891e5619-fe8a-5703-8683-51845abfa85f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5541 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} }_{1}At+{\\alpha }_{0}I \\\\  & ={\\alpha }_{1}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\\\ -5 & -1\\end{bmatrix}t+{\\alpha }_{0}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}{\\alpha }_{1}t+{\\alpha }_{0} & 2{\\alpha }_{1}t \\\\ -5{\\alpha }_{1}t & -{\\alpha }_{1}t+{\\alpha }_{0}\\end{bmatrix},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere ${\\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be }_{2}=-3\\text{i}t,\n$$\n\nwhich are complex conjugates. =\\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\\text{i}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\\\ {\\alpha }_{0}+3{\\alpha }_{1}\\text{i}t & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\\text{i}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we }_{1}t &=\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\\end{aligned}\\right.\\,⇒\\,\\left\\{\\begin{aligned}{\\alpha }_{1} &=\\frac{1}{3t}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\\\ {\\alpha }_{0} &=\\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\\end{aligned}\\right.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting ${\\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}-5{\\alpha }_{1}t & =-5\\cdot \\frac{1}{3t}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\\cdot t \\\\  & =-\\frac{5}{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\\\ -{\\alpha }_{1}t+{\\alpha }_{0} & =-\\frac{1}{3t}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\\cdot t+\\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\\\  & =-\\frac{1}{3}\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+\\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}(3\\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\n{e}^{At}=\\frac{1}{3}\\begin{bmatrix}3\\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & t^{n-1}+\\alpha_{n-2} A^{n-2}t^{n-2}+\\cdots+\\alpha_1 At+\\alpha_0 I,\n$$\n\nwhere $\\alpha_0, \\alpha_1, \\ldots, \\alpha_{n-1}$ are functions of $t$ and $I$ is the $n \\times n$ identity matrix. \n\nNow, we define the polynomial \n\n$$\nr(\\lambda)=\\alpha_{n-1}\\lambda^{n-1}+\\alpha_{n-2}\\lambda^{n-2}+\\cdots+\\alpha_1\\lambda+\\alpha_0.\n$$\n\nThen we have the following key fact:\n\n> For of diagonalization is that it allows us to easily determine the power of a matrix.\n\nAs an example, we consider the $2\\times 2$ matrix ![](images/53/53b7a9efd9f2ae1ef4adc7cee5f86f784722777b8c29f268dbd0e822ff1354f9.svg) with the diagonalization\n![](images/e3/e3111a91b80d238cf5255eb9a9884dcd3f80e914039c5e789e32c07b55cf5b06.svg)\n\nWe will use the diagonalization of $A$ to compute $A^{55}.$\n\nLet's start by computing $A^2.$ Using the properties of matrix multiplication, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =PD{P}^{-1}\\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\\\  & =PD\\cancel{{P}^{-1}\\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\\\  & =P(DD){P}^{-1} \\\\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nComputing $A^3,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & ={A}^{2}\\cdot A \\\\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}\\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\\\  & =P{D}^{2}\\cancel{{P}^{-1}\\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\\\  & =P({D}^{2}D){P}^{-1} \\\\  & =P{D}^{3}{P}^{-1}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe see that the matrix $P$ and its inverse $P^{-1}$ will always cancel each other out in the middle of the multiplication! So by induction, we have that\n\n$$\nA^{\\color{blue}55}=P \\cdot D^{\\color{blue}55} \\cdot P^{-1}.\n$$\n\nNow, we only need to find $D^{\\color{blue}55}.$\n\nSince $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\\\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\ {D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}D=\\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\\\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{3} & 0 \\\\ 0 & (-1)^{3}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFollowing this pattern, we get\n\n![](images/05/05e10fdc6944077a48b0214a41fae8d418a1b66c8d87a47d652158c84285c246.svg)\n\nTherefore, we can conclude that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{55} & =\\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}{\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}}^{55}\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} & -\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} & -\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} & -\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn general, given that $A = PDP^{-1},$ for any non-negative integer ${\\color{blue}k},$ we obtain \n\n$$\nA^{\\color{blue}k} = P \\cdot D^{\\color{blue}k} \\cdot P^{-1}.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b7628bf0-02d4-514e-a564-669610253cd2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3576 :tutorial/title "Raising a Diagonalizable Matrix to a Power"} :step/id #uuid So by induction, we have that\n\n$$\nA^{\\color{blue}55}=P \\cdot D^{\\color{blue}55} \\cdot P^{-1}.\n$$\n\nNow, we only need to find $D^{\\color{blue}55}.$\n\nSince $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\\\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\\end{bmatrix} \\\\ {D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}D=\\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\\\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}=\\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{3} & 0 \\\\ 0 & (-1)^{3}\\end{bmatrix}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFollowing this pattern, we get\n\n![](images/05/05e10fdc6944077a48b0214a41fae8d418a1b66c8d87a47d652158c84285c246.svg)\n\nTherefore, we can conclude that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{55} & =\\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}{\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}}^{55}\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} & -\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} & -\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}\\begin{bmatrix}\\frac{1}{5} & -\\frac{1}{5} \\\\ 0 & 1\\end{bmatrix} \\\\  & =\\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\\\ 0 & -1\\end{bmatrix}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIn general, given that $A = PDP^{-1},$ for any non-negative integer ${\\color{blue}k},$ we obtain \n\n$$\nA^{\\color{blue}k} = P \\cdot D^{\\color{blue}k} \\cdot =-{r}^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta +2{r}^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\  & ={r}^{2}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta First, let's write down our tree diagram.\n\n![](images/7f/7f19c4a682b30f1eea1d9c1be7da83bd77ba137173f25eb9c7e5cf253abba015.png)\n\nFrom the tree diagram, we can see that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\\frac{∂f}{∂x}\\cdot \\frac{∂x}{∂r}+\\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\cdot \\frac{∂y}{∂r} \\\\ \\frac{∂f}{∂\\theta } & =\\frac{∂f}{∂x}\\cdot \\frac{∂x}{∂\\theta }+\\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\cdot \\frac{∂y}{∂\\theta }.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, let's take the partial derivatives of $x=r\\cos\\theta$ and $y=r\\sin\\theta$ with respect to $r$ and $\\theta{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂x}{∂r} & =\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  &  &  & \\frac{∂y}{∂r} & =\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\ \\frac{∂x}{∂\\theta } & =-r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  &  &  & \\frac{∂y}{∂\\theta } & =r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting these results into the multivariable chain rule, we conclude that\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\\frac{∂f}{∂x}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta +\\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta , \\\\ \\frac{∂f}{∂\\theta } & =-\\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +\\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1b053bdf-59d9-5c48-bb1e-43f776bb9b90" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4974 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186125534 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125838 :tutorial/content "Given a function of three variables $f(x,y,z),$ we can find formulas for $f_r, f_\\theta,$ and $f_z,$ where $(r,\\theta,z)$ are cylindrical polar coordinates. The results that we need are as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\\frac{∂f}{∂x}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta +\\frac{∂f}{∂y}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\ \\frac{∂f}{∂\\theta } & =-\\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +\\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  \\\\ \\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\\frac{∂f}{∂z}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNotice that the first and second equations are identical to the equations derived for plane polar coordinates, as we would expect. \n\nThe difference here is that we now have a third equation that deals with the $z$-dependence. But since the $z$-coordinate is the same in both Cartesian and cylindrical polar coordinates, we can simply differentiate with respect to $z$ as usual.\n\nLet's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186125847 :tutorial/content "Up to now, we've been using the following formulas:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{f}_{r} & ={f}_{x}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta +{f}_{y}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  \\\\ {f}_{\\theta } & =-r{f}_{x}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta +r{f}_{y}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta \\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can treat the above as a system of equations in the \"unknowns\" $f_x$ and $f_y.$ Solving this system gives explicit expressions for $f_x$ and $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\\theta.$\n\nFor example, suppose we want an explicit formula for $f_x.$ We can eliminate $f_y$ by multiplying the first equation by $r\\cos\\theta$ and the second equation by $\\sin\\theta$ to give\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}r{f}_{r}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & =r{f}_{x}{cos}^{2}⁡\\theta +r{f}_{y}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta , \\\\ {f}_{\\theta }\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta  & =-r{f}_{x}{sin}^{2}⁡\\theta +r{f}_{y}\\operatorname{sin}⁡\\theta \\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta .\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubtracting the second equation from the first gives\n\n$$\nr f_r \\cos\\theta - f_\\theta \\sin\\theta = r f_x(\\sin^2\\theta + \\sin\\theta.\n$$\n\nWe can use a similar procedure to write $f_y$ in terms of functions of $r$ and $\\theta.$ Our results as summarized below:\n\n$$\n\\eqalign{\n\\dfrac {\\partial f}{\\partial x} &= $y=\\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $-\\frac{\\pi }{2}\\le x\\le \\frac{\\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\\,i+Q\\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that\n\n$$\n{∮}_{C}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\\text{div}\\,F\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhich is equivalent to\n\n$$\n{∮}_{C}P\\,dy-Q\\,dx={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\\text{d}A.\n$$\n\nThe region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.\n\n![](images/e5/e570374b37c116e32c3a7762b8cf09a28bdbb3e06b5e67e25837902a89bcd264.png)\n\nWe have that $P(x,y)=x+\\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y+\\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\\,\\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:\n\n$$\nD=\\{(x,y):-\\frac{\\pi }{2}\\le x\\le \\frac{\\pi }{2},\\,0\\le y\\le \\operatorname{cos}⁡x\\}\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\\,dy-Q\\,dx \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =2{\\int }_{-\\pi /2}^{\\pi /2}{\\int }_{0}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =2{\\int }_{-\\pi /2}^{\\pi /2}y\\,{|}_{0}^{\\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\\,dx \\\\  & =2{\\int }_{\\pi /2}^{\\pi /2}\\operatorname{cos}⁡x\\,dx \\\\  & =2\\operatorname{sin}⁡x\\,{|}_{-\\pi /2}^{\\pi /2} \\\\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\\\  & =4.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186172100 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171906 {:db/id 17592186173012 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173207 :tutorial/content "There is some nice intuition behind the flux form of Green's theorem that makes it easier to remember.\n\nSuppose that $\\mathbf F$ is a vector field on $\\mathbb R^2$ with component functions $P$ and $Q$ defined over a region $D.$ So, we have\n\n$$\n\\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\\,\\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\\,\\mathbf j.\n$$\n\nGreen's theorem in flux form states that the sum of the microscopic \"fluxes\" (divergences) of $\\mathbf F$ inside $D$ equals the macroscopic flux of $\\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D.$\n\n![](images/47/47a81125069be94b4ccda6f228ff1b8253f99595c6f3c4ae0ca710bdb796215f.png)\n\n    \n\nRecall that the divergence (i.e., the microscopic flux) of $\\mathbf F$ at a point is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F = \\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf F = \\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q }{\\partial y}.\n$$\n\nIf we sum (integrate) the divergence at every point over the entire domain $D,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_D \\left( \\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q }{\\partial y} \\right)\\textrm d A.\n$$\n\nThis expression gives us one side of Green's theorem in flux form.\n\nThe macroscopic divergence is simply the flux of $\\mathbf F$ across the boundary of $D{:}$\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C\\mathbf F\\cdot \\mathbf n \\, \\textrm d s\n$$\n\nEquating the sum of the divergences with the flux, we have\n\n$$\n\\iint\\limits_D \\left( \\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q }{\\partial y} \\right)\\textrm d A = \\oint\\limits_C\\mathbf F\\cdot \\mathbf n \\, \\textrm d s.\n$$\n\nThe flux form of Green's theorem can be summarized in a single picture, as follows:\n\n![](images/0f/0f8ba4b7e853e3b59e8677b0954c3cfae1b9c482750e13a742bd4d45eda8005d.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9016229b-93aa-58fc-857c-2a2d3f337ca4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5862 :tutorial/title "Intuition Behind Green's Theorem in Flux Form"} :step/id #uuid "e5c29654-0b83-51e0-a3d0-c6fbf08c8f2d" :step/math-academy-id 35877 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173010}} {:db/id 17592186173013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!\n\nTo see how, we first recall that the flux of $\\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\\,\\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s= \\oint\\limits_C P\\, \\textrm{d}y -Q\\, \\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nwhere $C$ is closed and $\\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$\n\nNow, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\\,\\text{d}y-Q\\,\\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\\,\\text{d}y+M\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={∮}_{C}M\\,\\text{d}x+N\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\\frac{∂M}{∂y})\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}-(-\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}))\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAs a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s = \\iint\\limits_D \\left(\\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} +\\dfrac{\\partial  Q}{\\partial y}\\right)\\textrm d A\n$$\n\nNow, recall that the divergence of $\\mathbf F$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F =  \\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q }{\\partial y}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s = \\iint\\limits_D \\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F\\,\\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\nGreen's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux line integral into an equivalent double integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f3b4b70-8b58-53d1-bc8d-a42daddfab4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5868 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "528120c2-edf7-5b3d-a8d3-0b481b460d90" :step/math-academy-id 35900 :step/next {:db/id 17592186173012}}] :activity/title "Green's Theorem in Flux Form" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172181} {:db/id 17592186173013 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173208 :tutorial/content "Green's theorem allows us to write line integrals as double integrals, and we've seen how Green's theorem simplifies circulation calculations. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\\,\\text{d}y-Q\\,\\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\\,\\text{d}y+M\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={∮}_{C}M\\,\\text{d}x+N\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\\frac{∂M}{∂y})\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}-(-\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}))\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAs a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s = \\iint\\limits_D \\left(\\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} +\\dfrac{\\partial  Q}{\\partial y}\\right)\\textrm d A\n$$\n\nNow, recall that the divergence of $\\mathbf F$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F =  \\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q }{\\partial y}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s = \\iint\\limits_D \\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F\\,\\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\nGreen's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux Even more, Green's theorem can also be used to simplify flux calculations!\n\nTo see how, we first recall that the flux of $\\mathbf{F}(x,y) =  P(x,y)\\,\\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\\mathbf j$ across $C$ can be calculated as follows:\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s= \\oint\\limits_C P\\, \\textrm{d}y -Q\\, \\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nwhere $C$ is closed and $\\mathbf n$ is the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$\n\nNow, let's set $M= -Q$ and $N=P$. Then, by the circulation form of Green's theorem, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\\,\\text{d}y-Q\\,\\text{d}x & ={∮}_{C}N\\,\\text{d}y+M\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={∮}_{C}M\\,\\text{d}x+N\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂N}{∂x}-\\frac{∂M}{∂y})\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}-(-\\frac{∂Q}{∂y}))\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nAs a result, we've obtained the **Green's theorem in flux form**, which we restate below:\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s = \\iint\\limits_D \\left(\\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} +\\dfrac{\\partial  Q}{\\partial y}\\right)\\textrm d A\n$$\n\nNow, recall that the divergence of $\\mathbf F$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F =  \\dfrac{\\partial P }{\\partial x} + \\dfrac{\\partial Q }{\\partial y}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, we can also write Green's theorem in flux form as\n\n$$\n\\oint\\limits_C \\mathbf F \\cdot \\mathbf{n} \\: \\textrm{d}s = \\iint\\limits_D \\textrm{div}\\,\\mathbf F\\,\\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\nGreen's theorem in flux form allows us to convert a flux line integral into an equivalent double integral." :tutorial/id #uuid "7f3b4b70-8b58-53d1-bc8d-a42daddfab4d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5868 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:activity/course {:db/id "Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,0),(2,0),(2,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field\n$F(x,y)={x}^{2}y\\,i+5xy\\,j$\nthrough $C$ as a repeated integral." :question/worked-solution "Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\\,i+Q\\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that\n\n$$\n{∮}_{C}F\\cdot n\\,\\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\\text{div}\\,F\\,\\text{d}A,\n$$\n\nwhich is equivalent to\n\n$$\n{∮}_{C}P\\,dy-Q\\,dx={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\\,\\text{d}A.\n$$\n\nThe region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.\n\n![](images/26/265d27ad87a7f114bd2a32a5f48cbfedb13192abf48f9b759c4ed635e71ff144.png)\n\nWe have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=5xy.$ So,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2xy,\\,\\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =5x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:\n\n$$\nD=\\{(x,y):-1\\le x\\le 2,\\,0\\le y\\le 2\\}\n$$\n\nTherefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\\,dy-Q\\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+5x)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{-1}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{2}x(2y+5)\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "1736de57-90cb-505e-97a3-07df8bb92125" :step/next {:db/id "Which of the following statements are true? \n\nI. The sum of $4{x}^{2}+1$ and $2{x}^{2}$ is a binomial.\n\nII. The sum of $3{x}^{2}-2x$ and $5$ is a binomial.\n\nIII. The sum of a binomial and a monomial is **sometimes** a binomial." :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.\n\n- Statement I is true. We have\n\n$$\n(4{x}^{2}+1)+(2{x}^{2})=6{x}^{2}+1,\n$$\n\nwhich is a binomial.\n\n- Statement II is false. We have\n\n$$\n(3{x}^{2}-2x)+(5)=3{x}^{2}-2x+5,\n$$\n\nwhich is *not* a binomial (it's a trinomial).\n\n- Statement III is true. The sum of a binomial and a monomial *could be* a binomial (see, for example, statement I). \n\n However, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *not always* a binomial (see, for example, statement II). \n\n So, the sum of a binomial and a monomial is *sometimes* binomial.\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and III only.\""} {:db/id 17592186048209} {:db/id 17592186050526} {:db/id :tutorial/content "Let's recap some of the rules for exponents.\n\n- **Product rule**: to multiply powers of the same base, add the exponents.\n\n- **Quotient rule**: to divide powers of the same base, subtract the exponents.\n\n- **Power rule**: to raise a power to another power, multiply the exponents.\n\n- **Power of product rule**: to raise the product of two numbers to a power, raise each number to that power, and then multiply.\n\n- **Power of quotient rule**: to raise a fraction to a power, raise both the numerator and the denominator to that power.\n\nWe can use a combination of these rules to simplify expressions containing exponents. linear equations have **infinitely many solutions.** \n\nFor example, consider the following equation: \n\n$$\nx+5 = x + 5\n$$\n\nLet's attempt to solve this equation by subtracting $x$ from both If we substitute any value, say $x=3,$ into the original equation, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\\\ 3+5 & =3+5 \\\\ 8 & =8.\\,✓\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nIt's important to note that substituting *any* value for $x$ into the equation will lead to a true statement. For example, the values \n\n$$\nx=42,\\qquad x=-\\dfrac 1 4, \\qquad x=1.2345\n$$\n\nare *all* solutions to the original equation.\n\nTo summarize:\n\n- Our original equation has *infinitely many solutions.*\n\n- The solution of the equation is \"*any (real) value of* $x$\"." :tutorial/id #uuid "edb6ae26-e191-5d7d-9ce8-ad9ee36655f2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 11389 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "eab36dd4-7684-5fb5-a213-f02f98e0da39" :step/math-academy-id 476188 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111679}} {:db/id 17592186111679 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110719 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110372 :question/id #uuid "6355ac1e-bb4d-5133-9917-04dfb2bc5a0d" :question/math-academy-id "e-18854"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ff4e9141-5743-55f1-a8be-3e28cb047eca" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048213}] :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186476103} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111133} {:db/id 17592186111138} {:db/id 17592186297181} {:db/id 17592186297182} {:db/id 17592186297196} {:db/id 17592186492000} {:db/id 17592186492056}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Equations With Infinitely Many Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "310129a9-81a2-54d5-b227-633c2cb1b8d6" :step/math-academy-id 476189 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111680}} {:db/id 17592186111680 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111818 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have an equation of the form\n\n$$\nax = bx,\n$$\n\nwhere $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a = b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.\n\nFor example, each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2x=2x,\\,\\frac{1}{3}x=\\frac{1}{3}x\\,-2.16x=-2.16x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo show that the general equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ we can substitute $a$ for $b$ in our equation as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}ax & =bx \\\\ ax & =(a)x \\\\ ax & =ax\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThen, we simplify this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}ax & =ax \\\\ ax-ax & =ax-ax \\\\ 0 & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe equation, $0=0,$ is always true, regardless of the value of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ and any value of $x$ is a solution to the equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "8428afc7-2e9a-55d0-9f13-7a2acdf8fd7d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13429 :tutorial/title "Conditions for an Equation To Have Infinitely Many Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "888ce267-7f48-5074-a1ab-42caf954a38c" :step/math-academy-id 476192 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111681}} {:db/id 17592186111681 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111815 :tutorial/content "Consider the equation\n\n$$\n2qx = 10x,\n$$\n\nwhere $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$\n\nNotice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$ \n\n$$\n\\underbrace{2q}_{\\large a} \\ x = \\underbrace{10}_{\\large b} \\ x\n$$\n\nIn this case, \n\n$$\na = 2q, \\qquad b = 10.\n$$\n\nWe know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if\n\n$$\n2q = 10.\n$$\n\nSolving this for $q,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\\\ \\frac{2q}{2} & =\\frac{10}{2} \\\\ q & =5.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$\n\nWe can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\\\ 2(5)x & =10x \\\\ 10x & =10x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nand simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\\\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\\\ 0 & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich is true for all values of $x.$\n\n**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "0d28dc5e-68de-53d0-a57c-9072a89eccbb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 11486 :tutorial/title "Problems Involving Unknown Parameters"} :step/id #uuid "2f94c8cb-7345-56bc-b884-f0ac3f242910" :step/math-academy-id 476193 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111682}} {:db/id 17592186111682 :step/content {:db/id 17592186110720 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186110368 :question/id #uuid "4a8f8deb-2ff1-56d2-888a-3e51eb805bc4" :question/math-academy-id "e-17212"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6cd2f04-e0d5-5df0-8e74-ea737501cdf8" :knowledge-point/question-generator {:db/id 17592186476197} :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186111134} {:db/id 17592186111135} {:db/id 17592186297170} {:db/id 17592186297183} {:db/id 17592186297184} {:db/id 17592186476179} {:db/id 17592186476183} {:db/id 17592186476185} {:db/id 17592186476189} {:db/id 17592186476193} {:db/id 17592186491998} {:db/id 17592186549009} {:db/id 17592186549054}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving For an Unknown Parameter"} :step/id #uuid "1e04eac3-4a93-5d72-9a90-2b1099628885" :step/math-academy-id 476194 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111683}} {:db/id 17592186111683 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111819 :tutorial/content "Each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:\n\n$$\n2x + 1 = 2x + 1, \\qquad \\dfrac13x -2 = \\dfrac13x -2, \\qquad 1-x = 1 - x\n$$\n\nMore generally, suppose we have an equation of the form\n\n$$\nax + b = cx + d,\n$$\n\nwhere $a, b, c,$ and $d$ are constants. Then, this equation has infinitely many solutions if \n\n$$\na = c\\quad \\text{and}\\quad b = d.\n$$\n\nNote that if we substitute $c=a$ and $d=b$ into this equation, we get the following: \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}ax+b & =cx+d \\\\ ax+b & =(a)x+(b) \\\\ ax+b & =ax+b\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSimplifying this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation gives the following:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}ax+b & =ax+b \\\\ ax+b-ax & =ax+b-ax \\\\ b & =b\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe final equation, $b = b,$ is always true. Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions, and any real value of $x$ is a solution." :tutorial/id #uuid "7498a4f8-36b5-5d1d-b953-893581bfa9aa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13430 :tutorial/title "Conditions for a General Linear Equation To Have Infinitely Many Solutions"} :step/id #uuid "1d109dfd-fdee-5718-a3d2-a9a96f41ffd0" :step/math-academy-id 476197 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111684}} {:db/id 17592186111684 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111817 :tutorial/content "Consider the equation\n\n$$\n(s - 2)x + t = 6x + 9,\n$$\n\nwhere $s$ and $t$ are constants. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the values of $s$ and $t?$\n\nNotice that this equation is in the form $ax+b = cx+d{:}$ \n\n$$\n\\underbrace{(s-2)}_{\\large a} \\ x + \\underbrace{t}_{\\large b} = \\underbrace{6}_{\\large c} \\ x + \\underbrace{9}_{\\large d}\n$$\n\nWe know that an equation of the form $ax+b = cx+d$ has infinitely many solutions when $a=c$ and $b=d.$\n\nSo, to determine the values of $s$ and $t$ such that the equation\n\n$$\n({\\color{blue}{{s - 2}}})x + {\\color{red}{{t}}} = {\\color{blue}{{6}}}x + {\\color{red}{{9}}}\n$$\n\nhas infinitely many solutions, we **equate the coefficients** of $x,$ and we **equate the constants:**\n\n- Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we have\n\n$$\n{\\color{blue}{{s - 2}}} = {\\color{blue}{{6}}}.\n$$\n\nSolving this equation for $s,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}s & =8.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Equating the constants, we get\n\n$$\n{\\color{red}{{t}}} = {\\color{red}{{9}}}.\n$$\n\nTherefore, if $s = 8$ and $t=9,$ our original equation has infinitely many solutions." :tutorial/id #uuid "dc5c5f3e-0731-5ab3-8afd-a2cf24228db1" :tutorial/math-academy-id Doing this, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\\\ 2(5)x & =10x \\\\ 10x & =10x\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nand simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\\\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\\\ 0 & =0\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhich is true for all values of $x.$\n\n**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "0d28dc5e-68de-53d0-a57c-9072a89eccbb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 11486 :tutorial/title "Problems Involving Unknown Parameters"} :step/id #uuid "2f94c8cb-7345-56bc-b884-f0ac3f242910" :step/math-academy-id 476193 :step/next {:db/id 17592186111682}} {:db/id 17592186111815 :tutorial/content "Consider the equation\n\n$$\n2qx = 10x,\n$$\n\nwhere $q$ is a constant. :question/worked-solution "We will write the equation of the line in the slope-intercept form $y=mx+b.$ So, we need to work out the slope $m$ and the $y$-intercept $b.$\n\nFirst, we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & =\\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\\\  & =\\frac{11-7}{3-2} \\\\  & =\\frac{4}{1} \\\\  & =4\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting the slope $m=4$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach\n\n$$\ny=4x+b.\n$$\n\nWe now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(2,7):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =4x+b \\\\ 7 & =4(2)+b \\\\ 7 & =8+b \\\\ 7-8 & =b \\\\ -1 & =b\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo the equation of the line is $y=4x-1.$"} :step/id #uuid "45872dd6-e531-5118-a656-32545845e64a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186503839}} {:db/id 17592186503816 :step/content {:db/id 17592186503680 :question/answer-fields =\\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\\\  & =\\frac{17-7}{5-4} \\\\  & =\\frac{10}{1} \\\\  & =10\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting the slope $m=10$ into the slope-intercept formula $y=mx+b,$ we reach\n\n$$\ny=10x+b.\n$$\n\nWe now need to find the $y$-intercept $b.$ We can find this by substituting the coordinates of a point on the line. Any point will do, so let's substitute $(4,7):$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}y & =10x+b \\\\ 7 & =10(4)+b \\\\ 7 & =40+b \\\\ 7-40 & =b \\\\ -33 & =b.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the equation of the line is :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the following exponential function:\n\n$$\nf(t) = C\\cdot 4^t\n$$\n\nIn addition, we're told that $f(3) = 128.$ Can we use this information to find the unknown constant $C?$\n\nTo solve this problem, we substitute $t=3$ and $f(t) = 128$ and solve for $C,$ as follows:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}128 & =C\\cdot {4}^{3} \\\\ 128 & =C\\cdot 64 \\\\ \\frac{128}{64} & =C \\\\ 2 & =C\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, $C=2.$ So our function expressed in full is\n\n$$\nf(t) = 2\\cdot 4^t.\n$$\n\nWe sometimes say that the **initial value** of the function is $2,$ because if we evaluate $f$ at $t=0,$ we get\n\n$$\nf(0) = 2\\cdot 4^0 = 2\\cdot 1 = 2.\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6820cdab-7e0a-5a90-adb1-880e4eb4a8de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8846 [{:db/id 17592186106814 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107037 :tutorial/content "The **power of product rule** states that if we want to raise the product $xy$ to some power $n$, we must raise each factor to the power $n$ and then multiply:\n\n$$\n(xy)^n=x^n y^n\n$$\n\nFor example,\n\n$$\n(xy)^4=x^4y^4.\n$$\n\nTo see why the power of product rule is true, let's take the above example and work it out again the long way, changing the order of factors in the multiplication. We get the same result:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}(xy)^{4} & = \\\\ (xy)(xy)(xy)(xy) & = \\\\ (x\\cdot x\\cdot x\\cdot x)(y\\cdot y\\cdot y\\cdot y) & = \\\\ {x}^{4}{y}^{4}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe power of product rule is just a shortcut for the process above." :tutorial/id #uuid "7aabbc0f-a3ca-5f05-b6ae-d7551b16ae1a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1482 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid [17592186046669 1005 17592186046872 17592186045417] [17592186046669 1005 17592186046963 17592186045417] [17592186046669 1007 "Linear Algebra" 17592186045417] [17592186046669 1008 "Our Linear Algebra course builds on students' prior experience with matrices and determinants to develop their understanding of crucial linear algebra concepts. These include systems of equations, vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvectors and eigenvalues, diagonalization, matrix functions, inner products, orthogonal projections, quadratic forms, and singular value decomposition. Real-world applications such as least-squares problems, Markov chains, and regression will also be explored.\nThis course is designed to give students a deep understanding of linear algebra, equipping them with the knowledge and skills necessary for advanced study in mathematics, computer science, physics, and engineering." 17592186045417] [17592186046669 1009 "After briefly looking at some essential set theory, logic, and vector geometry, students explore matrices in-depth. They will become fluent in Gaussian elimination, using it to solve systems of equations and compute inverse matrices.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces. They will explore vectors in N-dimensional space, linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, nullity, and the rank-nullity theorem. They also generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces.\nThis course develops students' understanding of linear transformations, including images, kernels, linear maps between different vector spaces, and change-of-coordinates matrices.\nStudents will learn how to find and solve the characteristic equation of a matrix and fluently compute eigenvectors. They will study matrix diagonalization and its properties, apply the rotational-scaling theorem, and explore matrix functions. They will also cover generalized eigenvectors and Jordan canonical decomposition.\nThis course covers various aspects of orthogonality in vector spaces, including orthogonal sets, complements, and orthogonal matrices. In addition, students will learn about orthogonal projections and the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process.\nStudents will explore quadratic forms, including positive-definite and negative-definite quadratic forms, and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. They will also classify quadratic curves and learn how to reduce a quadratic curve to its principal axes.\nFinally, this course explores singular value decomposition and other applications of linear Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. learn how to determine the center of mass of a thin lamina whose mass is unevenly distributed. \n\nWe describe the mass distribution across a lamina using its mass density function $\\lambda (x,y).$ This function tells us the *mass per unit area* at any point $(x,y)$ on the lamina.\n\nFor example, consider a thin plate with mass density function $\\lambda(x,y) = 6xy$ occupying the finite rectangular region $D$ between the lines $x=1,$ $x=2,$ $y=0,$ and $y=1.$ What is the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis?\n\nTo answer this, consider a point $(x,y) \\in D$ on the plate and a small rectangular piece with its bottom-left corner at $(x,y)$ and area $\\Delta{A},$ as shown below.\n\n![](images/8c/8cd947e542aaf7eb787abc7a846e87a2d03ccafa0987f3422928fdcba115da9e.png)\n\nIf $\\Delta{A}$ is very small, we can assume that our density function is approximately constant over the selected piece. As a result, the moment of this piece about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}Δ{M}_{y} & ≈x\\cdot Δm \\\\  & ≈x\\cdot 6xy\\,ΔA \\\\  & =6{x}^{2}y\\,ΔA.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTo find the total moment of the plate about the axis, we add together the moments of all such pieces and take the limit as $\\Delta{A} \\to 0.$ By doing this, we get\n\n$$\nM_y =  \\iint\\limits_D 6x^2y \\: \\textrm{d}A.\n$$\n\n \n\nCarrying out the integration, we find that the moment of the plate about the $y$-axis is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}6{x}^{2}y\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & ={\\int }_{1}^{2}{\\int }_{0}^{1}6{x}^{2}y\\,\\text{d}y\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & ={\\int }_{1}^{2}3{x}^{2}\\,\\text{d}x\\cdot {\\int }_{0}^{1}2y\\,\\text{d}y \\\\  & =[{x}^{3}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\\cdot [{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\\\  & =(8-1)\\cdot (1-0) \\\\  & =7.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe moment about the $x$-axis can be found similarly.\n\nIn general, the moments $M_x$ and $M_y$ of a lamina $D$ with mass density function $\\lambda(x,y)$ about the $x$-axis and about the $y$-axis, respectively, are given by the following formulas:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{M}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}y\\,\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A \\\\ {M}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}x\\,\\lambda (x,y)\\,\\text{d}A\\end{aligned}\n$$" 17592186045417] [17592186199455 1065 4906 17592186045417] [17592186199455 1066 #uuid "7aa18cfe-acd7-5e17-982c-58eabc063404" 17592186045417] [17592186199455 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186199456 1064 "When a lamina's mass density is constant, the center of mass depends only on the shape of the lamina. In cases like these, the center of mass is called the **centroid** of the lamina. The centroid of a shape corresponds to its geometrical center.\n\nSo, $\\lambda$ is constant, then the mass of the plate is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}m & ={∬}_{D}\\lambda \\,dA \\\\  & =\\lambda {∬}_{D}\\,dA \\\\  & =\\lambda \\cdot {A}_{D},\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwhere $A_D$ denotes the area of $D.$ As a result, \n\n$$\nm = \\lambda \\cdot A_D \\qquad \\Longrightarrow \\qquad \\dfrac{\\lambda}{m} = \\dfrac{1}{A_D}.\n$$\n\nSubstituting the above into the formula for the $x$-coordinate of the center of mass, we obtain \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\frac{{M}_{y}}{m} & =\\frac{1}{m}{∬}_{D}x\\,\\lambda \\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{\\lambda }{m}{∬}_{D}x\\,\\text{d}A \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{{A}_{D}}{∬}_{D}x\\,\\text{d}A.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nWe can similarly compute the 17592186045417] [17592186148596 1063 17592186148719 17592186045417] [17592186148714 1064 "A **polyhedron** is a $3$-dimensional shape where each side is a polygon. These flat polygonal sides are called **faces**.\n\n**Prisms** are polyhedrons made of two identical polygonal faces (called **bases**) connected by equal parallel line segments. If these line segments are perpendicular to the bases, we have a **right** prism.\n\nLet's take a look at some common prisms.\n\n- A **triangular (right) prism** consists of two identical triangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments.\n\n![](images/95/9563bd4f9c40ff5921998ed5840f8e5b43fb1af579a64a06a14782be4a86ece2.png)\n\n- A **rectangular (right) prism** consists of two identical rectangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments. Notice that each face is a rectangle.\n\n![](images/39/39ea3dd56722c7fb05ba275a054ff46479e3ee96851dafdd66fe09455a517f1a.png)\n\n- A **cube** is a special case of a rectangular prism that consists of six equal square faces.\n\n![](images/41/415d03a9a886793eee4b4d16e50af26002c0881279481b2e70773b8b7bff02a5.png)\n\nBy adding more sides to the polygonal base, we can make more prisms. For example, the following shape is a pentagonal prism.\n\n![](images/8f/8f4dd8fe8c120eabbe5a1ad6413f6f0cd9cd3d22efe8b13e25ac3d2a916f3258.png)\n\nWe can also construct hexagonal prisms, heptagonal prisms, etc." 17592186045417] [17592186148714 1065 2202 17592186045417] [17592186148714 1066 #uuid "af52fff0-b45a-59d7-85f8-cacc3a9cb9f9" 17592186045417] [17592186148714 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186148718 1064 "**Pyramids** are polyhedrons made of a polygonal base, with the other triangular faces meeting at a single point.\n\nLet's take a look at some common pyramids.\n\n- A **triangular pyramid** has a triangular base with $3$ other triangular faces that meet at a single point.\n\n![](images/d8/d8597d1e526e2af72255f7dce1cc13e01cf76f1c53522003b126be67a0a6c55d.png)\n\n- A **rectangular pyramid** has a rectangular base with $4$ triangular faces that meet at a single point. If the base is a square, we call this a **square pyramid.**\n\n![](images/26/26700acaf9eae64227988ddcfb43269c0eba6f6447229ec8854cc1ebfeab3334.png)\n\n- A **pentagonal pyramid** has a pentagonal base with $5$ triangular faces that meet at a single point.\n\n![](images/4c/4c73b984b3e4a2ccb0796646ebb4c547947fab7359914599d928a63819818725.png)\n\nSimilarly to prisms, we can add more sides to the polygonal base to make more types of pyramids." 17592186045417] [17592186148718 1065 2248 17592186045417] [17592186148718 1066 #uuid "5ebd5b00-1afa-5ee5-9321-47a3e76e71ef" 17592186045417] [17592186148718 1067 "Pyramids" 17592186045417] [17592186148719 1064 "Not all three-dimensional shapes are polyhedrons. A **hemisphere** is half of a sphere.\n\n![](images/84/84e7b63b5ec8761d4a3ac8a00b15a08f0dab7d4f95a536721df0c82e2999873f.png)\n\n- A **cylinder** is a solid shape with two parallel circular bases. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes.
